text:
A life-size statue of Florida Governor Ron DeSantis began melting shortly after it was unveiled in Tallahassee Tuesday, in a protest organized by environmental advocates over the state's approach to climate change.

The installation, called “DENIAL,” was created by advertising agency Uncommon, climate advocacy group 350 Action and production company M ss ng P eces. Made from gallium, a metal that melts at about 85.6 degrees Fahrenheit, the statue was designed to melt in Florida's heat, according to the creators.

Organizers say the installation criticizes Florida's decision to remove references to climate change from state law. DeSantis signed the legislation in May 2024, calling it a “common-sense approach” to energy policy.

See also: Trump arrives at Mar-a-Lago as Palm Beach road closures, No Kings rallies are planned

The law removed climate change references from several state statutes, prohibited offshore and nearshore wind turbines, and supported expanded use of natural gas. The governor's office also pointed to provisions involving nuclear reactor research, hydrogen-powered vehicles and electric grid security, according to the Associated Press.

DeSantis has also pushed back on claims linking climate change to stronger hurricanes, pointing to Florida's history of powerful storms. Scientists say the relationship is complex, but research indicates a warming climate can contribute to heavier hurricane rainfall and faster storm intensification. Long-term trends in overall hurricane frequency and intensity remain less certain, in part because historical records are incomplete, according to a PolitiFact report.

The statue is part of a campaign encouraging voters to support candidates who prioritize climate action ahead of the midterm elections.

text:
At a Rossford union office, a large American flag set the background for a Get Out the Vote rally headlined by former U.S. Sen. Sherrod Brown.

The rally was held at the Central Midwest Regional Council of Carpenters office, which was filled with members wearing blue shirts reading: “Our vote, our voice, our future.”

Along the walls were banners the read: “Infrastructure investments = union jobs” and “We build industry,” with a list of projects such as chip manufacturing facilities, renewable energy, food processing developments, and data centers.

“Look in the eye of a worker carrying a carpenter’s union card. It might be a millwright, might be a pile driver, might be a floor layer. Look them in the eye and say, ‘Your work ethic is broken,’” Mr. Brown said, criticizing a comment his opponent said earlier this year when discussing his Upward Mobility Act.

Mr. Brown is hoping voters return him to the Senate after losing re-election in 2024. He is running against U.S. Sen. Jon Husted (R., Ohio), who was appointed to the seat last year.

But on Saturday, Mr. Brown rallied with those union workers, encouraging them to get out to vote and drawing on his long record of supporting labor unions.

“We’re fighting for government that works for you not for the drug companies, not for the insurance companies, not for big oil, not for the crypto crowd,” he said. “We’re demanding a government that works for American workers.”

While data centers have become a political hot topic in Ohio and across the country, many unions support the developments as they provide high-paying construction jobs.

None of Saturday’s speakers spoke on data centers, although the Democrat has made them a key part of his campaign. He has called his opponent the “face of data centers in Ohio” and says local communities should get to decide if data centers are built in their community.

After the event, Mr. Brown said even though the projects bring union jobs, at the end of the day, those workers have bills too.

“Electricians are working on these projects, but electricians don’t want to see their utility bills go up, and they will unless we do something,” he said.

The Northwest Ohio Building and Construction Trades Council has endorsed Mr. Husted in this election cycle but has previously endorsed Mr. Brown. The carpenters council has endorsed Mr. Brown for 2026.

Patrick Day, a retiree with Carpenters Local 437 out of Portsmouth, Ohio, encouraged voters to get out and “tell [the trades council] that they were wrong.”

“We need you as foot soldiers,” Mr. Day said. “We need you out Monday morning and every day until Election Day, telling those people that they were wrong. That this man [Mr. Brown] is the one who saved you and your retirees’ pension plan.”

Mr. Day traveled four hours to be at Saturday’s rally and said he saw firsthand how Mr. Brown’s Butch Lewis Act, which saved pensions for more than 100,000 Ohioans, impacted his members.

“I saw how that reduction in benefits affected him,” Mr. Day said of one of his local members. “And then I saw the relief to him and his family when his pension benefits were once again made whole due to these acts.”

U.S. Rep. Marcy Kaptur (D., Toledo) co-sponsored the bill in the U.S. House of Representatives. She was also at the rally on Saturday, emphasizing the need for Democrats to gain control of the House.

“Thank you for caring about the House of Representatives where we are four votes short of a majority,” she told attendees. “We must hold this seat.”

Ms. Kaptur is running in a rematch against former Republican state Rep. Derek Merrin. The two ran against each other in 2024, and Ms. Kaptur won by less than one percentage point.

Ms. Kaptur said she supports U.S. Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D., N.Y.), who is positioned to become the next Speaker of the House if Democrats win the majority.

A spokesman for Mr. Merrin’s campaign criticized Ms. Kaptur for siding with “the far-left wing of the Democrat Party instead of the hardworking people” of northwest Ohio.

“Our region deserves new leadership, fresh energy, and a representative whose values are aligned with working families — that’s why Derek Merrin will prevail in November,” the spokesman said.

Both political parties are doing everything they can to mobilize their base to vote, as Republicans look to hold on to majorities in both chambers of Congress in a tough election cycle.

Mr. Husted has been traveling across the state to reach voters and has received some outside help. President Trump has visited Ohio twice this month to stump for the senator, and Vice President JD Vance has made separate visits, most recently in Lima earlier this month.

“Sherrod Brown spent 50 years talking a big game about labor, but abandoned unions when push came to shove in Washington,” a spokesman for Mr. Husted’s campaign said. “That’s why labor groups have thrown their support behind Jon Husted this cycle, including several groups that previously endorsed Sherrod Brown.”

Voters can cast their ballot early until Nov. 1. Nov. 3 is Election Day.

text:
DataOne, the Microsoft-linked New Jersey datacenter recently hit with a $1 million fine for running unpermitted generators, emitted large amounts of health-harming air pollution for nearly a year before state regulators stepped in, according to public records obtained by Floodlight.

The Vineland facility’s 62 gas-fired generators became public in August after a Floodlight/Guardian visual investigation found them operating without permits. The New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection fined the company over the fleet, but didn’t disclose how long the generators had been operating, nor how much air pollution they had released into the surrounding community over the past year.

Floodlight sent technical data about the generators — obtained through public records requests — to two experts to calculate the site’s emissions.

“Our best estimate is that the generators emitted about 140 tons of NOx,” said Xiaomeng Jin, an assistant professor at Rutgers Department of Environmental Sciences. Her analysis would rank DataOne in the state’s top five NOx polluters of 2025, per EPA data.

NOx is a dangerous group of smog-producing gases linked to asthma, heart attacks and even premature death. It’s “the most important air pollutant in the U.S. that affects most people,” Jin said.

Longtime Vineland resident Tiffany Leone-Vespa lives about a mile from the data center and said the noise from the generators sounds like an airplane in the back of her house.

“What health problems might I face in the future? Because I’ve been exposed to all of that. My kids have been exposed to it,” she said.

The site’s potential NOx emissions are even larger, according to Jin and Bruce Buckheit — a former EPA air enforcement division chief. Both concluded that at full use, DataOne’s fleet could emit more than 1,500 tons of NOx per year. That is nearly twice the amount that the Linden Cogeneration gas-fired power plant, New Jersey’s largest NOx emitter, is allowed to emit.

Operating the generators “results in very high levels of air pollution,” said Buckheit.

New Jersey labels any facility capable of emitting more than 25 tons of NOx per year a “major source” and DataOne’s potential emissions are “well over” that limit, Buckheit said. Obtaining a major source permit requires extensive environmental reviews, best available pollution controls and public comment periods — all before construction can even begin.

That didn’t happen at DataOne, despite the operation being capable of emitting more than half the NOx put out by New Jersey’s entire power sector.

“That is basically offsetting some of the air quality improvements [regulators] have achieved for decades,” Jin said.

DataOne did not respond to Floodlight’s emissions analysis. Instead, its spokesperson sent the same statement as they did in response to NJDEP’s decision to fine them, saying the company is “transitioning to low-emission, quiet fuel cells as part of the site’s permanent power solution and have the necessary approvals in place for this solution.”

The company disagrees with NJDEP’s determination and had argued the generators did not require permits — but plans to apply for them now.

A Microsoft spokesperson wrote that “we expect our suppliers and partners to meet all applicable legal and regulatory obligations” and the company was working with DataOne “to support their completion of the facility’s transition to its permanent long-term power solution.”

In press releases, New Jersey regulators said the tractor-trailer-sized generators were detected during a July 29, 2026, site inspection but not during an earlier visit in December. However, the fleet was there to find, according to a letter DataOne later sent to NJDEP.

The letter, obtained by Floodlight through a public records request, notes that the generators first began to arrive in July 2025. Sixteen generators started operating in October 2025, with another 16 brought online in early February. By June, all 62 had been fired up.

By the time state inspectors noticed them, the unpermitted fleet had collectively run for more than 46,000 hours in total, according to the letter.

“How did 62 generators get installed and operated and nobody did anything until now? That blows me away,” Leone-Vespa said. “Clearly somebody wasn’t doing their job.”

A spokesperson for NJDEP declined to comment.

For many Vineland residents, confirmation that DataOne’s generators have been running for nearly a year is a bittersweet vindication. Locals have reported strange noises emanating from the facility for months, with more than 100 noise complaints submitted to the Cumberland County Department of Health since March, according to records obtained by Floodlight. Many of the complaints list generators as the suspected source.

“They’re just running these monster generators. And they think, by right, they have every ability to do so at the expense of anyone else,” said local flower farmer Michael Atkinson.

Atkinson’s family has been farming a patch of land beside the data center for more than 70 years. He said DataOne is “one of the richest and worst neighbors that I have ever had to deal with in my entire life.”

During a Vineland town hall meeting in late January, DataOne CEO Charles-Antoine Beyney told residents that his data center would be “polluting less than a farm.”

Born in Bordeaux, Beyney told the crowd, “I’m too French to just kill my lungs, the lungs of your kids and all the community around us.”

Beyney confirmed during that speech that DataOne was running generators, and he said NJDEP was aware — claiming the agency had been at the site that same morning and was “on us big time.”

While the generators may have evaded state regulators for a year, local officials knew about them for much longer.

A City of Vineland inspection activity report noted that “Phase 1 generators are online” in early February. And in May, a Cumberland County Health Department inspector responding to a noise complaint visited the site and reported that the source of the noise appeared to be two generators, “possibly more.”

The inspector noted that the noise “exceeded a nighttime violation.”

As part of the record fine levied against DataOne, the state is mandating the company apply for and obtain the required permits or cease operations, but is allowing them 45 days to do so, according to a NJDEP spokesperson.

During that time, regulators are allowing the facility to continue running the generators — which are capable of emitting more than four tons of NOx in nearby neighborhoods each day.

“I just don’t understand how this is being allowed,” Leone-Vespa said. She hopes independent air monitoring can help protect her community in the future. Until then, she has little faith in New Jersey regulators to watch out for them.

“It’s like they don’t care about the residents.”

text:
Combating global warming requires reducing greenhouse gas emissions, and carbon neutrality is one of the goals through which companies, organizations, and products demonstrate this commitment. Also known as carbon neutrality, it refers to the balance between CO₂ emitted and CO₂ removed or offset. At the institutional level, the term climate neutrality is also used, a related concept applied to long-term climate goals. Distinguishing these concepts from “net zero” and understanding the strategies for achieving carbon neutrality, from reducing emissions at the source to offsetting only residual emissions, enables a precise understanding of climate commitments.

What Is Carbon Neutrality

Carbon neutrality is the state in which carbon dioxide (CO₂) emissions generated by an activity, a product, or an organization are balanced by an equivalent amount of CO₂ removed from the atmosphere or offset. To be carbon neutral, one must therefore measure one’s greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, reduce them, and offset the remaining ones. Removal occurs, for example, through carbon absorption by forests and soils or via dedicated technologies; offsetting is achieved by purchasing carbon credits generated by projects that avoid or remove emissions elsewhere.

Carbon Neutrality, Climate Neutrality, and Net Zero: What’s the Difference?

Carbon neutrality, climate neutrality, and net zero refer to different goals, though they are often used interchangeably in everyday language:

Carbon neutrality: balances CO₂ emitted with CO₂ removed or offset and refers to a single activity, product, or organization;

climate neutrality (climate neutrality): considers all greenhouse gases, not just CO₂, and is the term used at the institutional level and by the European Union for the long-term goal;

net zero: requires reducing emissions at the source to zero or to residual levels compatible with reference climate pathways and neutralizing residual emissions through carbon removals.

The meaning of net zero does not, therefore, coincide with zero emissions in an absolute sense: the net-zero goal consists of reducing net emissions to zero, that is the difference between residual emissions and removed emissions. The standards of the Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi) require companies to follow pathways compatible with achieving net zero by 2050 at the latest. Version 2.0 of the Corporate Net-Zero Standard, published in June 2026, reaffirms the priority of reducing emissions throughout the value chain and requires that, upon achieving net zero, any remaining emissions be offset through appropriate carbon removals.

Decarbonization is the process by which these goals are achieved: the gradual reduction of greenhouse gas emissions that precedes and enables any form of carbon neutrality.

How to Become Carbon Neutral: The Key Leverage Points

To achieve carbon neutrality, a priority order is followed: first, emissions are reduced at the source, and only then are residual emissions addressed. This is also the approach outlined in the ISO 14068:2026 standard, which prioritizes emissions reductions and removals along the value chain over offsetting. The starting point is to measure, through an emissions inventory (carbon footprint), where emissions originate and where it makes sense to take action.

Reduction at the source relies on three key levers:

energy efficiency: consuming less energy while maintaining the same level of service, for example through better-insulated buildings and optimized industrial processes;

electrification: replacing fossil fuels with electricity in end-use applications, such as transportation, heating with heat pumps, and process heat;

renewable sources: powering electrification with solar, wind, or hydroelectric energy, which does not emit CO₂ during generation.

Offsetting addresses residual emissions that cannot yet be eliminated, including those associated with the sectors and processes that are most difficult to decarbonize (hard-to-abate).

In its 2026–2028 Strategic Plan, Enel forecasts approximately 20 billion euros in investments in renewables to add about 15 GW of new capacity and exceed 80 GW by 2028, compared to approximately 68 GW by the end of 2025. According to the ESG Focus for Investors 2026, in 2025, absolute greenhouse gas emissions, both direct and indirect, totaled 62.5 MtCO₂eq, a 67% decrease compared to 2017.

The 2030 and 2050 Targets

The Paris Agreement is the primary international framework for climate action and long-term decarbonization: it aims to limit the rise in global average temperature to well below 2 °C above pre-industrial levels, with a goal of 1.5 °C. According to the IPCC, pathways compatible with 1.5 °C bring net CO₂ emissions to zero around 2050.

The European Union and many other countries have set a target of climate neutrality by 2050; in Europe, this is mandated by law. According to the Council of the EU, compared to 1990 levels, the interim targets are to reduce net greenhouse gas emissions by at least 55% by 2030 and by 90% by 2040. For the European Union, 2030 is not a net-zero deadline, but an intermediate milestone on the path toward climate neutrality by 2050.

Through Enel’s Zero Emissions Ambition, the Group aims for net-zero emissions across all Scopes by 2040, with targets certified by the SBTi.

Carbon Neutrality in Daily Life and in Businesses

In everyday life, carbon neutrality translates into choices that reduce emissions and, for the remaining portion, offset them: electricity supplied from renewable sources, low-impact transportation, and the purchase of products with verified carbon neutrality claims, meaning the manufacturer has reduced and offset emissions according to defined criteria.

For a company, the concept applies to production processes, facilities, and the supply chain and can be verified through an independent audit, for example, in accordance with the ISO 14068:2026 standard. Some examples:

electric corporate fleets, with charging stations in parking lots;

building energy efficiency improvements, such as heat pumps instead of old boilers, LED lighting, and energy management software;

low-impact logistics and packaging, using recycled materials instead of virgin plastic;

long-term PPAs (Power Purchase Agreements) with renewable energy producers to source electricity from renewable sources and reduce emissions associated with energy consumption.

When encountering a product or service that claims to be carbon neutral, it’s important to verify which emissions are included and whether the claim has been verified by an independent third party.

text:
Hyundai Compact EV is expected to debut in India in January 2027. This upcoming sub-four-metre electric SUV was earlier expected to arrive by the end of 2026, but its launch timeline has now been pushed to 2027.

Hyundai had earlier indicated a debut by March 2027 at its 2026 CEO Investor Day. Later, Hyundai Motor India MD and CEO Tarun Garg told Autocar Professional that the electric SUV could arrive by the end of 2026. Now, according to the latest information, its debut could happen in January 2027.

Join Our Youtube Channel to stay updated with daily car & bike news instantly!

This upcoming model is being developed specifically for India. Hyundai aims to expand its presence in the compact electric SUV segment, where manufacturers like Tata and Mahindra are also strengthening competition with new electric models. However, Hyundai has not yet revealed the official name, price, or complete specifications of this EV.

Also Read: Hyundai New Compact EV Spied Charging In India: Fresh Spy Shots Reveal Key Details

Hyundai Compact EV: Platform and Battery Options

The Hyundai Compact EV, internally codenamed HE1i, will be based on the company’s E-GMP (K) platform. This platform is also used in the Hyundai Inster EV sold in international markets. The India-spec model will be produced at its Sriperumbudur plant in Tamil Nadu.

Hyundai plans to offer this electric SUV in two versions: Standard Range and Long Range. The battery capacity, power output, and driving range of both variants have not been officially confirmed yet. Therefore, the figures for the international-spec Inster should not be considered as the final specifications of the India-spec model.

For reference, the overseas Hyundai Inster comes with 42kWh and 49kWh battery packs. According to the company’s claimed WLTP figures, their range is up to 300km and 355km respectively. The Standard Range version produces 97hp power and 147Nm torque, while the Long Range version produces 115hp and 147Nm.

The Hyundai Compact EV coming to India is also reported to have two battery options, but its final range and performance may differ from the international version. A clearer picture of its actual range will emerge only after Indian driving conditions, vehicle specifications, and homologation are determined.

Hyundai Compact EV: Svolt’s Role in Battery Supply, Local Cells Later

Upcoming Hyundai Compact EV will initially use Svolt-supplied battery cells. Locally sourced battery cells also play a role in the company’s long-term planning. Hyundai plans to work towards battery localization in India through an association with Exide.

However, the shift to local cells may happen later due to delays in Exide’s battery production timeline. This means that the battery sourcing strategy may differ for initial production and future batches. The actual impact of local sourcing on costs, supply chain, and vehicle pricing is not yet clear.

Focusing on battery manufacturing and local supply chain in India is important for the EV industry. However, the extent to which localization will benefit Hyundai’s compact EV pricing will remain to be determined until the company’s official announcement.

Also Read: India-Spec Hyundai Bayon Revealed Ahead of October 26 Price Announcement

Features: Level 2 ADAS and Next-Generation Infotainment

Hyundai has confirmed that the upcoming Hyundai Compact EV will feature Level 2 ADAS and a next-generation infotainment system. The infotainment setup could include the brand’s Pleos Connect system, which has been seen in some newer Hyundai models. However, the exact screen sizes and connected features of the India-spec model are not yet confirmed.

The international Hyundai Inster gets dual 10.25-inch displays, which include a digital instrument cluster and infotainment system. Features like automatic climate control, a 360-degree camera, and blind-spot monitoring are also available on the overseas model.

It’s too early to say whether these features will be available on the India-spec compact EV. Hyundai has only confirmed Level 2 ADAS and next-generation infotainment for now. The final feature list is expected to be revealed variant-wise closer to the launch.

Who will be the Hyundai Compact EV’s rivals?

Upon launch in India, Hyundai Compact EV could compete with models like the Tata Nexon EV, Mahindra XUV 3XO EV, and Kia Syros EV. Driving range, charging convenience, cabin space, safety technology, and ownership cost will be important factors for buyers in this segment.

Simply offering an electric powertrain won’t be enough for Hyundai. The company will need to deliver features, along with pricing and practical range, that address Indian buyers’ daily commuting and occasional highway travel needs. The option of Standard Range and Long Range versions can give buyers a choice based on their budget and usage.

Auto India Daily Verdict

The January 2027 debut of upcoming Hyundai Compact EV is currently a reported timeline, not an official launch date. Key highlights of this model include India-specific development, two expected range options, Level 2 ADAS, and a next-generation infotainment system. Manufacturing in Sriperumbudur also highlights this EV’s importance for the Indian market.

Currently, the biggest unanswered questions concern battery capacity, India-specific driving range, charging capabilities, and pricing. Until Hyundai confirms these details, it would be inaccurate to directly apply international Inster specifications to the India model. If Hyundai offers practical range along with competitive pricing, this compact electric SUV could become an important new option in the Indian EV market.

title: Permitting Reform Could Impact Consumers on Their Power Bills - Energy News Beat
description:
A new Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) proposal to streamline expansions of liquefied natural gas (LNG) facilities highlights both the opportunity and the limits of piecemeal reform.
Source: Paris Apodaca ⁠Dailycaller Broader Permitting Reform and Consumer Impacts Blackmon and others have repeatedly argued that the United States faces a permitting shortage rather than a resource shortage.
Permitting reform is not a silver bullet, but it is one of the highest-leverage steps available to expand stable supply and moderate pressure on power bills.
ICF analysis for API: Permitting reform impacts on residential electricity bills (~$55.6 billion cumulative 2026–2035), jobs, and tax revenue.

text:
America does not primarily have an energy shortage. It has a permitting shortage. A new Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) proposal to streamline expansions of liquefied natural gas (LNG) facilities highlights both the opportunity and the limits of piecemeal reform. As energy analyst Stuart Turley notes, LNG expansion alone will not lower costs for consumers without broader regulatory overreach reform throughout the natural gas value chain—and beyond, across all energy sources. The same delays, litigation risks, and multi-year reviews that slow LNG and pipelines also constrain power plants, transmission lines, refineries, and even renewable projects, feeding higher construction costs, tighter supply, and upward pressure on power bills.

We highly recommend reading and following both the Daily Caller, with great energy writers like Simon and Paris, and David Blackmon.

FERC’s LNG Fast-Track Proposal

On October 16, 2026, FERC unanimously proposed a blanket authorization program that would allow certain LNG facility expansions and modifications to proceed without full project-specific reviews under the Natural Gas Act. Minor changes that do not increase authorized capacity, expand the footprint, or exceed design limits could proceed automatically. Capacity increases within the existing footprint would require 60 days’ notice; larger projects such as new processing units, storage tanks, or marine berths would need 90 days’ notice, still subject to safeguards. Source: Paris Apodaca ⁠Dailycaller

Energy analyst David Blackmon called it “a very significant move to streamline permitting and get the government out of the way of one of America’s most dynamic expanding industries.” He pointed to cases in which an LNG operator waited more than two years simply for approval to build a safety- and efficiency-related flow line. “If approved, this authority would have avoided that and other bureaucratic delays,” he said. FERC Chairman Laura V. Swett framed the proposal in terms of energy dominance: “American energy dominance requires us to build and maintain the energy infrastructure our country needs without unnecessary delay.” The proposal mirrors an existing program for interstate natural gas pipelines and includes standardized environmental and engineering safeguards. Public comments will be accepted for 60 days after Federal Register publication. Source: Paris Apodaca ⁠Dailycaller

Turley’s caution is equally important. “LNG expansion by itself will not lower costs; it has to have regulatory overreach reform throughout the value chain,” he said. Expanded LNG exports can place upward pressure on domestic natural gas prices even as other reforms lower supply-chain costs. Restrictions on production, pipelines, and transportation remain binding constraints. Faster LNG infrastructure is helpful for energy security and exports, but it is not a complete answer for residential or industrial power bills. Source: Paris Apodaca ⁠Dailycaller

Broader Permitting Reform and Consumer Impacts

Blackmon and others have repeatedly argued that the United States faces a permitting shortage rather than a resource shortage. More than 650 major infrastructure projects, representing roughly $1.1–1.5 trillion in investment, remain stuck in federal review. McKinsey has estimated that construction costs rise 24–30 percent over long permitting timelines, driven largely by materials, labor, and overhead while reviews and litigation continue. An ICF analysis commissioned by the American Petroleum Institute found that comprehensive federal permitting reform could cut residential electricity bills by a combined $55.6 billion from 2026 through 2035 across 22 states studied, while supporting about 705,000 jobs and nearly $24 billion in tax revenue by 2030. Average residential rate reductions of roughly 0.71 cents per kWh (rising toward 0.95 cents by 2035) translate into annual household savings that vary by state, with larger impacts in places like Virginia.⁠Blackmon.substack

A bipartisan Senate package—the American Affordability and Jobs Act (sometimes described as “Freedom to Build”)—aims to address core problems: narrowing NEPA reviews to impacts tied to the project rather than every hypothetical downstream effect, imposing a 150-day clock on certain lawsuits and limiting standing, preventing courts from vacating completed permits over paperwork defects (remand rather than halt), keeping Clean Water Act Section 401 focused on actual water quality rather than serving as a backdoor climate veto, and making statutory deadlines enforceable. These changes would apply across energy types, including transmission, generation, and pipelines. Environmental and safety standards remain; the goal is to end process that treats delay as a virtue.⁠Blackmon.substack

It is impossible to isolate a single precise dollar figure for “permitting costs” to every U.S. energy consumer—the interactions of federal, state, and local rules, litigation, financing costs, and forgone supply are too complex. Analysts have nonetheless quantified large effects. Beyond the ICF and McKinsey figures, other work shows that delays in transmission and generation development raise system costs by tens of billions annually in modeled scenarios, with net costs to energy users several times larger than any capital-cost savings from slower spending. Project-specific examples (transmission lines, solar, storage) routinely show 6–25 percent or higher cost increases from federal or local permitting delays, which flow into rate bases. Broader federal regulatory compliance costs have been estimated in the trillions annually across the economy, with energy, climate, and appliance rules among the drivers that raise household expenses. The direction is clear: longer, more uncertain processes raise the cost of building the infrastructure that keeps the lights on and fuels affordable.

Blue-State vs. Red-State Permitting: Oil Wells as a Window into All Energy

Energy News Beat’s comparison of oil-well permitting in Colorado, California, and Texas illustrates how state-level differences compound federal ones and affect supply reliability. As of mid-September 2026 data:

Texas (development-oriented): Standard W-1 drilling permits typically process in 2–4 business days. Trailing 24-month permits ~3,232; high spud activity (hundreds in recent 90-day windows). 2025 oil output ~5.76 million b/d. Statewide spacing rules with relatively limited local veto power; the statutory posture emphasizes preventing waste and protecting correlative rights, with development presumed.

Colorado: OGDP-to-hearing averages 257–297 days in recent years; full state-plus-local packages often 12–18 months. Trailing 24-month permits only ~335. 2,000-foot statewide setbacks, local surface-siting authority, continuous monitoring, methane rules, and net-zero-oriented statutes have sharply reduced activity near residences and slowed new wells. Output has plateaued in the 420–475 thousand b/d range after earlier growth.

California: Paper targets for certain notices are short, but CEQA, local land-use vetoes, and phase-down politics dominate real timelines. Trailing 24-month permits ~1,853 (many reworks rather than new shale-style drills); recent 90-day spuds extremely low (single digits in some snapshots). Long-term production decline continues in the ~300 thousand b/d range. Kern County saw limited 2026 streamlining, but overall policy has constrained new development.

Texas’s volume and speed support high output and a deep operator base. Colorado and California’s longer clocks, setbacks, and environmental/litigation overlays have produced lower new-well activity relative to resource potential. These patterns are not limited to oil. Pipelines, gas-fired power plants, nuclear projects, transmission lines, and even large wind or solar farms face analogous multi-year federal NEPA processes, state siting battles, and lawsuit risks. In higher-regulation states, local and state rules frequently add layers that make firm, dispatchable capacity harder to build. The result is greater reliance on existing assets, imports, or intermittent resources that require backup—raising system costs and volatility that appear on power bills.

Reform for Stable Power Across All Sources

More permitting reform would accelerate baseload and firm capacity—natural gas combined-cycle plants, nuclear (including advanced designs), hydropower, and the pipelines and transmission that serve them—alongside any renewables that can clear reviews efficiently. Data-center load growth, electrification, and manufacturing reshoring are increasing demand. When new firm generation or delivery infrastructure is delayed, operators run older plants longer, buy more expensive power, or curtail loads, all of which increase costs. Streamlined processes reduce the 24–30 percent construction-cost premium from timelines, lower financing risk, and allow capital to flow into capacity that stabilizes the grid rather than relying solely on weather-dependent resources plus storage and backup.

LNG and pipeline reforms help by supporting abundant, flexible gas supply that underpins both power generation and industrial demand. Broader reforms (federal NEPA and Clean Water Act fixes, state-level streamlining modeled on Texas-style efficiency rather than Colorado- or California-style constraints) would extend the benefits to every major energy pathway. As Blackmon has emphasized in recent commentary, the bipartisan package offers a practical path; Turley’s point remains that partial measures are insufficient without consistent reform across the value chain.

Consumers ultimately pay for the capital, financing, and reliability costs embedded in delayed or canceled projects. Analysts’ estimates—tens of billions in cumulative residential bill reductions from comprehensive reform, double-digit percentage cost increases from prolonged timelines—indicate the scale. Permitting reform is not a silver bullet, but it is one of the highest-leverage steps available to expand stable supply and moderate pressure on power bills.

text:
Nearly half a million dollars in regional environmental grants were awarded on Thursday to three organizations working to manage the impact of climate change, pollution and sea level rise on Martha’s Vineyard.

Cong. Bill Keating joined Peter Wharton, chair of the Martha’s Vineyard Commission, and Thomas Ardito, director of the Southeast New England Watershed Grant Program, to award $249,990 to the commission to implement a permeable reactive barrier to continue to improve water quality in Lagoon Pond, $242,000 to The Trustees of Reservations for salt marsh and barrier beach restoration on Chappaquiddick, and an additional $6,000 to The Great Pond Foundation to purchase water quality monitoring equipment.

“We’re leveraging science, technology, environmental expertise and we’re empowering the local communities to do what they know their needs are,” said Mr. Keating. “That’s what’s great about this program.”

The grants were awarded via the Environmental Protection Agency’s Southeast New England Program to empower the Vineyard community by funding projects that aid climate resiliency efforts around the Island.

“Nature is healing itself with watershed protection, with marshlands,” said Mr. Keating. “All we’re doing is aiding and literally channeling this, as is the case on Chappaquiddick, channeling nature so that it’s healing itself, and in the nitrogen issue, which is fascinating.”

A permeable reactive barrier was first installed at Lagoon Pond in 2020. According to Dr. Jessica Thomas, a professor of mathematics and physics at Roger Williams University, areas that have installed similar permeable barriers have seen 99 per cent reduction in harmful bioavailable nitrogen release.

“Permeable reactive barriers are an innovative technology for dealing with nitrogen,” said Ms. Thomas. “This is a technique that we can use to try to address that and it’s a natural technique.”

Nitrogen is a common ecological issue facing coastal communities and is most often released into the groundwater via nearby septic systems. Permeable reactive barriers are designed to function as a passive on-site method for groundwater treatment using seed oils to absorb excess nitrogen.

“We inject vegetable oil into the groundwater to intercept [nitrogen molecules] and that vegetable oil will create an environment for the natural microbes to take a bioavailable nitrogen, which is our problem nitrogen, and change it into nitrogen gas, which can off-gas right into the atmosphere and is the most abundant gas in the atmosphere,” said Ms. Thomas.

Following a brief discussion, those in attendance were invited to join Alejandra Narvaez, the coastal project manager at The Trustees of Reservations, on a tour of the salt marshes situated on Chappaquiddick. There, Ms. Narvaez discussed the history of salt marshes on the Island and how The Trustees plan to bolster areas that are highly susceptible to sea level rise.

According to Ms. Narvaez, models suggest that by 2070 the Dike Bridge, which grants access to various Chappaquiddick beaches via over-sand vehicles, will be submerged during daily tidal fluctuations.

“That’s why we’re intervening now,” she said during the tour. “We’re maintaining the natural vegetation to keep up with sea level rise.”

The process to protect salt marshes and barrier beaches involves a combination of efforts that include ditch remediation, which can take anywhere from three to five years, said Ms. Narvaez, and reconnecting channels via runnelling to reach an equilibrium and maintain natural tidal flow.

Typically, runnels are dug approximately seven inches into a salt marsh and are constructed in a ‘V’ shape to allow for natural reshaping as sea levels continue to rise.

“We want a light touch restoration,” said Ms. Narvaez. “We are basically remediating or healing these ditches.”

Mercedes-AMG unveiled the all-electric Mercedes-AMG GT SUV on Saturday, October 17, 2026, the first full-size SUV the Affalterbach division has developed entirely in-house.
The 2028 model arrives at US dealerships in summer 2027 as a GT 63, GT 55 and GT 53.
The GT 63 and GT 55 SUV peak at 710 kW.
The GT 63 SUV’s 128 kWh Battery Pushes DC Charging to 710 kW The SUV out-charges the 4-Door because the GT 63 and GT 55 get a larger pack: 128 kWh usable across 22 modules, against 106 kWh and 18 modules in the GT 53 SUV and the 4-Door.
Rotary dials on the center console adjust throttle response, handling balance and traction control on the GT 63, and are optional on the GT 55.
text:
Mercedes-AMG unveiled the all-electric Mercedes-AMG GT SUV on Saturday, October 17, 2026, the first full-size SUV the Affalterbach division has developed entirely in-house. The flagship GT 63 SUV uses three axial flux motors for a peak 1,153 horsepower and reaches 60 mph in an estimated 2.4 seconds.

The 2028 model arrives at US dealerships in summer 2027 as a GT 63, GT 55 and GT 53. Mercedes has not announced US pricing. It is the production version of the electric performance SUV EVXL first covered as a winter-testing prototype in December 2024.

The AMG GT 4-Door Coupe that launched the same platform in May peaks at 600 kW on a DC fast charger. The GT 63 and GT 55 SUV peak at 710 kW.

The GT 63 SUV’s 128 kWh Battery Pushes DC Charging to 710 kW

The SUV out-charges the 4-Door because the GT 63 and GT 55 get a larger pack: 128 kWh usable across 22 modules, against 106 kWh and 18 modules in the GT 53 SUV and the 4-Door. Mercedes rates the bigger pack at 710 kW, the smaller at 600 kW.

Mercedes quotes 10 to 80 percent in 12 minutes at the 710 kW peak, and 282 miles (454 kilometers) of WLTP range added in as little as 10 minutes. On a 400 kW station, the same session takes 16 minutes. Mercedes-Benz USA’s launch release labels its charging rates and times preliminary, with no certified values yet.

The 800-volt pack uses tall, narrow cylindrical cells bathed directly in non-conductive oil, the cooling approach Mercedes credits for both the charging rate and repeatable power. It switches to 400-volt mode at older stations, and Mercedes lists NACS among the five DC plug standards it supports.

The GT 63 SUV's six round taillights and active roof spoiler. Photo credit: Mercedes-Benz

The 1,153-HP GT 63 SUV Weighs 5,941 Pounds and Has No EPA Rating

Peak output for the GT 63 SUV is 1,153 hp and 1,475 lb-ft, with 711 hp available continuously and a 63-second boost window. The 2.4-second 0 to 60 mph time uses a 1-foot rollout; without it, Mercedes estimates 2.6 seconds. Top speed is limited to 168 mph.

That output puts the GT 63 SUV just ahead of the Porsche Cayenne Turbo Electric, which makes 1,139 hp on launch control and charges at up to 400 kW.

The DIN curb weight is 2,695 kilograms, or 5,941 pounds. Mercedes quotes 385 to 435 miles (620 to 700 kilometers) of WLTP range. The US release carries no EPA estimate.

The GT 55 SUV uses the same three motors and pack at 805 hp. The GT 53 SUV swaps in two synchronous motors and the 106 kWh pack for 536 hp. Storage runs to 21.4 cubic feet (606 liters) in the trunk and 2.8 cubic feet (79 liters) in the frunk.

AMGFORCE Sport+ Plays a Recorded V8 and Shakes the Seat

The AMGFORCE Sport+ drive program plays a recorded V8 in the GT 63 and GT 55 SUV, or a six-cylinder in the GT 53, and pairs it with simulated gear changes, paddle shifting and seat vibration. Mercedes says it built the sound from over 100 measurements taken with 16 microphones.

Inside, the 10.2-inch driver display and 14-inch center screen form one unit, and a second 14-inch screen is optional for the passenger. Rotary dials on the center console adjust throttle response, handling balance and traction control on the GT 63, and are optional on the GT 55.

The Mercedes-AMG GT SUV cockpit. Photo credit: Mercedes-Benz

The reference cars for the sound included the AMG GT R, and a slider lets the driver turn the effect down to “Silent.” Porsche added simulated gears to the 2027 Taycan in June, a feature its own development driver had publicly dismissed. Stefan Weckbach, who runs Mercedes-AMG, summed up the SUV’s pitch as “SUV by shape. GT by nature.”

EVXL’s Take

The 710 kW peak makes the headline, but I’d pay for the bigger pack behind it. Mercedes says a 400 kW charger takes the GT 63 SUV from 10 to 80 percent in 16 minutes. Porsche quotes a little under 16 minutes for the Cayenne Electric’s 113 kWh pack, so on the same charger the Mercedes refills 128 kWh of usable capacity in about the time the Porsche needs for a smaller battery. That gap holds whether or not a 710 kW station ever shows up on your route. The release doesn’t say what the SUV pulls from a Tesla Supercharger, where the Cayenne tops out at 200 kW. I’d want that number from Mercedes before calling this the faster road-trip SUV.

Source: Mercedes-Benz USA

EVXL uses automated tools to support research and source retrieval. All reporting and editorial perspectives are by Haye Kesteloo.

authors: Leah Bowers, Deseret News, Deseret News), www.facebook.com
description:

"Utah already is a model for other states for developing geothermal energy," Mitchell said.
"At the prices stated by Fervo with tax credits included, PacifiCorp anticipates proxy geothermal would be economic and the model would select proxy geothermal over other proxy resource options like gas.
Without tax credits, PacifiCorp anticipates the prices stated by Fervo would still make proxy geothermal competitive with proxy gas in the IRP model."
text:
SALT LAKE CITY — Fervo Energy announced a 396 megawatt power purchase agreement with Google on Sept. 1 — enabling southwestern Utah's Cape Station geothermal plant development, coming online in 2028.

But Fervo's geothermal giant comes with a catch: None of the energy is going to Utahns ... yet.

California got there first

Most of Cape Station's early capacity is contracted under long-term agreements to California power providers, such as Southern California Edison, Clean Power Alliance and Desert Community Energy.

California utilities purchased these initial blocks because the state's regulation explicitly mandates the procurement of "clean firm" renewable energy.

Google is purchasing the almost 400 megawatts of power which, the company hopes, will eventually power a data center on Utah soil.

The agreement also includes an option for Google to scale up its purchase by an additional 600 megawatts, reaching nearly 1 gigawatt by June 2030 — about the same amount of power Utah's Huntington coal plant can generate at any given moment.

Google and Fervo also signed a broader 3 gigawatt non-binding framework agreement to evaluate future data center power arrangements across Fervo's pipeline.

"This agreement reinforces that EGS (enhanced geothermal systems) is ready to power the next generation of computing infrastructure," said Tim Latimer, CEO and co-founder of Fervo Energy, in a press release. "As demand for reliable electricity grows, customers like Google need energy resources that can be deployed at scale, operate around the clock, and deliver where power is needed."

Overall, Fervo predicts Cape Station will be able to deliver 4.3 gigawatts of power at peak — and the rest of the potential power lies unclaimed. The leftover 3.4 gigawatts (after Google and California contracts are fulfilled) is equivalent to running three full-scale legacy coal plants at maximum output.

And Fervo is actively advertising them.

The state's dominant power provider may not be far behind. Pacificorp, which operates as Rocky Mountain Power in Utah, stated in the 2027 Integrated Resource Plan Public Input Meeting Oct. 14 that at the prices stated by Fervo with federal tax credits included, it anticipates geothermal "would be economic" and its model "would select proxy geothermal over other proxy resource options like gas."

Even without tax credits, PacifiCorp said Fervo's pricing "would still make proxy geothermal competitive with proxy gas."

Though no purchase agreement has been signed yet, PacifiCorp's statement signals Utah ratepayers could eventually benefit from the technology being built in their backyard.

Utah's energy appeal

"It checks all the boxes," said Mitchell, referring to Fervo's next-gen technology.

For the "old style" of geothermal generation, Mitchell said it required three things: the heat in the Earth, cracks in the rocks or crust, and a way to harvest the heat out of the Earth — usually water.

"And so you need the cracks to push the water through to harvest the heat, and then that brings the heat to the surface, and then that turns a turbine and creates energy," he explained.

"And that's why geothermal exists in a few spots — and it's great where it exists — but it's not everywhere," Mitchell added.

Utah is third in the nation in installed geothermal capacity, though it only makes up about 3.2%. California and Nevada hold over 90% of the nation's capacity.

But the technology being used differs significantly among the three states.

Nevada and California's geothermal plants are largely conventional — the "old style" Mitchell described. The states are home to geysers and lakes, where the hot fluid necessary for this technique is easy to find.

Though the state may be behind, many emerging Utah projects — like Fervo — use "enhanced" geothermal techniques: drilling deep into hot rock, fracturing it, and circulating water through to build an artificial reservoir.

The federal push

In places like Utah, the ground's permeability is a motivating factor. Other nearby states have similar benefits, leaving geothermal developers looking west to develop the technology.

"Utah already is a model for other states for developing geothermal energy," Mitchell said. "We have a relatively good permitting environment here, and we're seeing geothermal companies work very closely with the Bureau of Land Management offices ..."

Federal agencies — such as BLM — have started to promote geothermal-focused policies.

In August, the bureau authorized the drilling of up to 10 geothermal temperature-gradient holes in Iron County — shallow, lower-cost test wells used to measure how quickly temperatures increase before jumping into expensive, massive wells.

The U.S. Department of Energy is also funding Utah FORGE — an enhanced geothermal research site in Beaver County. Operated by the University of Utah, researchers are testing new techniques to create geothermal energy in other parts of the U.S. where no natural hot water exists.

Utah's opening

"Hopefully, we'll have very, very little water consumption also. We'll have zero air emissions, no air quality impacts, no carbon emissions. It's also dispatchable like natural gas," Mitchell said. "We want our data centers to be investing in the right technologies that are going to be viable for long periods of time."

Mitchell argues that in a world of increasing demand for power, geothermal is a dispatchable, clean energy that can be built quickly.

"What this really means is that we have a pathway for reducing the emissions and water consumption of our energy system into the future," he said.

With 3.4 gigawatts of Cape Station's potential still unclaimed — and California and Google already proving the demand — the question is whether Utah will stake a claim on the clean energy being built in its own backyard.

"At the prices stated by Fervo with tax credits included, PacifiCorp anticipates proxy geothermal would be economic and the model would select proxy geothermal over other proxy resource options like gas. Without tax credits, PacifiCorp anticipates the prices stated by Fervo would still make proxy geothermal competitive with proxy gas in the IRP model."

"For the 2027 IRP, PacifiCorp is planning to model a single proxy near-field enhanced geothermal system (NF EGS) binary resource option limited to 500 MW selectable in both Oregon and Utah for the entirety of the study horizon, first eligible in 2030. The costs for the proxy geothermal resource option would be based on Fervo's cost estimates, beginning with an overnight capital cost of $5,500 per kilowatt in 2030 and declining to $3,000 per kilowatt by 2036."

Crucially, PacifiCorp agreed to update its 2027 IRP model to incorporate Fervo's cost curve—starting at $5,500/kW in 2030 and scaling down to $3,000/kW by 2036, complete with federal tax credits

name: EPA
title: Which Is the Most Underestimated Climate Threat in the US? - Gizmodo
authors: Ellyn Lapointe, Webb Wright, Passant Rabie
description:
All of this got me wondering, which climate threat is the U.S. most underestimating?
To me, climate threats mean both climate hazards and their broader societal impacts.
Climate threats are shaped by weather and climate events occurring and what lies in the places where extreme events happen and people’s ability to respond and recover.
If you talk to most climate scientists, they will say that the biggest underappreciated near-term climate risk is extreme precipitation events.
My fear is not a specific climate threat per se.
text:
With each fraction of a degree Earth’s temperature rises, so does the threat of extreme weather. In the United States, climate change is exacerbating disasters that endanger the public and cost the nation hundreds of billions of dollars per year. Despite this, federal support for climate change mitigation and adaptation, as well as disaster preparedness and response, has crumbled under President Trump.

His energy agenda has sought to destroy renewable energy growth and inject new life into the nation’s fossil fuel industry. In February, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) rescinded the legal basis for greenhouse gas regulation in the United States. The Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) lost over 17% of its staff in 2025 alone, and the administration also withheld billions of dollars meant to help states protect residents, their homes, and the critical infrastructure they depend on from natural disasters.

I could go on. As the risks mount and the resources for addressing them disappear, knowing where the biggest gaps in preparedness lie becomes all the more important. The urgency of this situation was laid bare this summer—the hottest on record for the United States—during which communities struggled to cope with life-threatening heat waves, rampant wildfires, powerful storms, and flash flooding.

All of this got me wondering, which climate threat is the U.S. most underestimating? I posed this question to multiple experts, and while it’s clear that the federal government has hampered the nation’s ability to weather all kinds of climate-driven disasters, they pointed to several threats that may be particularly underappreciated.

Andra Garner

An assistant professor in the Department of Environmental Science at Rowan University. Garner’s research focuses on the impacts of climate change on natural hazards, including the effects of sea-level rise on tsunamis and the evolving characteristics of tropical cyclones and storm surge in a warming world.

The short, blunt answer to this question is, “all of them.” Otherwise, we’d be doing much more to help our communities become more resilient in the face of climate-driven hazards. The U.S. would be working harder to assume a leadership role on the international stage in the effort to address climate change and to find a way to curb emissions.

We would also be doing all that we could to eliminate one of the biggest barriers to climate action: funding from the fossil fuel industry that supports politicians and lobbyists to act in ways that prevent meaningful legislation that would otherwise help regulate the polluters that are driving this crisis.

But, if I had to identify a particular type of climate-driven threat that is commonly underestimated, I’d again say that the answer is not any single type of event, but rather what the climate community calls “compound hazards,” climate-driven hazards that happen either concurrently or in close succession to one another.

Consider the recent, powerful nor’easter that impacted the U.S. northeast, bringing strong winds, rainfall, and storm surge from Virginia to Maine. Climate-driven coastal flood impacts were certainly felt during this storm, but coastal defenses (including recently replenished beaches and dunes in many parts of New Jersey and Delaware) prevented complete devastation.

However, many of these defenses were also heavily compromised, as erosion ate away at beaches and dunes. So, should another coastal storm occur in the coming months, many of these communities will be unprotected, potentially facing far worse impacts and more costly damages.

Or consider hurricanes, which produce hazards like storm surge, rainfall, and exceptionally strong winds—all made worse in a warming climate. Similarly, heat waves are becoming more intense and lasting longer, with overnight lows that offer little relief, especially in humid regions.

Protocols exist to prepare for an approaching hurricane, or to help keep residents safe during heat waves. But how do we prepare for and help a community that experiences a hurricane landfall, immediately followed by an extreme heat wave, when electricity might be out for millions?

In a world where climate hazards are continuing to become more extreme, these types of compound hazards present a unique threat that remains difficult to address and requires more attention.

Deepti Singh

An associate professor in the School of the Environment at Washington State University Vancouver, where she leads the Climate Extremes and Impacts lab. Singh’s research aims to advance the physical understanding of climate extremes and their interactions that result in compound hazards, as well as their sources of predictability in the Earth system.

It’s hard to name a single threat the U.S. is underestimating. To me, climate threats mean both climate hazards and their broader societal impacts. Climate threats are shaped by weather and climate events occurring and what lies in the places where extreme events happen and people’s ability to respond and recover. I think we’re underestimating the extreme events themselves and their toll on society, particularly on health and the economy.

Heat is a big one. It is among the deadliest climate extremes globally and in the U.S., despite being reasonably well-understood and highly predictable, which enables timely early warnings. The ecological and human health impacts are very likely underestimated.

Colder places are unprepared, as we saw from the acute and devastating impacts of the 2021 Pacific Northwest heat wave, which killed an estimated 1,400 people and a billion marine animals in the region. Meanwhile, places like Florida, Arizona, and Louisiana experience chronic heat—exposure to dangerous heat that seriously affects health, but whose impacts are not as immediate or visible. Many of these places don’t have early warning systems for heat, and images of people frolicking in water fountains or rivers often used in reporting don’t motivate people to take it as seriously as death and destruction from, say, a hurricane.

Wildfires are another. Increasing heat and drought severity are fueling increasing wildfire activity across the West. Fires threaten infrastructure and ecosystems while producing smoke that is really harmful to human health near to and far beyond the burn areas. Fires also leave landscapes vulnerable for years, if not decades, and they are hard to anticipate.

We can forecast high fire weather conditions, but not precisely when and where fires will ignite, whether from human activity or lightning, or how quickly they will spread, especially with the long lead times needed to prepare. The 2020 fire season was a preview—large fires burned across California, Oregon, and Washington, and smoke blanketed the entire country. That risk will continue, and we are not adequately planning for it.

The impacts of these events are also underestimated. Billion-dollar weather disasters are increasing rapidly, with 21 already since the start of 2026. The human and ecological impacts unfold over months.

Most importantly, there is limited data for tracking these impacts in the most vulnerable communities, including low-income communities, communities of color, and indigenous communities that lack monitoring infrastructure and resources. Our models to anticipate future risks are only as good as the data underlying them. So, threats to the communities most at risk are also the ones we are less likely to anticipate and be prepared for.

Finally, communities are now facing compounding threats—multiple extremes happening at once or back-to-back disasters that hit communities while they are still recovering from a previous disaster. Our emergency resources are limited and are being depleted (for example, recent FEMA cuts), just as increasing extreme events are pushing communities beyond the boundaries of what they can manage.

Jesse Keenan

The Favrot II Associate Professor of Sustainable Real Estate and Favrot II Associate Professor of Sustainable Real Estate and Urban Planning, Director of the Center on Climate Change and Urbanism, and Director of the Climate Change Science and Practice Minor Program at Tulane University. Keenan’s research focuses on the intersection of climate change mitigation and adaptation in the built environment, including aspects of design, engineering, regulation, planning, and financing.

Climate impacts come in all shapes and sizes, from highly disruptive extreme events to not-so-obvious chronic nuisances. In recent years, my colleagues and I have investigated a simple research question: To what extent is there an alignment between people’s actual risk exposure to climate impacts and their perception of those risks?

In the first paper from this research, published in Nature Communications, we evaluated the alignment between heat risk and people’s worry about extreme heat. Our research showed significant misalignments in the Pacific Northwest and in Appalachia. This means that these areas have a fair amount of risk exposure, yet people do not seem to be too concerned.

This presents a real problem if communities and local governments delay making heat-related adaptation investments because it is incorrectly viewed as an otherwise low-risk problem. Conversely, in places whose climate is already pretty hot, such as Texas, the alignment between risk and exposure is pretty robust. All across the country, people’s historical experience, existing risk exposure, and way of life have a lot do with how people evaluate and perceive their risk.

But, existing research about people’s perception of risks tends to focus on known and likely risks. If you talk to most climate scientists, they will say that the biggest underappreciated near-term climate risk is extreme precipitation events. When it rains, it can really pour. However, there is category of risks called low-probability high-impact events that most people are grossly unaware of. In fact, if they knew more about these events, they would probably be more concerned with how we prepare for them.

One event that keeps me up at night is associated with a scenario where we have an extreme heat wave that contributes to the collapse of the grid. Without power, people roast alive. With rapidly increasing loads from data centers in urban areas, we are facing a compound risk scenario that—in a place like Phoenix—could easily lead to more causalities and deaths than all American terrorist attacks and combat casualties this century—combined.

Brad Udall

A senior water and climate research scientist/scholar at Colorado State University’s Colorado Water Center. Udall’s expertise includes climate change, hydrology, and related policy issues of the American West.

My fear is not a specific climate threat per se. It is, instead, that humans are failing to meaningfully reduce greenhouse gas emissions, let alone get to net zero emissions by mid-century.

Despite 30 plus years of scientific outcry pleading for emissions reductions, we have yet to see an emissions peak, we don’t have the technologies nor are we making the investments to reach net zero, and the world is backsliding everywhere into new decades-long committed emissions.

In the absence of significant efforts to curtail emissions, every potential threat is a worry. Only by reducing emissions will we reduce our overall risk from all threats. Arguing about which individual threat is worse is the wrong focus given our inability to deal with the root cause of the problem.

Recent work by Carbon Brief suggests that, under current policies, global warming of 5.4 degrees F (3 degrees C) by 2100 has a 75% chance of occurring, and 7.2 degrees F (4 degrees C) of warming by 2150 occurs 25% of the time.

In a rational world, a 5.4-degree F (3-degree C) rise should be completely unacceptable and 7.2 degrees F (4 degrees C) unthinkable, yet there is little discussion about these outcomes. Furthermore, the failure of the press and the scientific community to explain potential post-2100 emissions and warming trajectories has been a grave mistake. In addition, two recent studies show that since about 2015, the rate of warming has approximately doubled, heightening the long-term danger of destabilizing temperature increases.

Capitalism, acceptable standards for consumer behavior, and our governance institutions are all major problems. We allow fossil fuel producers to sell a planet-wrecking product without any consideration of the costs of that product despite having cost-effective green alternatives available in many cases (for example, carbon-free electricity and vehicles). We are taught that freedom means being able to consume anything we want, no matter the climate consequences of those actions. And our democracies, under threat from authoritarians who almost universally oppose meaningful climate action, seem unable to rise to the occasion.

It doesn’t have to be this way. We have the knowledge and many of the technologies to avoid the worst. A meaningful carbon tax would make capitalism our friend, instead of our enemy. We need to use our substantial collective wealth to protect us from what should be completely unacceptable risks, not sleepwalk into irreversible, dire outcomes.

text:
DETROIT (AP) — A group of environmental organizations sued the Trump administration on Oct. 2 over its recent relaxation of key vehicle fuel economy rules, a decision that the group says will make vehicles less efficient, contribute to more pollution and increase gas consumption.

On Sept. 28, the Trump administration lowered Corporate Average Fuel Economy, or CAFE, standards that set out how far new vehicles need to travel on a gallon of gasoline.

The announcement was made as the Trump administration negotiated with Iran over reopening the Strait of Hormuz.

About a fifth of the world’s oil passes through the strait on a typical day, and the fight over its control has sent energy prices soaring across the globe.

The environmental groups filed the petition for review in the U.S. Court of Appeals against Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Jonathan Morrison, the administrator of the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, which sets the rules.

“We’re taking the Trump administration to court for this reckless rollback that prioritizes Big Oil and automaker profits over American families,” Katherine Garcia, director of Sierra Club’s Clean Transportation for All program, said in a statement.

“It is unlawful for Trump to turn back the clock on fuel-efficient cars, forcing drivers to waste more money on gas and communities to breathe toxic air.”

The Center for Biological Diversity, the Conservation Law Foundation, the Environmental Defense Fund and Public Citizen, along with the Sierra Club, filed the suit.

The Transportation Department and NHTSA lowered the standards to an industry fleetwide average of roughly 34.9 miles per gallon for passenger cars and light trucks in the 2031 model year, down from a projected 50.4 miles per gallon under rules set by the Biden administration.

The administration said the change would provide Americans more vehicle choice and encourage consumers to buy newer, safer vehicles.

Experts say reducing fuel economy requirements in vehicles does not necessarily lower their cost, nor would it automatically translate to new vehicle sales.

Duffy said the new rule also cuts the “illegal mandate that forced automakers to produce more expensive electric vehicles that American families didn’t want.”

There has never been a mandate that manufacturers sell EVs or Americans buy them; the rules and other cleaner vehicle standards incentivized automakers to sell a mix of electric, hybrid electric and increasingly-efficient gasoline-powered vehicles.

When reached for comment, a DOT spokesperson referred to statements made by Duffy: “This administration understands the freedom of every American family starts with affordable cars. That’s why our new standards will make that dream more achievable by letting auto manufacturers produce the cars that fit families’ needs at a lower price.”

Auto companies and industry groups broadly welcomed the change, saying the rules under the Biden administration were too stringent and did not benefit consumers.

But environmental organizations decried the changes.

“With gas prices at historic highs, Trump picked the worst possible time to roll back federal mileage standards,” David Pettit, an attorney at the Center for Biological Diversity’s Climate Law Institute, said in a statement.

“Oil companies will profit from less efficient cars, but drivers will take a hit to their wallets and our kids will breathe dirtier air. We’ll all pay the price for more tailpipe pollutants spewing everywhere from playgrounds to wild places. We’re asking the courts to put a stop to this callous giveaway to Big Oil and Big Auto.”

Gas prices have hovered around $4.50 and diesel has hit unprecedented heights in recent weeks, according to AAA.

The DOT said that the rule would cut yearly oil consumption in 2050 by about 1.3 billion barrels as compared with yearly oil consumption in 2024, but NHTSA had estimated the 2024 standards would have saved 14 billion gallons of gasoline from being burned by that year.

Fuel economy requirements have been in place since the 1970s energy crisis and over time have led to improved average efficiency in vehicles.

President Donald Trump has made a number of moves to undercut cleaner vehicles in the United States.

These include eliminating electric vehicle tax credits, scrapping vehicle emissions standards, repealing the fines for automakers who don’t meet mileage rules and attempting to block the nation’s EV charging buildout.

text:
A coalition of 17 groups that want the Montana Public Service Commission to consider the effects of climate change in its decisions is taking its case to court.

Earthjustice and Western Environmental Law Center filed a complaint Thursday against the Public Service Commission.

It asks the Missoula County District Court to find the PSC has a constitutional obligation to account for climate risks in its decisions.

“Climate change poses an urgent threat to Montana and its people,” the complaint said.

It said the Public Service Commission can allow utilities to keep investing in fossil fuels or encourage them to pursue “cleaner and ultimately less costly alternatives.”

But it said the PSC has “refused to recognize and regularly disregards” the costs of climate, such as smoke that hurts asthmatic children, floods that destroy homes, and anglers who can’t fish.

The groups include healthcare providers, youth organizations and clean energy and climate advocates.

Amy Cilimburg, with lead plaintiff Climate Smart Missoula, said the PSC’s failure to regulate with climate in mind affects the health of Montanans and their ability to afford power.

“When the PSC fails to consider climate change in its decisions, Montanans bear the high costs and risks that come with fossil-fuel electricity, as well as the unaffordable and unconstitutional effects of a changing climate,” Cilimburg said in a statement.

In February 2024, more than 40 organizations and businesses asked the PSC to address its “obligations to consider climate impacts,” but the PSC denied the request in September 2025 and again last month.

The PSC regulates monopoly utilities and is made up of five elected commissioners, all of whom are currently Republican.

The complaint asks the court to vacate the PSC’s decisions and find the commission has a constitutional responsibility to consider climate as part of the state’s obligation to “maintain and improve a clean and healthful environment.”

The PSC could not be reached for comment Thursday afternoon.

When the commission voted to deny the petition by the groups in 2025, its legal counsel said the PSC is an administrative agency, so it didn’t have the authority to do what the groups wanted — to declare the constitution requires the PSC to consider the adverse impacts of climate change.

Then-chief-legal-counsel Lucas Hamilton also said the constitutional right to a clean and healthful environment appears along other rights the PSC must consider, such as to pursue life’s basic necessities — including water service.

In a news release about the lawsuit, the groups said the PSC took nearly two-and-a-half years to make a decision on their petition but never addressed its substance.

In the meantime, the PSC was making “consequential decisions,” they said.

They pointed to the PSC’s decision to approve “NorthWestern Energy’s request to charge customers for the high construction and operation costs for the Yellowstone County Generating Station.”

In December 2024, the Montana Supreme Court affirmed the constitutional right to a clean and healthful environment includes “a stable climate system” in the historic Held vs. State of Montana decision.

In a statement, Sarah Lundquist, executive director of Families for a Livable Climate, said youth fought for their constitutional rights in the Held case and have been advocating “for climate justice” ever since.

Families for a Livable Climate is part of the lawsuit.

“Now it’s our turn,” Lundquist said. “The Public Service Commission has enormous influence over Montana’s energy future, and we must ensure climate change is at the center of its decisions. It is our responsibility as adults to protect the future our kids deserve.”

Groups filing lawsuit

Earthjustice and Western Environmental Law Center represent Climate Smart Missoula, Citizens for Clean Energy, Earthworks, Families for a Livable Climate, Forward Montana, Helena Hunters and Anglers, Helena Interfaith Climate Advocates, Montana Chapter of the American Academy of Pediatrics, Montana Environmental Information Center, Montana Health and Climate, Montana Public Interest Research Group, Montana Renewable Energy Association, NW Energy Coalition, Park County Environmental Council, Renewable Northwest, Sierra Club Montana Chapter, and 350 Montana in the lawsuit.
