title: Why does it take 60 countries to build a single car? - Dagens.com
description:
From raw lithium mined in Chile to microchips stamped in Taiwan, it takes a massive, fragile supply chain spanning dozens of countries to build a single modern vehicle.
A single car might be designed in Munich, assembled in South Carolina, wired with electronics from Taiwan, and powered by a battery cell forged in China.
Stellantis—the conglomerate behind Jeep, Dodge, and Peugeot—explicitly notes that its direct supply chain spans more than 60 different countries.
The electric battery bottleneck The transition to electric vehicles has made this international web even more complex, largely due to the intense geographical concentration of battery manufacturing.
But the obvious downside to relying on 60 different countries for a single product is extreme vulnerability.
text:
The badge on your car’s grille is a marketing illusion. From raw lithium mined in Chile to microchips stamped in Taiwan, it takes a massive, fragile supply chain spanning dozens of countries to build a single modern vehicle.

When you buy a German luxury sedan, a Japanese crossover, or an American pickup truck, the badge on the grille implies a clear national origin. But that badge is a marketing sleight of hand.

According to a breakdown by Motor1, identifying the true origin of a modern vehicle is nearly impossible. A single car might be designed in Munich, assembled in South Carolina, wired with electronics from Taiwan, and powered by a battery cell forged in China. The family car is no longer a product of a single factory; it is the final output of a fragile, interconnected manufacturing web that spans the globe.

The assembly line is just the last stop

Automotive manufacturing operates on a massive tier system. Automakers rarely build their own brakes, seats, or wiring harnesses from scratch. Instead, they purchase complete sub-assemblies from Tier 1 suppliers, who in turn buy sensors, plastics, and microchips from Tier 2 and Tier 3 suppliers scattered across different continents.

The sheer scale of this logistics network is staggering. Stellantis—the conglomerate behind Jeep, Dodge, and Peugeot—explicitly notes that its direct supply chain spans more than 60 different countries.

This global dispersion completely skews the concept of domestic manufacturing. As highlighted by the 2026 Cars.com American-Made Index, a vehicle physically assembled in the United States routinely relies on engines, transmissions, and critical electronics manufactured overseas. Stamping “Made in the USA” on the door jamb often just means the final bolts were tightened there.

The electric battery bottleneck

The transition to electric vehicles has made this international web even more complex, largely due to the intense geographical concentration of battery manufacturing.

While a traditional gas engine can be cast and assembled regionally, an EV battery requires specialized minerals that cross multiple borders before they ever reach an assembly plant. Lithium is sourced heavily from Australia and Chile, cobalt is mined in the Democratic Republic of Congo, and nickel comes primarily from Indonesia.

But the true bottleneck happens during refinement and cell production. According to the International Energy Agency’s Global EV Outlook 2026, China currently accounts for roughly 70 percent of all electric car production and a staggering 80 percent of global battery-cell manufacturing. That means even if an EV is assembled in Michigan or Berlin, its core propulsion system is fundamentally tied to Chinese manufacturing.

A highly vulnerable network

Automakers utilize this sprawling global strategy to secure competitive pricing and build vehicles at an unprecedented scale. But the obvious downside to relying on 60 different countries for a single product is extreme vulnerability.

Dear Editor: A GOP representative recently called renewable energy rebates “radical,” stating, “These costly regulations threaten our energy supply and drive up prices.”

While it makes no sense how wind and sun, which are not subject to volatile markets and don’t need to be repeatedly extracted and transported, threaten energy supply, it got me questioning how “costly” renewable rebates compare to fossil fuel subsidies. So I Googled “How much did it cost tax payers to subsidize oil and gas in the Big Beautiful Bill?" Here is what it said:

“The 'BBB' adds ~$3.5-$4 billion annually in new subsidies for the oil and gas industry, increasing federal payouts to the fossil fuel industry to $34 billion per year including existing subsidies. Over the next decade, it provides $40-$80 billion in new tax breaks and benefits for fossil fuel companies.

"Key giveaways:

"$1.1 billion allowing companies to deduct drilling costs from the Corporate Alternative Minimum Tax.

"$7 billion by cutting the methane fee.

"$6 billion from reduced oil and gas royalty rates.

"$50.2 billion for carbon oxide sequestration tax credits.

"$65 billion for bonus depreciation.”

But they cut incentives for rooftop solar and other energy-saving credits for everyday Americans. Which could save us billions in oil wars — I mean, you can't invade the Sun. And, by the way, renewable infrastructure is cheaper.

Meanwhile, during Line 5 reroute construction, Canadian pipeline company Enbridge has reported six spills of gas liquids, diesel, hydraulic fluid and hydrocarbons, 10 frac-outs, built an unpermitted and unapproved bypass, and breached an aquifer — without accountability. Who’s radical?

Yvonne Besyk

Salem

text:
Qcells announced plans to launch new versions of its residential solar panel series featuring U.S.-made aluminum frames by the end of 2026.

The updated residential product offerings, which include the company’s Q.Tron AC and Q.Peak Duo AC lines, will incorporate aluminum frames extruded, anodized, and fabricated at supplier Aluko Group’s integrated facility in Halls, Tennessee. The initiative is aimed at helping residential installers and third-party ownership TPO providers qualify for the Investment Tax Credit ITC domestic content bonus adder.

Under the Treasury Department’s domestic content guidance, solar hardware must meet specific domestic manufacturing thresholds to qualify for the 10% tax credit bonus. Qcells noted that keeping all three core stages of frame manufacturing, including extrusion, anodization, and fabrication, within the United States provides greater clarity for installers and financing partners when evaluating compliance.

The domestic frame offering comes as the statutory domestic content threshold for clean energy projects begins stepping up toward 55% for projects commencing construction in 2027.

“Through this partnership to produce modules with domestic frames, we are furthering our commitment to U.S. manufacturing, supporting clean, affordable energy and giving our customers the certainty they need to qualify projects for the domestic content bonus,” said Il Hyeong No, head of Qcells North America’s residential business.

Supply chain localized in Tennessee

Aluko Group’s manufacturing plant in Lauderdale County, Tennessee, is expected to reach full commercial production by the end of 2026. Once operational, the plant will have a planned annual capacity to manufacture enough frames to support 4 GW of solar modules.

Aluko plans to invest more than $107 million into the facility over five years, creating 285 full-time jobs. The company operates what it describes as the only facility in the U.S. performing all three major frame production steps under one roof.

“By carrying out extrusion, anodizing, and fabrication here in the United States, we are delivering a product that offers transparency and confidence at every step of the process,” said Jinwoo Park, president of Aluko Group.

The move expands Qcells’ broader domestic manufacturing push across its vertically integrated operations in Dalton and Cartersville, Georgia, where the company operates large-scale module and component assembly operations.

authors: Alexis Papazoglou, empirical finance, corporate governance, corporate social responsibility, spans applications of accounting, Energy Policy, Environmental Policy
description:

text:
Recent energy crises have shown the degree to which Britain is exposed to global events. But thanks to advances in renewable energy technology, such as solar panels, Britain’s homes are increasingly decentralising the energy system, and becoming less reliant on oil and gas price fluctuations, argues Erhan Kilincarslan.

Enjoying this post? Then sign up to our newsletter and receive a weekly roundup of all our articles.

For most of the past century, British homes had a straightforward relationship with the energy system. They consumed electricity generated elsewhere, paid monthly bills and had little control over either the source or the price of their energy. That relationship is beginning to change.

Across the UK, a growing number of homeowners are installing rooftop solar panels, home batteries and smart energy technologies that allow them to generate, store and manage electricity themselves. In doing so, homes are evolving from passive consumers into active participants in Britain’s energy system.

The implications extend far beyond lower electricity bills. They could change the economics of home ownership itself.

The solar panel boom

The growing interest in household solar is no coincidence. The cost of photovoltaic (PV) systems has fallen substantially over the past decade as manufacturing has expanded and the technology has become more efficient. At the same time, government policies, including zero per cent VAT on eligible residential solar installations and the Smart Export Guarantee, which allows households to receive payments for surplus electricity exported to the grid, have strengthened the financial case for investing in rooftop solar.

Recent evidence suggests that demand remains exceptionally strong. Britain recorded a record 269,000 solar installations in 2025, the highest annual total on record, with rooftop systems accounting for more than 95 per cent of new installations. At the same time, interest in home battery systems has accelerated as households seek greater control over their energy costs and reduce their dependence on the grid.

The UK government is moving forward with plans to introduce low-cost plug-in solar panels that can be installed on balconies, terraces and other small outdoor spaces.

Technology is also expanding beyond traditional rooftop systems. The UK government is moving forward with plans to introduce low-cost plug-in solar panels that can be installed on balconies, terraces and other small outdoor spaces, potentially extending the benefits of solar generation to millions of renters and flat owners who have traditionally been excluded from the market. If widely adopted, these systems could broaden access to household renewable energy and accelerate the shift towards more decentralised electricity generation.

By lowering installation costs and reducing the need for home ownership, plug-in solar could broaden participation in Britain’s energy transition in much the same way that rooftop solar transformed owner-occupied housing over the past decade. Yet the growing popularity of household solar cannot be explained by falling costs alone.

The energy crisis

The past few years have exposed how vulnerable British households remain to global energy markets. Russia’s invasion of Ukraine triggered Europe’s worst energy crisis in decades, sending wholesale gas prices to record levels and sharply increasing household energy bills across the UK. The episode served as a stark reminder that events taking place thousands of miles away can have immediate consequences for domestic finances.

More recently, renewed tensions in the Middle East have once again unsettled global oil and gas markets, highlighting the continued sensitivity of energy prices to geopolitical developments. Although Britain imports relatively little energy directly from the region, it remains exposed through interconnected international markets, where disruptions to global supply can feed through into higher wholesale prices and ultimately household energy bills.

For many homeowners, these repeated shocks have reinforced a simple lesson: generating at least some electricity at home offers not only environmental benefits but also a degree of protection against increasingly uncertain global energy markets.

This represents an important shift in thinking. Solar panels are increasingly viewed not simply as environmental investments but as financial assets capable of reducing long-term household expenditure and improving resilience against future price shocks. The transformation extends even further when battery storage enters the equation.

Rather than exporting surplus electricity during the day and buying it back in the evening, homeowners can increasingly store their own electricity for later use or combine battery systems with smart tariffs that charge when electricity is cheap and discharge when prices rise. The result is a home that no longer simply consumes electricity but increasingly generates, stores and manages its own energy.

Energy economists increasingly describe households equipped with rooftop solar and battery storage as “prosumers” because they both produce and consume electricity, reflecting a fundamental shift in the relationship between homes and the energy system. This transformation has wider implications for Britain’s electricity system.

Decentralising the energy system and transforming the home

Traditionally, electricity has been generated at large centralised power stations before being transmitted across the country through the national grid. As more households generate and store their own electricity, the energy system is becoming increasingly decentralised, with homes playing a more active role in balancing supply and demand. Millions of properties producing relatively small amounts of electricity can collectively become part of the country’s energy infrastructure, reducing pressure on the grid and improving system flexibility while supporting the wider integration of renewable energy.

As more households generate and store their own electricity, the energy system is becoming increasingly decentralised, with homes playing a more active role in balancing supply and demand.

This is not merely a theoretical possibility. In countries such as Germany and Australia, rooftop solar already accounts for a substantial share of electricity generation, demonstrating how decentralised energy production can complement conventional power generation. Britain appears to be moving steadily in the same direction as household solar and battery adoption continues to expand.

The housing market may eventually reflect this transition. Just as buyers routinely consider school catchment areas, broadband speeds or insulation standards, energy performance is becoming an increasingly important consideration for many households. Properties equipped with rooftop solar, battery storage and high energy efficiency ratings may become more attractive as buyers seek lower running costs and greater protection against future energy price volatility.

Of course, rooftop solar will not solve every challenge facing Britain’s energy system. Not every property is suitable, batteries remain expensive and large-scale investment in electricity networks, offshore wind and nuclear generation will remain essential.

But the cumulative impact of millions of household decisions should not be underestimated.

For decades, British homes have been viewed primarily as places to live and stores of wealth. Increasingly, they are becoming something else as well: energy assets capable of generating income, reducing costs and strengthening resilience against future energy shocks.

The next stage of Britain’s energy transition may depend not only on giant infrastructure projects but also on millions of small investments made by ordinary homeowners. If that trend continues, some of the country’s next generation of power stations may already be standing on suburban streets across Britain.

name: American Energy
title: Trump Tried to Defund Them, But Green Banks Keep Financing Clean Energy Projects
authors: Jeff St. John, Rachel Santarsiero, Anna Rogers, Martha Pskowski, Marianne Lavelle, Stephanie Mencimer, Sophie Hurwitz, Adam Rogers, Inae Oh, Mother Jones
description:
The report includes summaries from about 70 case studies of the work that’s been helped along by financing from green banks.
The technologies behind the projects that green banks finance aren’t risky in and of themselves, Adler said.
Green banks are also sharing technical resources to help each other lower financing costs, Adler said.
Montgomery County Green Bank in Maryland has blended financial technology support and layered financing to make home renewable-energy and energy-efficiency improvements more affordable.
But as the Green Bank 50 report highlights, many green banks operate on budgets of less than $2 million per year.
text:
This story was originally published by Canary Media and is reproduced here as part of the Climate Desk collaboration.

A community solar project built for New Orleans’ oldest historically Black Catholic order of nuns. An all-electric affordable housing complex in Salt Lake City. A program offering low-income Maryland households inexpensive loans for rooftop solar and energy efficiency.

These are just some of the recent projects financed in the US by green banks, entities that use public funds to boost lending for clean energy and climate-adaptation efforts in tough-to-finance sectors. And they’ve done it even as the Trump administration’s clawbacks of federal climate funding force them to scale down their Biden-era plans.

“We’ve continued to move capital in very challenging times,” said Dan Adler, executive director of the U.S. Green Bank 50, a coalition of 56 green banks and other organizations. To fill in the gaps, they’ve sought out financing partners ranging from commercial banks and credit unions to corporate and philanthropic funders. ​“We’re making a virtue out of a necessity,” he said.

The Green Bank 50 laid out what its members have been able to accomplish over the last two years in its inaugural impact report, released in September, which collected data from 48 green banks nationwide. Over the course of 2024 and 2025, those organizations put about $1.4 billion of their own capital, along with $11 billion in additional private capital, into more than 40,000 projects.

The report includes summaries from about 70 case studies of the work that’s been helped along by financing from green banks. Some are large-scale projects, like the $10 million community solar array being built on land owned by the Sisters of the Holy Family in New Orleans, which has committed to providing up to 350 low-income households with reduced utility bills using the solar power it will generate. Loans for that project came from the nonprofit Inclusive Prosperity Capital, the United Church of Christ Cornerstone Fund, and Pelican Community Capital, which is a Louisiana community development lender affiliated with the Baton Rouge Area Foundation.

Inclusive Prosperity Capital is among the many green banks that has had to make do without promised grants from the Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund. It won $249 million from the program, which was created by the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act and provided $20 billion in green bank grants and another $7 billion in Solar for All grants. The Trump administration terminated both programs last year.

“We had projects with financial commitments, training courses for developers and lenders, a predevelopment mentorship program, staff hired and trained, and more,” Inclusive Prosperity Capital CEO Kerry O’Neill said. ​“We hope recent court decisions will result in our return to this important work.”

In August, a federal judge ruled the administration’s freeze of the $20 billion to be unlawful, and this month, two separate federal judges have ruled the Solar for All termination illegal. But the administration has yet to release the funds, and is expected to appeal to the US Supreme Court.

The loss of federal funds has severely curtailed the scale of work planned by the Green Bank 50 partners. Climate United Fund, a partnership that was awarded $7 billion but had its funds frozen, has been unable to follow through on plans to finance U.S.-built electric trucks, energy-efficiency and clean energy upgrades, and loans to Native American–led clean energy projects.

The 48 green banks surveyed in the impact report have about $6.8 billion in their funding pipelines. But Adler conceded that the loss of federal funds has put some worthy projects out of reach. ​“When money is coming down from the sky at basically 0 percent [interest], you can do very interesting projects—and we’re prepared to do that again,” he said.

“But now we have to focus on tight discipline with private capital as our key partner,” he said. ​“You can’t do the higher-risk projects, so you work on what’s addressable.” The goal, he said, is to find projects that are still considered too risky or unproven for private-sector lenders, ​“but if you do it with green banks a few times, then private capital can take over.”

That’s in fact the founding principle of the green bank movement, he noted. Some of the first green banks formed in Connecticut and New York state in the 2010s have become significant drivers of private-sector lending for building energy efficiency and electrification, solar for schools and municipalities, and other categories of investment important to meeting state and local climate policies.

The technologies behind the projects that green banks finance aren’t risky in and of themselves, Adler said. But the classes of customers that green banks work with—such as affordable housing providers and solar developers working in low-income communities—can be. ​“Whether they’ve been redlined out of the traditional capital markets, or the deals are not as big as traditional lenders are motivated to engage in, we’re taking on the credit risks and the deal structure and size risks,” he explained.

Green banks have continued to find ways to reduce those risks. One method is bundling funds from multiple lenders, which reduces an individual lender’s risk. That’s how Inclusive Prosperity Capital and its partners financed the community solar project for the Sisters of the Holy Family.

It’s also how the New York City Energy Efficiency Corp., a 16-year-old green bank, supported a 396-unit, all-electric affordable housing project in Salt Lake City. The green bank worked with Utah nonprofit SustainEnergyFinance to set up a $4.5 predevelopment loan—a form of financing that can be hard to underwrite for first-time projects—so that the project’s developer could move into the next phases of construction.

Green banks are also sharing technical resources to help each other lower financing costs, Adler said. He cited the Solar and Energy Loan Fund, a Florida-based green bank that has financed nearly $80 million in home energy-efficiency, solar, and storm-hardening projects. That organization has developed a platform, now being used by 13 other green banks and similar lenders across the country, that standardizes much of the underwriting and loan-processing expertise it’s built up over the past decade, said David Graber, the green bank’s chief of staff.

“We provide the back office and the capital. Partners bring the local trust and the projects,” Graber explained. The Solar and Energy Loan Fund estimates that each lending partner on the platform avoids hundreds of thousands of dollars a year in costs it would otherwise incur running a full lending operation on its own.

Montgomery County Green Bank in Maryland has blended financial technology support and layered financing to make home renewable-energy and energy-efficiency improvements more affordable. In March 2026, the organization launched a $4 million initiative that offers households low-interest loans for rooftop solar, heat pumps, and other projects.

Qualifying homeowners can access solar loans with a subsidized interest rate of 2.99 percent for the first 15 years, with a higher rate applying afterward, said Rokas Beresniovas, the green bank’s head of partnerships and business development.

As utility bills rise, mobilizing investment for these kinds of efforts is more important than ever, Adler said. But as the Green Bank 50 report highlights, many green banks operate on budgets of less than $2 million per year.

“We could do a lot more,” he said. ​“But we’re looking at what we’re able to finance.”

text:
The ever-burning flame at the Lena Road Landfill in east Manatee County will be going dark about 18 months from now.

The flame is actually a flare stack that safely releases excess gas from the mounds of buried, decomposing waste, but Manatee County is moving ahead with plans to capture that gas and turn it into a commodity.

A groundbreaking ceremony was held at the landfill Oct. 9 for a $50 million renewable natural gas facility. At 3333 Lena Road, the landfill is east of Interstate 75 and south of State Road 64.

The facility is the result of a partnership between Manatee County, Johnson Controls and Nopetro Energy. The county provided the land.

Johnson and Nopetro are funding the $50 million project, with Johnson serving as the integrated developer and Nopetro serving as the owner and operator of the plant.

Charles McGinnis, a vice president for Johnson Controls, says Manatee County is guaranteed to collect at least $883,000 in annual royalties once the plant is operational, and that number could increase up to $2.1 million.

In addition to the gas itself, the plant will generate energy credits, which can also be sold.

The Environmental Protection Agency explains renewable energy monetization on its website: A credit is issued for every megawatt-hour of electricity generated and delivered to the electric grid from a renewable energy resource. Selling credits generates revenue, but the seller forfeits “the ability to make any claims about ‘using’ renewable energy.”

For local residents, the project offers better air quality because it will reduce the emissions from the biogas that’s currently being flared into the atmosphere at the Lena Road Landfill.

The plant is expected to eliminate the amount of carbon dioxide that, in comparison, would be produced by 5.3 million gallons of car gasoline each year.

“It’s environmentally great for everybody,” Manatee County Commissioner Mike Rahn says. “It helps bring dollars back into Manatee County, and we get green tax credits that will help bring down some of the costs that we have to pay at the landfill.”

He notes some county equipment at the landfill can be powered using the gas, too.

Rahn says more counties are starting to capture their biogas instead of wasting it.

According to McGinnis, the value of biogas is much higher than it’s been in previous years.

“Because the value of renewable natural gas has increased substantially, now projects have become financially viable that weren’t before,” McGinnis says. “Manatee County is one of those counties that’s at the forefront of innovation, and they saw this happening. They were already taking some of the renewable natural gas and using it themselves in their biosolids drying process.”

According to the American Biogas Council, landfills are the largest source of captured biogas in the United States, “driving record investment” in renewable natural gas production.

The “Biogas in America 2026” report states, “The nation’s 598 landfill gas capture systems provide about three-quarters of all biogas captured in the U.S. and produce 64% of the nation’s renewable natural gas.”

Additionally, developers brought 20 new landfill gas projects online in 2025. One of those projects was led by Nopetro in Vero Beach, in Indian River County.

A year later, Nopetro Energy CEO and co-founder Jorge Herrera says the operation is going so well that Indian River County has been making improvements to its landfill to produce and capture more gas.

Manatee County, company officials say, can do the same.

To simplify a complex system, Herrera says to picture straws. The straws have holes in them, and they can be stuck into the ground throughout the landfill.

More straws can collect more gas. As the organics start to decompose, the molecules get sucked into the straws and moved to the plant to be refined into usable gas

Currently, the majority of the gas produced at the landfill is being burned off into the atmosphere.

Indian River County has a population of about 174,000. Nopetro estimates that its Vero Beach plant can provide as much as 80% of the natural gas used in the county.

Herrera says Manatee County’s production will be about 20% higher, but its population is also 2.5 times that of Indian River. A ballpark estimate, he says, is the Lena Road plant could meet about a third of the county’s natural gas demands.

In 20 years, Manatee County will have the option to either extend its contract with Nopetro or take ownership of the facility. However, the latter is not likely.

“These are very complex assets,” Herrera says. “From that perspective, I don’t think I’ve witnessed across the country an example where a government has taken on the responsibility of a production plant like this because it’s so specialized. It’s basically like saying, ‘Take an oil refinery and run it.’”

Nopetro has been in business for 17 years.

“We didn’t need to become an energy company ourselves,” Commissioner George Kruse says. “We wouldn’t know what we’re doing. We needed to find the right partners, and Petro Energy is bringing its renewable natural gas experience. Johnson Controls helped develop the project and its performance strategy. Mead & Hunt is designing and constructing the facility, and Manatee County is bringing an asset that was here all along. That’s exactly what a public-private partnership is supposed to be.”

Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins (left) speaks with Shyam Sankar, of Palantir, and David Friedberg, of The Production Board, during the launch of the America.gov on Sept. 29 in Washington.

U.S. Secretary of Agriculture Brooke L. Rollins announced a historic $3.3 billion loan to Oglethorpe Power Corporation to help finance its Smarr Combined-Cycle electric generating facility in Monroe County, Georgia, during a visit to the construction site.

This loan is the largest ever delivered in the history of USDA Rural Development’s Rural Utilities Service and comes at a critical time for investing in U.S. energy. As stated by President Trump, the United States is experiencing a surge in electricity demand from rapid technological advancements. This project strengthens the nation’s electrical grid, and lower-cost financing will help keep electricity affordable for Georgia families.

“Historic times call for historic actions, and this tremendous investment in America’s electric power grid is evidence of President Trump’s focus on powering our nation forward,” said Secretary Brooke L. Rollins. “Great things are happening with our rural electric cooperatives nationwide, and Oglethorpe Power is one example in Georgia through this project, which will generate reliable electricity, create jobs, and bring significant investment to rural America.”



Oglethorpe Power is a generation cooperative owned by 38 electric distribution cooperatives that serve nearly 5 million people across Georgia. It supplies wholesale power through a diverse energy portfolio that includes natural gas, coal, nuclear and hydroelectric resources. Oglethorpe services 157 of Georgia’s 159 counties either in part of in total. The Tennessee Valley Authority provides service to 12 northern counties in the state.

“This historic loan will allow us to build the reliable generation Georgia families, farms and businesses need at a lower cost, helping our member cooperatives keep electricity affordable for the communities they serve,” said Annalisa Bloodworth, President and CEO of Oglethorpe Power. “We are grateful to USDA and RUS for their longstanding partnership and for providing the lower-cost financing that helps electric cooperatives make critical investments in reliable, affordable power.”

description:

According to KPIX, Governor Gavin Newsom recently signed the Clean Energy Choice Act, introduced by Assemblymember Marc Berman (D-Menlo Park).
The Clean Energy Dream Home features a range of appliances that can replace gas-powered systems, including heat pumps for heating, cooling, and hot water, an induction cooktop, and an electric fireplace.

“Except this one produces no pollution.” Heat pumps were another major feature of the display.
text:
On the heels of new legislation aimed at helping Californians switch from gas to electric-powered homes, a Silicon Valley-based agency is bringing its “Clean Energy Dream Home” showroom to communities around the Bay Area.

During SF’s Fleet Week last week, a 18-by-8-foot mobile showroom created by Silicon Valley Clean Energy (SVCE) was set up along the Embarcadero, as KPIX reports. The display, powered by a Ford electric pickup truck, offers visitors a look at electric appliances designed to reduce household pollution and slash energy bills, while making homes healthier and more comfortable.

The showcase comes as California makes it easier for homeowners to ditch gas. According to KPIX, Governor Gavin Newsom recently signed the Clean Energy Choice Act, introduced by Assemblymember Marc Berman (D-Menlo Park). It requires utilities to offer financial incentives to homeowners who disconnect from gas and electrify their homes when gas service line repairs are scheduled.

“This is the all-electric home of the future,” said Nik Kaestner, senior building decarbonization coordinator for the San Francisco Environment Department, speaking to KPIX.

The Clean Energy Dream Home features a range of appliances that can replace gas-powered systems, including heat pumps for heating, cooling, and hot water, an induction cooktop, and an electric fireplace.

Kaestner demonstrated to KPIX that the induction stove, which uses electromagnets to heat cookware directly instead of burning gas, brings water to a boil considerably faster than a gas stove, keeping energy from escaping into the kitchen.

Electric fireplaces are also a source of clean energy.

“If you have an all-electric home, you may still want the comfort and warmth from a fireplace,” Kaestner said, speaking to KPIX. “Except this one produces no pollution.”

Heat pumps were another major feature of the display. The systems use electricity to transfer heat rather than generate it through combustion, allowing a single unit to heat and cool a home. Heat pump water heaters can also replace conventional gas models.

Kaestner said reducing indoor pollution is one of the central advantages of electrification.

“The most important benefit for an all-electric home is that it’s a healthier home because there is no gas combustion happening within your four walls,” he told KPIX.

Pacific Gas and Electric says customers can save an average of $714 per year by replacing gas heating systems with heat pump technology, as California moves away from new natural gas heaters, as KPIX reports.

Homeowners can also search for available rebates and incentives through Switch Is On, BayREN, and California’s home energy programs.

text:
The United States is making an unprecedented attempt to revive three shuttered nuclear plants to meet rising energy demand, including from large-scale data centers.

No commercial nuclear reactor is known to have resumed generating electricity after beginning the decommissioning process that takes one out of service, though some reactors have restarted after long outages.

The Department of Energy is lending as much as $4.4 billion to restart the Palisades Power Plant in Michigan, the Crane Clean Energy Center on Pennsylvania's Three Mile Island and the Duane Arnold Energy Center in Iowa to restore a combined 2.25 gigawatts of electricity, which can power roughly 2 million homes and businesses. All three of the plants closed before their licenses expired, largely because the electricity they produced was considered too expensive.

Not anymore. Two of the plants have contracts with Big Tech companies that will pay a premium to get large amounts of carbon-free energy for data centers. President Donald Trump's administration is pushing hard to deploy nuclear power for artificial intelligence and manufacturing. It's also lending billions of dollars for upgrades to produce more electricity from currently operating nuclear plants.

Restarting a reactor is a fairly quick way to get a lot of electricity, and it's cheaper than building a new, large reactor, said nuclear engineering expert Todd Allen.

"There's a demand in the country for more power," he said. "You have these assets that were previously hooked up. They were previously operable, and you can relatively quickly get them generating electricity again, compared to your other possibilities. For anyone who wants zero carbon, nuclear provides that. For the Trump administration, which really wants nuclear, this fits that story also."

Restarting reactor like restoring a car

Allen compared restarting a decommissioned nuclear plant to restarting a car that sat idle for a few years. The driver still needs a valid license and all the parts need to work correctly.

"That's what they're trying to do with these nuclear plants, but it's a much bigger, complicated system," said Allen, associate dean for research at the University of Michigan's College of Engineering.

With a nuclear plant, the owner has to bring nuclear workers back and ensure their training is current, make sure everything is working and that maintenance is up to date, ensure they have enough fuel and ask regulators to restore their operating license, he added.

Allen said it's a lot to track, but it's relatively straightforward.

Expert says restarts are risky

Edwin Lyman, at the Union of Concerned Scientists, said the taxpayer money being used should go toward addressing safety risks. For example, most U.S. plants were built between 1970 and 1990 and designed to withstand natural disasters of that era, said Lyman, director of nuclear power safety at UCS. But climate change is making extreme weather events more frequent and severe.

"It's possible, if they set the right level of safety and spend the necessary funds to meet that, they could restore these plants to operable condition," he said. "That's not happening at this point."

title: The Subsidy Cliff and Your Power Bill: Wind, Solar, Storage and the Grid
description:
The average residential price went from 11.54¢ to 16.48¢ per kilowatt-hour, up 43% (EIA; EIA 2024 Table 4).
California curtailed about 4 million MWh of wind and solar in 2024, up 29%, and 93% of it was solar (EIA).
Solar, wind and batteries connect through power electronics, or inverters, which do not provide inertia on their own and must be programmed to ride through disturbances.
Download the data: every figure in the charts and tables is in “The Subsidy Cliff and Your Power Bill – Wind, Solar, Storage and the Grid – Data.xlsx.” Appendix A.
“High” states had a 2024 wind+solar share of 35% or more (6 states); “low” states under 5% (16 states).
text:
Washington spent billions to put wind, solar and batteries on the grid, and the biggest wave yet is arriving right as the tax credits run out. Here is what the data says about your bill, what it does not say, and why grid stability is the question to watch.

By Stuart Turley, host of the Energy News Beat podcast • Published Oct. 17, 2026 • Market and news items as of Oct. 16, 2026, 10 a.m. CT • Analysis and opinion; Stu’s views are labeled as his • Not investment advice

Start with your wallet

As of EIA Short-Term Energy Outlook, Oct. 6, 2026 (next update Nov. 10)

Pull out your last power bill. By EIA’s forecast, the average American household will spend about $1,931 on electricity this year, up from about $1,710 in 2024 (EIA STEO; ENB calculation, price × usage). That is about $221 more a year, or roughly $18 a month, and EIA expects another bump in 2027. Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (LBNL) and The Brattle Group put the climb more starkly: residential prices are up about 33% since 2019 in nominal terms, and the typical bill is about $480 a year higher (LBNL/Brattle, July 2026).

Over the same years, the grid changed. In 2010, wind and solar made 2.3% of U.S. electricity. By 2024 they made 15.6% (EIA state generation data; ENB calculation). The average residential price went from 11.54¢ to 16.48¢ per kilowatt-hour, up 43% (EIA; EIA 2024 Table 4). And federal taxpayers helped pay for the build-out: EIA counted about $11.1 billion of federal support for solar and wind in fiscal 2022 alone, nearly three times the 2016 level (EIA subsidy report; ENB sum).

Stu’s thesis, as he frames it: the more wind, solar and storage we bolt onto the grid, the more consumers pay for the grid, and the problem gets bigger, not smaller, when the subsidies end, because the projects keep coming fast and someone still has to keep the lights on. That is Stu’s view. This article tests it against the best data we could find, including the studies that disagree with him. Where the evidence backs him up, we say so. Where it does not, we say that too.

Part 1. How big are the subsidies?

The credits in plain English

As of IRS and Federal Register guidance through Aug. 2025; statute as enacted July 4, 2025

For three decades, wind got a production tax credit (PTC), paid per kilowatt-hour for ten years, and solar got an investment tax credit (ITC), a percentage off the cost of building. The 2022 Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) replaced them, starting in 2025, with “technology-neutral” versions: Section 45Y (production) and Section 48E (investment). Any zero-emission power source could claim them (CRS).

How much per kWh? For 2025, the 45Y credit is 0¢ per kWh for projects that meet prevailing-wage and apprenticeship rules, and 0.6¢ for those that do not (Federal Register, Aug. 25, 2025). For context, that 3¢ is close to a fifth of what the average household pays for a kWh.

How much off the build cost? The 48E investment credit is generally 30% with labor rules met, plus possible 10-point bonuses for domestic content and “energy communities” (CRS).

Storage got its own credit. Since 2023, stand-alone batteries can claim the investment credit without being paired with solar (CRS). That is one reason battery construction exploded.

Developers can sell their credits for cash to companies with tax bills. The marketplace Crux (a tax-credit broker) estimates about $42 billion of credits changed hands this way in 2025, up from about $32 billion in 2024 (Crux; figures as reported by Crux). The One Big Beautiful Bill kept transferability but barred sales to “specified foreign entities” (SEIA fact sheet, solar trade group).

What the One Big Beautiful Bill changed

As of statute signed July 4, 2025; IRS Notice 2025-42 issued Aug. 15, 2025

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (Public Law 119-21) did not repeal the credits for everyone. It put wind and solar on a short fuse and left most other technologies on a long one (OBBBA Sec. 70513; CRS).

Rule Wind and solar Battery storage and other zero-emission sources Start-construction deadline July 4, 2026 (one year after enactment) No near-term deadline If construction started late Must be placed in service by Dec. 31, 2027 Not applicable Continuity safe harbor Projects that began by July 4, 2026 generally have 4 calendar years to finish Same Phase-down Credits end for late projects 100% for construction starting in 2033, 75% in 2034, 50% in 2035, 0% after Foreign-entity (FEOC) limits Apply from 2026 Apply from 2026 Transferability Kept (not to specified foreign entities) Kept

Sources: OBBBA text; IRS Notice 2025-42; CRS IN12719; Taxpayers for Common Sense, a nonpartisan budget watchdog; SEIA, solar trade group.

Then Treasury tightened the screws. IRS Notice 2025-42 made the Physical Work Test the only way for most wind and solar projects to prove they started construction. The old “5% safe harbor,” where spending 5% of project cost counted as a start, was ended except for small solar (IRS Notice 2025-42). In plain English: you had to actually be building something, on site or at a factory under a binding contract, by July 4, 2026.

What it costs taxpayers: estimates before and after

As of JCT estimates of July 1, 2025 and Dec. 3, 2025; EIA subsidy report of Aug. 2023 (latest edition)

Before the cuts. When the IRA passed in 2022, the Joint Committee on Taxation (JCT) scored its energy credits at about $271 billion over ten years (CRS). The estimates then ballooned as companies used the credits faster than expected. A later CBO/JCT update put the energy credits near $786 billion for 2024–2033, as summarized by the Tax Foundation and cited by the libertarian Cato Institute, which also cites a Goldman Sachs estimate of $1.2 trillion (Cato). Academic modelers using EPRI’s model estimated about $780 billion through 2031 for the clean-electricity, carbon-capture and EV credits (MIT CEEPR/Brookings).

After the cuts. JCT estimated the One Big Beautiful Bill’s changes would save about $165.7 billion on the 48E investment credit and $24.9 billion on the 45Y production credit from fiscal 2025 to 2034, or roughly $190.6 billion together (JCT JCX-34-25; ENB sum). All of the bill’s energy-credit changes together saved about $499 billion (JCT). The Clean Air Task Force (an environmental group that supported the credits) says JCT now values the key clean-electricity credits at about $280 billion through 2034, versus about $490 billion in JCT’s 2023 score (CATF).

What is still being spent. The credits did not stop overnight. JCT’s December 2025 tax-expenditure tables show the main electricity credits (Sections 45, 45Y, 48 and 48E) costing about $27 billion in fiscal 2025 and peaking near $37 billion in 2026, before falling to about $12 billion by 2029, a five-year total of about $122 billion (JCT JCX-45-25; ENB sums). Those lines include some non-wind, non-solar projects, so read them as an upper bound for wind and solar.

What EIA counted. EIA’s last subsidy report covers fiscal 2016 to 2022. Federal support for all renewables roughly doubled, from $7.4 billion to $15.6 billion (2022 dollars). Solar got $7.5 billion and wind $3.6 billion in fiscal 2022 (EIA). EIA has not published a newer edition.

The other subsidy: state mandates and RECs

As of LBNL State Electricity Resource Standards data update, June 2026

Federal tax credits are only half the story. LBNL counts 27 states plus D.C. with renewable portfolio standards (RPS), and several more with clean-electricity standards. They require utilities to buy a rising share of renewable or clean power, usually by purchasing renewable energy certificates (RECs). Those costs land on your bill, not your tax return.

LBNL estimates RPS compliance costs averaged about 5% of retail electricity bills in RPS states. In seven states it was under 1%; in four it topped 10%, with Virginia the highest, at about 20% in LBNL’s state chart, and D.C., New Jersey and Massachusetts also high (LBNL). LBNL says the highest costs come from solar carve-outs.

REC prices vary widely. New England’s Class I RECs ran around $40 per MWh, and PJM Tier I RECs about $25 (LBNL).

“Carve-outs” that require in-state solar are the most expensive. The mandate-critical think tank Always On Energy Research found solar RECs (SRECs) costing $407/MWh in D.C., $337 in Massachusetts and $206 in New Jersey, and estimated the in-state solar mandates cost the average customer about $298 in New Jersey and $227 in Maryland (Always On; Energy Bad Boys). Those are an advocacy group’s calculations; we report them as theirs.

Plain-English takeaway: Taxpayers carry the federal credits. Ratepayers carry the state mandates. Either way, a household pays.

Part 2. Do more wind and solar mean higher bills?

The national picture: yes, they moved together

As of EIA 2024 annual data (latest complete state-level year)

Put the national numbers side by side and Stu’s instinct looks right. Every year from 2010 to 2024, the wind-and-solar share went up, and nearly every year, the average residential price went up. The correlation is r = 0.94, where 1.0 would be a perfect match (ENB calculation from EIA and EIA price data).

But here is the catch every statistics teacher warns about. Over the same years, the price of a gallon of milk, a pickup truck and a college degree also went up. General consumer prices rose about 44% from 2010 to 2024 (BLS CPI-U annual averages; ENB calculation), almost exactly as much as residential electricity. Two lines that both rise over time will always correlate. In fact, year-to-year changes in the two series correlate far more weakly (r ≈ 0.26, Fact Checker calculation), a sign the 0.94 mostly reflects two rising trends. To get closer to cause and effect, you have to compare places that added a lot of wind and solar with places that did not.

The state-by-state test: the link mostly disappears

As of EIA 2010 and 2024 state data

So we ran that test for all 50 states and D.C. We measured how much each state’s in-state wind-and-solar share rose from 2010 to 2024 and how much its average residential price rose (EIA generation; EIA 2010 prices; EIA 2024 prices; ENB calculation). The result: r = -0.04. That is no meaningful relationship, and if anything a slight tilt the other way. For 2019–2024 alone, the tilt is a bit stronger and still negative (r = -0.26).

State Wind + solar share 2010 → 2024 Residential price 2010 → 2024 Change Iowa 15.9% → 63.8% 10.4¢ → 13.4¢ +29% South Dakota 13.6% → 59.5% 9.0¢ → 12.9¢ +43% Kansas 7.1% → 51.9% 10.0¢ → 14.2¢ +41% Oklahoma 5.3% → 40.7% 9.1¢ → 12.2¢ +34% Texas 6.4% → 29.1% 11.6¢ → 14.9¢ +29% California 3.4% → 29.9% 14.8¢ → 32.0¢ +117% Massachusetts 0.1% → 11.0% 14.6¢ → 29.4¢ +101% United States 2.3% → 15.6% 11.5¢ → 16.5¢ +43%

Source: EIA state generation and price data; ENB calculation. Shares are in-state utility-scale generation; prices are nominal averages.

The six states where wind and solar made 35% or more of in-state generation in 2024 (Iowa, Kansas, South Dakota, Oklahoma, Colorado and New Mexico) averaged 13.6¢ per kWh and a 36% price rise since 2010. The 16 states under 5% averaged 17.0¢ and +39% (ENB calculation, simple averages of states).

Why would that be? The Plains states built wind because the wind is strong and the land is cheap, and much of it was built for economics, not to meet a mandate. Meanwhile, some of the biggest price jumps came in states with little wind or solar at home but other heavy costs: California’s wildfire liabilities and transmission, New England’s gas pipeline limits and mandates, and West Virginia’s and Kentucky’s coal-heavy utilities rebuilding and recovering costs.

What the state test cannot see. This is a simple test, and it has limits worth saying out loud. It counts power generated in a state, not power bought from neighbors, so Massachusetts looks “low renewable” even though it pays for offshore wind contracts and out-of-state RECs. It does not separate mandate-driven projects from market-driven ones. And it does not capture costs spread across a whole region, like PJM’s capacity market. So it does not disprove Stu’s thesis. It does say that “more wind and solar in a state means higher prices” is not what the raw state data shows.

Where the costs do show up: wires

As of EIA Today in Energy, Nov. 2024; LBNL/Brattle, July 2026

The money is moving into the poles and wires. EIA reports major utilities spent about $320 billion in 2023, up from $287 billion in 2003 (real dollars). Transmission spending nearly tripled to $27.7 billion, and distribution spending reached $50.9 billion. EIA says part of that is to replace aging equipment, harden the grid against storms and wildfires, and “manage the intermittency of renewable resources” (EIA).

LBNL and Brattle found transmission charges rose about 0.8¢/kWh in ISO New England, 0.6¢ in New York, and 0.4¢ in California and PJM from 2019 to 2025, partly to connect new renewable projects, while distribution costs pushed retail prices up in 22 states from 2024 to 2025 (LBNL/Brattle). Wind farms in West Texas and solar in the desert are far from cities, so somebody has to build the line to carry their power.

Capacity markets: PJM’s shock

As of PJM 2028/29 auction results, July 14, 2026

PJM runs the largest U.S. grid, serving about 67 million people in 13 states and D.C. Its capacity auction pays power plants to be available when needed. The clearing price went from $28.92 per megawatt-day for 2024/25 to $269.92, then hit the cap at $329.17, $333.44 and $325 (PJM 2024/25; PJM 2026/27; PJM 2027/28; PJM 2028/29). The 2028/29 auction cost about $16.4 billion and still came up 6,831 MW short of its reliability target (PJM).

Why is this relevant to wind and solar? Because of how PJM counts them. PJM rates each resource by its Effective Load Carrying Capability (ELCC), the share of its nameplate it can count on in the riskiest hours, which are increasingly winter mornings and evenings. For 2027/28, fixed-tilt solar gets 7%, tracking solar 8%, onshore wind 41% and a 4-hour battery 58%, versus 95% for nuclear and 74% for a gas combined-cycle plant (PJM ELCC). A 100 MW solar farm counts as about 7 or 8 MW of reliable capacity.

But be fair about who drove the price. PJM’s independent market monitor says data-center load drove about $6.3 billion, or 38%, of the 2028/29 auction cost, and $29.4 billion of $63.6 billion across the last four auctions (Utility Dive, quoting Monitoring Analytics). Firm plant retirements, slow interconnection and new accreditation rules also played a part. LBNL estimates capacity costs pushed average PJM wholesale costs up about 0.9¢/kWh in 2025 compared with 2024, with another 0.6¢ expected in 2026 (LBNL/Brattle). ENB has covered the strain in PJM’s emergency actions and the 76% bill jump.

Integration, balancing and curtailment

As of EIA, CAISO market monitor 2025 annual report, Xcel 2021 study

Balancing costs exist but are usually modest per MWh. Xcel Energy’s Colorado study (a utility that owns wind and solar) estimated integration costs of about $2.84/MWh for wind and $0.72/MWh for solar in its base case, rising with gas prices (Xcel).

Curtailment is the tell that the grid is saturated at midday. California curtailed about 4 million MWh of wind and solar in 2024, up 29%, and 93% of it was solar (EIA). The CAISO market monitor reported downward dispatch of wind and solar up another 22% in 2025 (CAISO DMM). When power is thrown away, its fixed costs are still paid.

Gas still has to stay on. EIA notes California keeps some gas plants online to meet reliability standards even when solar is abundant, which is part of why curtailment happens (EIA).

What high-renewable places abroad pay

As of exchange rates Oct. 16, 2026 (ECB); prices as noted

Look overseas and the high-renewable examples are expensive. German households pay about 37.0 euro cents per kWh, roughly 41.6¢ in U.S. terms; grid fees alone are 9.24 cents, and taxes and levies about a third of the bill (BDEW, German utility association; ECB; ENB conversion). Germany moved its renewable surcharge off power bills and onto the federal budget, which paid about €16.5 billion of the €18.5 billion that went to renewable generators in 2025 (pv magazine). The cost did not disappear; it moved to taxpayers.

In Great Britain, the price cap from Oct. 1 is 26.32p per kWh, about 35.1¢, excluding VAT (suspended on electricity from October 2026 to March 2027), plus a daily standing charge. Ofgem says it went up because of higher wholesale gas prices caused by the conflict in the Middle East (Ofgem; ENB conversion). South Australia gets about 44.5% of its power from wind and about a third from solar (AEMO), and its default residential offer is about A$2,334 a year including GST for 4,000 kWh, roughly 40.6¢ per kWh all in (AER; as reported in a search-index excerpt of the AER determination, because the AER site would not load for us; ENB conversion). California pays 32.0¢. Texas, with a similar wind-and-solar share, pays 14.9¢ (EIA).

Texas versus California is the most useful comparison. Both get about 30% of their power from wind and solar. One pays twice what the other does. The difference is mostly not the turbines and panels. It is wildfire costs, transmission, rooftop-solar rules, taxes, mandates and market design.

The mandate-critical case: Energy Bad Boys and Always On

As of Energy Bad Boys and Always On Energy Research publications, Nov. 2025–Oct. 2026

Isaac Orr and Mitch Rolling, the “Energy Bad Boys” of Always On Energy Research (a mandate-critical energy think tank), have built the most detailed state-by-state case for Stu’s side (Always On). Their findings, labeled as theirs:

States with 100% clean-energy mandates sought 32% larger rate increases since 2020 than states without them (Energy Bad Boys).

In their 50-state profiles with the free-market Institute for Energy Research, the price gap between “blue” and “red” states widened from 6¢ (44%) in 2011 to 6.33¢ (61%) in 2025, and MISO utilities in Illinois, Michigan and Minnesota, all 100% mandate states, raised rates 28% from 2018 to 2024 versus 14.9% elsewhere (Energy Bad Boys).

Their “Always On” cost method, which charges wind and solar for the backup needed to serve demand every hour, puts Minnesota wind at about $272/MWh and solar at about $472/MWh (Energy Bad Boys). Their 2022 study for the Center of the American Experiment (a conservative think tank) estimated Gov. Tim Walz’s proposed 100%-by-2040 carbon-free standard would cost $313.2 billion through 2050 (2022 dollars) (CAE).

Their battery study with the National Center for Energy Analytics found a renewables-only path for PJM could cost more than $4 trillion through 2045, versus about $668 billion for gas and nuclear, and noted PJM lost about 4,500 MW of net firm capacity since 2020 while adding about 17,000 MW of wind and solar (Energy Bad Boys). Clean-energy advocates, including former DOE official Jigar Shah, have disputed this framing, as the post itself notes.

They also argue that adding gigawatts of low-capacity-factor wind and solar, plus the transmission to connect them, lowers the overall utilization of the generation fleet, which means more steel and wire per kWh delivered (Energy Bad Boys).

Their core argument is the same as Stu’s: the cost of wind and solar is not the panel, it is the backup, the wires and the mandate. ENB has featured their work before, including on coal plant costs.

Part 3. The other side, fairly

LBNL and Brattle: market wind and solar did not drive price hikes

As of LBNL/Brattle Retail Price Trends, July 2026 update

The most thorough national study of what drives retail prices comes from LBNL and Brattle (a national lab and a consulting firm). Their 2026 update finds U.S. average prices rose 5.3% in 2025 and 29% since 2019 in nominal terms, but only about 3% after inflation since 2019, and are about 6% lower than in 2010 after inflation (LBNL/Brattle).

Their conclusion on wind and solar: “market based” wind and solar supported by tax incentives “do not appear to have driven price increases,” while binding state RPS policies often did raise prices (LBNL/Brattle).

Instead, they point to: fuel and wholesale costs (generator gas prices rose 36% in 2025); distribution spending; transmission; storm recovery; wildfire costs (more than 4¢/kWh in California); PJM capacity prices (adding about 3.1¢ in D.C., 2.0¢ in New Jersey and 1.5¢ in Maryland); and rooftop-solar net metering, which added more than 2¢ in California but less than 0.5¢ in about 40 states (LBNL/Brattle). Note the overlap with Stu’s thesis: transmission, capacity and net metering are all partly tied to how renewables are added and paid for.

Lazard: cheapest new power, with or without credits

As of Lazard LCOE+ v19.0, June 2026

Lazard, an investment bank, publishes the most quoted cost comparison. Its 2026 edition puts unsubsidized utility solar at $40–98/MWh and onshore wind at $37–99, versus $51–129 for a new gas combined-cycle plant (Lazard). With credits, wind drops to as low as $11. Lazard also estimates that renewables stay “broadly cost-competitive” with gas even after adding firming costs, using an illustrative method.

The critique, which Stu and the Energy Bad Boys make often: a levelized cost compares a megawatt-hour that shows up when the weather allows with one that shows up when you need it. That is the point of ENB’s piece on redefining LCOE. Lazard’s firming analysis is an attempt to answer that, but it is a stylized calculation, not a grid study.

Texas: wind and solar can push wholesale prices down

As of ERCOT market monitor 2025 State of the Market report, June 2026

ERCOT’s independent market monitor, Potomac Economics, reports that in 2025 natural gas prices rose 61%, yet the all-in wholesale price rose only 13.8%, from about $34 to $38 per MWh. More than 6 GW of solar came online, solar’s share of generation rose from 10.4% to 13.9%, and battery capacity grew about 80% to more than 17,000 MW (ERCOT IMM). Zero-fuel-cost power at midday and batteries shaving evening peaks both damp prices. Texas residential prices rose less than the national average from 2010 to 2024 (EIA; ENB calculation).

The caveat is reliability, not price. Texas also had Winter Storm Uri in 2021. Cheap energy most hours is not the same as power in the worst hour.

Correlation versus causation: our honest read

Here is where we land, label by label:

Supported by the data: Nationally, wind and solar share and residential prices rose together. Federal subsidies are large. State mandates, especially in-state solar carve-outs, raise bills in the states that have them. Transmission and capacity costs are rising, and some of it is tied to adding weather-dependent resources and retiring firm ones.

Not supported by the data we have: That states with more wind and solar saw bigger price increases. The cross-state correlation is essentially zero.

Stu’s view, beyond the evidence: That wind, solar and storage are the main cause of rising grid costs, and that the problem will grow as subsidies sunset. That is a reasonable hypothesis about where costs are hiding (wires, backup, accreditation), but the national studies attribute most of the recent increase to other drivers, including gas, wildfires, storms, distribution upgrades and data centers.

Part 4. The sunset rush: build now, pay later?

A record wave arriving

As of EIA Feb. 20, 2026; Bloomberg Oct. 16, 2026

Developers told EIA they plan to add a record 86 GW of capacity in 2026, up from 53 GW in 2025: 43.4 GW of solar, 24.3 GW of batteries, 11.8 GW of wind and only 6.3 GW of gas. Texas alone holds about 40% of the planned solar and 53% of the batteries (EIA).

Bloomberg’s Oct. 16 report. On Friday, Bloomberg News published “US clean energy set to reach new highs as tax credit cliff looms” by Leslie Kaufman and Will Wade (Bloomberg). The story is paywalled, and ENB could not read the full text. What we can attribute:

From the Bloomberg headline: U.S. clean energy is set to reach new highs as the tax-credit cliff approaches (Bloomberg).

From the Bloomberg Technoz syndication (Bloomberg’s Indonesian partner, which published a translated version): the U.S. is on track for record clean-energy installations this year and next as developers race to use expiring tax credits and data-center demand surges; the report is based on BloombergNEF’s U.S. Clean Energy Market Outlook released Oct. 16; the syndication’s headline cites about 89 GW this year; and BNEF analyst Hall Wellborn said data-center growth still drives renewables but the picture is “tarnished” by more gas infrastructure, which reduces the climate benefit (Bloomberg Technoz, ENB translation).

We did not see BNEF’s full outlook and have not used any other figures from the Bloomberg story.

This matches other investor data. BloombergNEF reported U.S. renewable investment in the first half of 2026 up 54% from a year earlier, with solar at $45.8 billion and wind more than doubling to $13.8 billion, and said projects that preserved credit eligibility can keep coming online until 2030 (BNEF). Crux estimates about 170 GW of projects were safe-harbored before the July 4 deadline (E&E News). Rhodium Group expects record solar installations in 2026–27 (Rhodium). Behind them sits a huge queue: about 2,290 GW of projects were waiting to connect at the end of 2024: about 1,400 GW of generation, including 956 GW of solar and 271 GW of wind, plus about 890 GW of storage (LBNL Queued Up).

This is the heart of Stu’s point: the subsidies are sunsetting, but the projects are not. Thanks to the four-year safe harbor, wind and solar that started by July 4, 2026, can keep arriving through about 2030, and storage has credits well into the 2030s. ENB covered the policy turn in “With Wind and Solar Subsidies Ending, How Will the Energy Mix End Up?”.

PPA prices: the cost shift begins

As of LevelTen Q2 2026 index, July 21, 2026 (Q3 index due Oct. 20, 2026)

Corporate buyers are already feeling it. LevelTen Energy, which runs a renewable power marketplace, reported North American wind power purchase agreement (PPA) prices up 17.5% year over year in the second quarter, while solar slipped 4.8% from the prior quarter (LevelTen). LevelTen’s market-averaged offer prices were about $83.79/MWh for wind and $61.40 for solar, as reported by mgrid.org from American Clean Power’s summary of the LevelTen index (mgrid). LevelTen said the pipeline of credit-eligible projects “will effectively freeze” after the third quarter and that PPA prices could enter “uncharted territory” with “substantial premiums” (LevelTen). LBNL also found solar and wind PPA prices up about 60% and 100% in real terms since 2020 (LBNL/Brattle).

So who absorbs the costs?

When a subsidy ends, the cost of building a wind or solar farm does not change. Who pays it does.

Taxpayers, for now. Projects already safe-harbored will claim credits for years. JCT’s tables show tens of billions a year still flowing through 2027 (JCT).

Ratepayers, next. Without credits, developers need higher PPA prices, which utilities pass through. Energy Innovation (a clean-energy policy think tank that supported the credits) projected the cuts would raise household energy costs about $170 a year by 2035 (Energy Innovation). Princeton’s REPEAT project (academic modelers focused on decarbonization) estimated about $165 per household per year in 2030 and more than $280 in 2035 (REPEAT). Both groups favored keeping the credits; their numbers are model projections, not measurements.

Everyone in a capacity market. When firm capacity is short, as in PJM, every customer pays the higher clearing price (PJM).

Data centers, if regulators make them. Several states and utilities are writing large-load tariffs so new data centers pay for their own grid upgrades. See ENB’s data-center rates coverage.

Stu’s view is that ending subsidies is right, because it makes each resource show its true cost, and that the bigger risk is the pace of intermittent additions relative to firm power. The pro-credit modelers argue the opposite: that cheap solar and wind lower wholesale prices, so cutting credits raises bills. Both can be partly right, and the outcome depends on the backup bill.

Part 5. Grid stability: the part that keeps Stu up at night

NERC’s warnings

As of NERC 2025 LTRA (Jan. 2026) and 2025–26 Winter Reliability Assessment (Nov. 2025); 2026–27 winter assessment not yet released as of Oct. 16, 2026

NERC, the grid’s reliability watchdog, says 13 of 23 assessment areas face elevated or high risk of supply shortfalls over the next ten years. Over 105 GW of generation is slated to retire in a decade, and summer peak demand is projected to grow by 224 GW. Most new resources in the next five years are solar and batteries, which NERC describes as inverter-based and, for solar, weather-dependent (NERC 2025 LTRA).

Winter is the weak spot. NERC’s last winter assessment flagged elevated risk in New England, the Maritimes, parts of the Southeast, the Northwest, the Basin and ERCOT. In Texas, it noted winter peaks come before sunrise and after sunset, when solar is not producing, and that keeping batteries charged through a multi-day storm like Uri would be “increasingly challenging” (NERC WRA). The 2026–27 winter assessment usually comes out in November.

Inertia, inverters and what Odessa taught us

As of NERC Odessa reports, 2021 and 2022

Big spinning generators (coal, gas, nuclear, hydro) store energy in their rotating mass, called inertia, which slows the grid’s frequency drop when something trips. Solar, wind and batteries connect through power electronics, or inverters, which do not provide inertia on their own and must be programmed to ride through disturbances.

Odessa 2021: A fault at a gas plant near Odessa, Texas, on May 9, 2021, led 1,112 MW of solar to drop offline unexpectedly (NERC). ERCOT had roughly 7,200 MW of solar then, so about 15% of it tripped (ENB calculation).

Odessa 2022: On June 4, 2022, a similar fault caused 1,711 MW of inverter-based resources to trip plus 844 MW of conventional generation, pushing frequency down to 7 Hz (NERC). NERC traced many of the trips to inverter protection and plant control settings, issues that can be fixed with better standards.

The good news: these are fixable with better standards and settings, and NERC has been pushing them. The concern: as inverter-based resources grow, the cost of getting it wrong grows too.

Spain’s April 2025 blackout: what the official report said

As of ENTSO-E Expert Panel final report, Mar. 20, 2026

On April 28, 2025, Spain and Portugal went dark. The official investigation by ENTSO-E (Europe’s grid operators’ association), with the EU regulator ACER and national regulators, published its final report on March 20, 2026 (ENTSO-E; full report). It found the blackout came from a combination of factors: oscillations, gaps in voltage and reactive-power control, rapid output reductions and disconnections, and uneven stabilization.

Many renewable plants ran in fixed power-factor mode, so their reactive power did not respond to voltage changes (ENTSO-E report).

Conventional plants also fell short: they met their reactive-power reference less than 75% of the time (ENTSO-E report).

On inertia, the panel was direct: even with significantly higher inertia values, the loss of synchronism would not have been avoided (ENTSO-E report).

That is an important correction to the instant takes. Spain was not simply “too much solar, not enough spinning mass.” It was a voltage-control failure in a grid with lots of solar, rules that did not ask that solar to help, and conventional plants that did not deliver. The lesson for America is the same either way: grid rules have to keep pace with the resource mix.

Storage: helpful, but not a winter blanket

Batteries are the fastest-growing grid resource. ERCOT had more than 17,000 MW and about 31,500 MWh of storage by the end of 2025, or about 1.85 hours of average duration (ENB calculation from the ERCOT IMM). That is great for the evening peak and frequency response. NERC says batteries can improve frequency response where other inverter-based resources provide little (NERC LTRA). But a two-hour battery does not cover a five-day freeze or a week of still, cloudy weather. The Energy Bad Boys cite a 113-hour stretch when PJM wind output stayed below 1,000 MW (Energy Bad Boys). PJM rates a 4-hour battery at 58% and an 8-hour battery at 70% (PJM ELCC).

Part 6. What consumers and investors are saying

Consumers

As of AP-NORC/EPIC poll fielded July 6–24, 2026; Pew survey March 16–22, 2026

Bills are top of mind. Pew found 75% of Americans say their home energy costs have gone up, and among them, 64% say utilities wanting to make more money is a major reason and 40% cite grid upgrades (Pew).

Support for renewables is still broad. In the AP-NORC/EPIC poll, 63% support incentives for new renewable energy projects, but only 38% would pay a $1-a-month carbon fee (AP-NORC/EPIC).

Data centers are the new worry. 63% are extremely or very concerned data centers will raise their electricity prices, and 73% say data centers should pay for grid upgrades (AP-NORC/EPIC).

Translation: Americans like the idea of renewables. They do not want to pay more for them, and they want whoever drives new demand to cover the cost.

Investors

As of BNEF Aug. 26 and Oct. 16, 2026; LevelTen July 21, 2026; Crux via E&E News Aug. 18, 2026

BloombergNEF (research provider): record U.S. clean-energy installations this year and next as developers race the cliff, per Bloomberg’s Oct. 16 report as syndicated (Bloomberg Technoz); first-half 2026 investment up 54% (BNEF).

Crux (tax-credit broker): about 170 GW safe-harbored and a record $180 billion of investment expected in 2026 (E&E News).

LevelTen (renewable marketplace): a frozen pipeline of credit-eligible projects and “substantial premiums” ahead (LevelTen).

Lazard (investment bank): renewables remain the cheapest new energy on a levelized basis, with or without credits (Lazard).

Investors are not walking away from wind and solar. They are pricing in a scarcity premium once the credits are gone, and a lot of that premium will be paid by utility customers.

What to watch next

20, 2026: LevelTen’s Q3 PPA price index, the first full quarter after the July 4 start-construction deadline (LevelTen).

10, 2026: EIA’s next Short-Term Energy Outlook, with updated bill forecasts (EIA).

November 2026: NERC’s 2026–27 Winter Reliability Assessment (NERC).

31, 2027: the placed-in-service deadline for wind and solar that did not start construction by July 4, 2026 (IRS).

2029–2030: the last safe-harbored wind and solar projects come online (CRS).

2033–2036: storage and other zero-emission credits phase down (Taxpayers for Common Sense).

The bottom line

Wind, solar and batteries are now a big part of America’s grid, and taxpayers paid a lot to put them there. Nationally, bills have climbed alongside them. But the state-by-state data does not show that more wind and solar, on its own, means a bigger price hike. The costs Stu worries about show up in specific places: mandates, transmission, capacity markets and backup. Those are real, they are growing, and they deserve far more attention than the sticker price of a solar panel.

The subsidy cliff will not stop the build-out right away. A record wave is arriving through 2030, and when the credits run out, ratepayers pay through PPAs and capacity charges. The questions that matter for your wallet are who pays for the backup and the wires, and whether the grid can stay stable on a winter morning. Appendix D. Methodology

Wind + solar share by state. From EIA’s “Net Generation by State by Type of Producer by Energy Source” file, we used the Total Electric Power Industry rows and divided Wind plus Solar Thermal and Photovoltaic generation by Total generation, for 2010, 2019 and 2024. This is utility-scale, in-state generation; it excludes small-scale rooftop solar and does not account for imports, exports or out-of-state REC purchases.

Residential prices. 2010 and 2019 values are EIA-861 average residential prices (Total Electric Industry). 2024 values are from EIA’s 2024 Electric Sales, Revenue and Average Price, Table 4. For the national series, 2021 is EIA-861 and 2022–2023 are EIA Short-Term Energy Outlook annual averages. All prices are nominal cents per kWh.

Pearson correlation coefficients (r) computed across 50 states plus D.C. (n = 51), with a normal-approximation p-value. Results excluding Hawaii and Alaska are essentially unchanged (r = −0.025). We tested four specifications; none shows a positive cross-state relationship. Correlation is not causation in either direction.

Group averages. “High” states had a 2024 wind+solar share of 35% or more (6 states); “low” states under 5% (16 states). Averages are simple, unweighted state averages.

Bill estimate. EIA STEO average residential price × average monthly residential use × 12. ENB calculation.

JCT tax-expenditure sums. We added corporate and individual columns for Sections 45 (renewable electricity production), 45Y, 48 (energy credit) and 48E for each fiscal year in JCX-45-25. These include some non-wind, non-solar property (e.g., geothermal, fuel cells, some storage), so they overstate the wind-and-solar portion.

Converted at ECB euro reference rates for Oct. 16, 2026: USD 1.1253, GBP 0.84385 and AUD 1.6171 per euro (implying £1 ≈ $1.3335 and A$1 ≈ $0.6959). International prices are not perfectly comparable: Germany and South Australia include fixed charges; the UK figure is the unit rate excluding the standing charge.

Bloomberg article. The Oct. 16, 2026 Bloomberg article is paywalled and returned an access block. We used only its headline, the Bloomberg Technoz syndication (in Indonesian, translated by ENB) and BloombergNEF’s own public pages. We did not use any figure we could not read.

Advocacy sources. Studies from groups with a policy position (Always On Energy Research, Energy Bad Boys, Center of the American Experiment, Cato, Clean Air Task Force, Energy Innovation, SEIA, REPEAT) are labeled where they appear, and their figures are reported as theirs, not ENB findings.

Appendix F. Glossary

PTC / ITC: production tax credit (per kWh, 10 years) / investment tax credit (percent of build cost).

45Y / 48E: the technology-neutral clean-electricity production and investment credits that started in 2025.

Safe harbor / begin construction: IRS rules for when a project counts as started; once started, projects generally have four years to finish.

Transferability: selling tax credits for cash to another taxpayer.

RPS / REC / SREC: renewable portfolio standard / renewable energy certificate (1 MWh of renewable output) / solar REC.

Capacity market (BRA): PJM’s Base Residual Auction, which pays resources to be available three years ahead.

ELCC: effective load carrying capability, the share of a resource’s capacity counted as reliable in the riskiest hours.

Curtailment: deliberately reducing wind or solar output because the grid cannot use or move it.

Inertia: stored rotational energy in spinning generators that slows frequency changes.

IBR: inverter-based resource (solar, wind, batteries).

LCOE: levelized cost of energy, the average lifetime cost per MWh, which does not by itself include backup or grid costs.

PPA: power purchase agreement, a long-term contract to buy a project’s output.
