text:
This analysis and news roundup come from the Canary Media Weekly newsletter. Sign up to get it every Friday.

It’s a great time to have an electric vehicle — and more Americans are getting the message.

Despite President Donald Trump’s pledge to refrain from striking Iran before next month’s midterm elections, oil markets are still roiling. The average price for a gallon of gasoline across the country has been stuck at over $4 for months now, making it considerably cheaper to drive an EV than a gas-powered car, even if you only charge up at pricey public stations.

Of course, going electric was a pretty sweet deal a year or so ago too, when the federal government still offered tax credits for certain EV purchases. The end of those incentives sent EV sales off a cliff, but now they’re finally on the rebound. U.S. consumers bought 262,649 new EVs in the third quarter of this year, marking two straight quarters of sales growth after last year’s face-plant, according to Cox Automotive.

That number is nowhere close to the record 437,487 new EVs sold in the third quarter of last year, when Americans rushed to take advantage of federal tax credits before they expired. But this time the growth is likely to continue, Cox Automotive says, as gas prices show no sign of going down soon.

The current hot streak extends to used EVs too. Americans bought 44,350 used EVs in August, up 26% from July and up 15% from a year prior, Cox reports — and one vehicle in particular is helping drive the surge. Ford canceled production of its F-150 Lightning in late 2025 after years of sluggish sales, but the discontinued truck is now dominating the resale market. Analysts say the price tag for a brand-new Lightning was too high to attract a lot of buyers, but it’s a worthwhile deal at a reduced cost.

Of course, Americans aren’t the only ones facing gasoline price spikes and turning to EVs as a result. European drivers bought nearly 600,000 EVs in September, marking the continent’s biggest sales month on record, according to Benchmark Mineral Intelligence. And overall, global EV sales rose 17% in September compared to the month before.

Sky-high gasoline prices probably won’t continue indefinitely, but America’s EV market rebound might. One reason? Automakers are rolling out more and better all-electric options in the U.S. (even though cheap Chinese models are banned). Ford’s next electric pickup will be far more affordable than the Lightning, Subaru’s new electric SUV charges faster than its predecessor, and Rivian recently began selling a less expensive version of its popular SUV, to name a few improvements.

It all means there’s a good chance that steady, sustainable growth will persist, and that the boom-and-bust cycle of the last few years may finally have ended.

More big energy stories

Will Trump’s latest offshore wind attack disrupt permitting talks?

Trump’s Department of the Interior revived its fight against offshore wind this week as it asked a federal court for permission to reevaluate a key permit for Revolution Wind. The project off the Connecticut and Rhode Island coasts has been generating power since the spring, and is part of a growing wind fleet that delivered 4,619 GWh of power to New England in the first nine months of the year. The DOI’s request comes as part of an anti-wind group’s lawsuit against Revolution, and its potential impact on the project’s operations permit likely won’t play out for months.

It’s not the best time for the White House to go after offshore wind again. Congress is currently working to advance long-awaited bipartisan energy permitting legislation, and some House Democrats say the renewed attack on Revolution is giving them second thoughts about the package. Still, the bill’s Democratic co-authors in the Senate, Martin Heinrich (N.M.) and Sheldon Whitehouse (R.I.), have noted that the bill contains protections that would prevent a presidential administration from rolling back permits for an energy project like this one is.

Trump’s deal with Russia likely won’t ease diesel prices

Another of Trump’s energy decisions is generating pushback, including from members of his own party. In an attempt to ease a diesel shortage in the U.S., Trump announced a deal in which Russia will sell millions of gallons of the fuel to the U.S. Analysts say the move will do little to actually ease diesel prices in this country, as Russia’s fuel exports have fallen dramatically over the past year amid Ukrainian attacks on its refineries. Trump’s recent move to release more tax-exempt diesel fuel into the U.S. transport market won’t have much effect either.

Diesel prices have been rising for months in the U.S. and around the world as the war in Iran limits supplies. The International Energy Agency predicts that these strains on the market will persist into 2027.

Clean energy news to know this week

Keep the money rolling: Green banks, which fund clean energy projects in traditionally hard-to-finance sectors, have still managed to get lots of projects off the ground in spite of funding rollbacks during the Trump administration. (Canary Media)

Where’s the hydrogen? Years after the announcement of two hydrogen hub projects that were supposed to bring jobs and economic benefits to Pennsylvania and neighboring states, progress has completely stalled. (Inside Climate News)

Clean jobs erased: The U.S. had about 37,000 fewer clean energy jobs at the end of 2025 compared to the year before, marking the first decrease after four years of consistent growth, though overall energy jobs fell as well. (Canary Media)

Save it for later: The levelized cost of energy for four-hour battery storage is now 65–75% cheaper than that for gas peaker plants across the globe, a new Wood Mackenzie analysis finds. (Utility Dive)

Coal cost concerns: Democrats and clean energy advocates are making a campaign issue out of the Trump administration’s orders to keep coal plants open in Michigan and Indiana. (Capital and Main)

title: Digging deeper: $20 million to kickstart next-generation geothermal in California
description:
Why geothermal matters for California Geothermal energy is a clean firm energy source, providing zero-carbon, always available electricity.
The availability of clean firm resources like next-generation geothermal can reduce annual electricity supply costs by $10-44 billion by 2045.
Maximizing the impact of California’s geothermal funding The $20 million in state funding can help kickstart a next-generation geothermal industry in the state and crowd in additional private capital if implemented successfully.
Fund next-generation geothermal projects.
Developing the first next-generation geothermal project in a region is seen as risky by investors.
text:
California’s 2026 budget included $20 million for geothermal exploration, mapping, characterization, and development. The funding is designed to overcome early-stage exploration risk, which is a major barrier to project deployment in the state. The program’s cost share model will ensure every state dollar is matched by non-state funding, bringing the total potential investment to $40 million. If implemented successfully, this program could help derisk the subsurface in high-potential geologic regions, which could crowd in large amounts of private investment and launch next-generation geothermal projects throughout the state to provide the clean firm energy that California needs.

Why geothermal matters for California

Geothermal energy is a clean firm energy source, providing zero-carbon, always available electricity. California is a global leader in conventional geothermal, which produces power from existing pockets of hot water in the Earth’s subsurface. But in recent years, the geothermal map has expanded dramatically with the advent of next-generation geothermal: power that can be created anywhere the Earth’s subsurface is warm, without looking for pockets of hot water. CATF’s modeling indicates that just 1% of the highest-temperature geothermal resources available in California at currently accessible depths (superhot rock geothermal) could produce 35 gigawatts of power, translating to nearly 300,000 gigawatt-hours of power annually – about the same amount the entire state consumed in 2023.

Geothermal can provide enormous benefits to California.

The availability of clean firm resources like next-generation geothermal can reduce annual electricity supply costs by $10-44 billion by 2045.

Clean firm energy reduces the amount of new generating capacity necessary to achieve California’s clean energy targets. It also provides flexibility for the required pace of renewables deployment while helping address land-use constraints through its smaller surface footprint.

As California advances its clean energy goals, next-generation geothermal can provide an onramp for experienced oil and gas workers to bring their expertise to the state’s clean firm power sector – supporting good-paying jobs in communities with a legacy of energy development.

Public investment in appraisal can unlock geothermal development

Next-generation geothermal projects are planned or underway in Utah, Nevada, Oregon, New Mexico, and Texas, but relatively few projects have been announced in California despite the state’s rich subsurface heat endowment. High upfront costs and insufficient understanding of large portions of California’s geology remain significant barriers to development.

Appraisal – drilling the first full-scale wells on a site and creating connectivity between them – are critical to understanding subsurface conditions and assessing whether a project is viable, but they are expensive, costing as much as $20 million (or more) depending on well depth and geology. Because appraisal drilling has high costs and involves significant uncertainty about resource viability, it can be difficult to attract private financing for this phase. These risks recur in each new geologic region, with the first appraisal wells holding the highest risk. Information gained through appraisal wells will reduce uncertainty for subsequent projects, especially if data is shared publicly. By sharing the upfront costs of appraisal and making subsurface data publicly available, state funding can help reduce risks for early developers and unlock geothermal development across California.

Maximizing the impact of California’s geothermal funding

The $20 million in state funding can help kickstart a next-generation geothermal industry in the state and crowd in additional private capital if implemented successfully. Key features of an effective design for the program include:

Catalyze the development of new projects. The highest-impact use of these funds is to launch projects which would not have otherwise occurred, rather than simply supporting projects already moving forward. The state should prioritize applicants who illustrate that state funding would be catalytic for their proposed project.

Fund next-generation geothermal projects. California is home to many conventional geothermal projects, including the world’s largest producing geothermal field, and it is a mature technology that has existed for decades. Next-generation geothermal has much larger potential in California but faces greater early-stage technical and financial risks as an emerging energy source. Limiting the state funding to next-generation geothermal can help address these risks and catalyze the development of a new industry in the state.

Focus funding on appraisal drilling (i.e., drilling the first full-scale wells and creating connectivity between them). Appraisal drilling is the riskiest stage of geothermal development, and private capital is generally unwilling to fund it.

Prioritize meaningful eligible award amounts calibrated to the high cost of exploratory drilling. The total program size is $20 million with a statutorily-mandated 50% cost share. The maximum eligible award amount should be large enough to meaningfully reduce financial risk and attract developer participation. For example, funding two projects at $10 million each would cover approximately half the cost of a typical appraisal well (though costs vary by location and project details), while reducing exploration risk in multiple locations and generating subsurface data that could support future development.

Spread funding across companies. To ensure that multiple companies can contribute to California’s geothermal future, limit this funding to only one award per company.

Fund projects in at least two distinct geological regions of the state, including at least one project in a new region. California has a long history of conventional geothermal development, concentrated near four locations: the Geysers, Salton Sea, Mammoth, and Coso. For next-generation geothermal to fulfill its full potential, more projects will need to be sited in more regions of the state, beyond those four locations. The first project in any new region is riskier than later projects, so private financiers are often unwilling to support those projects. Funding at least one project in a new geologic region – one without a history of geothermal development – will help derisk that location.

Provide funding certainty. Developing the first next-generation geothermal project in a region is seen as risky by investors. State funding can play a unique role in absorbing this early-stage technical risk, enabling the activities necessary to crowd in private investment and generating information to determine project viability. California should ensure that eligible drilling and stimulation costs will be reimbursed provided the funded activities are completed in accordance with the grant requirements, regardless of whether the wells ultimately achieve connectivity or sufficient flow rates. Certainty about reimbursement is necessary for developers to be able to find private financing for projects in this program.

Have a line of sight to full-scale development. When determining which applications to fund, the state should prioritize applicants who seem likely to be able to turn successful appraisal drilling into a full-scale project. The most important consideration is whether applicants have a technology and approach that is economically viable and could produce power at competitive prices. The state should also consider transmission access (e.g., availability of nearby interconnection capacity) and permitting (e.g., applicants with a history of successful development, line of sight on permits, and/or strong relationships with communities and key stakeholders near the project site). Integrating these factors into application decisions will help ensure that the program results in commercial-scale geothermal development.

text:
(Oct 16): The US is on track to install record amounts of clean energy this year and next as developers race to claim expiring federal tax credits and as soaring data-centre electricity demand stimulates growth.

But the same data-centre boom is also driving a major expansion of natural gas, undercutting the climate benefits of the renewables buildout.

The findings are part of BloombergNEF’s latest US Clean Energy Market Outlook, released on Friday.

“When we look at the picture holistically, we still see data center growth as a tailwind to renewable energy, but it is tainted by the growing gas pipeline,” said Hall Welborn, an author of the report.

BNEF expects the US to add a record 89 gigawatts (GW) of clean energy this year and to surpass that level in 2027. The surge is coming even as developers contend with more expensive financing, trade barriers and uncertainty over equipment costs and availability.

At the same time, 67.8GW of new gas-fired power could be added through 2030, according to BNEF. With just 14.3GW of gas generation slated to close over that period, the pipeline would amount to a substantial net increase.

The rapid growth of artificial intelligence (AI) and data centres is increasingly shaping US energy forecasts. BNEF now expects installed data-centre capacity to reach 118GW in 2030, which is 52% higher than its projections made only last December. Average data-centre power demand could reach 120GW by 2035, roughly five times current levels, with AI-related computing responsible for nearly half.

A significant portion of new data centres will be powered by on-site natural gas systems. While the US is the world’s largest supplier of the fossil fuel, all that demand is going to tax domestic supply, and BNEF expects the industry to swing from surplus production to a deficit as soon as 2028.

Yet the boom is also improving the outlook for clean-energy projects. BNEF revised up by 15% its forecast through 2036 for onshore wind additions, to 99.7 gigawatts, partly in light of data-centre demand.

The outlook for batteries has improved even more. BNEF now projects that 383GW of storage will be installed through 2036, 35% more than it expected earlier this year. Federal incentives for storage remain in place even as support for some renewable projects winds down.

Solar will continue to account for the biggest share of new clean generation. The analysts expect 48.9GW to be installed in 2026 alone as developers push ahead with projects that secured eligibility for expiring tax incentives. However, the utility-scale solar forecast for the period 2026 to 2036 has been revised down by 7.5%, to 430GW, due to new tariffs and the tax-credit phaseout.

Technology companies are themselves underwriting a large portion of the clean-energy expansion. More than 15GW of corporate clean-power contracts were announced through August, according to BNEF. Meta Platforms Inc and Alphabet Inc’s Google represented nearly three-quarters of that total.

Rising electricity needs are also renewing interest in nuclear power, although new reactors remain expensive and can take years to develop. More immediate gains can come from restarting closed reactors and increasing output from existing plants. Those projects, along with a limited number of new plants, are expected to add 13.7GW of nuclear capacity by 2036.

name: Louisiana and Evs
title: Americans want electric cars – they just can't find them | National News
authors: John Paul Helveston, George Washington University
description:
If there was ever a moment for Americans to switch to electric vehicles, this was it.
Some observers took that as evidence that high gas prices alone wouldn’t push Americans toward fully electric cars, but that conclusion misses half the story.
But the data doesn’t support the claim that electric vehicle sales stalled in 2026 because Americans don’t want them.
A look ahead Rather than move to increase electric vehicle supply and make them more affordable, federal policy continues to hinder the U.S. electric vehicle sector.
As long as gas stays expensive, the gap between the electric vehicles Americans want and the electric vehicles dealers can sell them is likely to remain.
text:
Within three months of the U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran on Feb. 28, 2026, the average price of gasoline for American drivers climbed from US$2.94 to $4.35 a gallon. If there was ever a moment for Americans to switch to electric vehicles, this was it.

From March to May 2026, in fact, sales of hybrid electric vehicles were 18% higher than over the same months in 2025.

But sales of fully electric vehicles were 16% lower from March to May 2026 compared with the same months in 2025. Some observers took that as evidence that high gas prices alone wouldn’t push Americans toward fully electric cars, but that conclusion misses half the story.

I study car buyers and their preferences, and there is an important distinction between what consumers want and what they can actually buy. Sales reveal what cars people actually bought, but not necessarily what they actually wanted.

When the supply of some kinds of cars can’t keep up with demand, prices rise, and that’s exactly what happened for electric vehicles in 2026.

An industry in retreat

In 2026, hybrids and all-electric vehicles faced the same jump in demand from the oil crisis. While there were plenty of hybrids available to meet that demand, the same was not true for EVs.

Hybrid production had been growing for years, led by Toyota, which sells about half of the hybrids bought in the United States. As a result, even as sales surged, hybrid inventories on dealer lots were 19% higher in March 2026 than they had been a year earlier.

However, EV production had been in retreat since the tax and spending law President Donald Trump signed in July 2025 ended federal tax credits for EVs. Buyers had been able to get up to $7,500 for new EVs and $4,000 for used ones, but that ended after Sept. 30, 2025.

Automakers responded by cutting back their EV production. General Motors laid off more than 3,400 workers at its EV and battery plants and shifted its Tennessee plant to make batteries for energy storage, not cars. Ford wrote off $19.5 billion from its EV business, ended production of the all-electric F-150 Lightning and converted a Tennessee EV plant to build gas-powered trucks.

Buyers, for their part, rushed to beat the tax credit deadline, pushing EVs to 11.3% of new vehicle sales in September 2025. But by November 2025, after the tax credits ended, their share dropped to 4.3%.

As 2026 progressed and gas prices began to rise, so did EV demand. New EV inventories declined, shrinking from about 130 days of supply in the first quarter of 2026 to 78 days by August – just two days above the supply level of gas-burning cars.

Discounts on new EV models shrank too. My analysis of online listings from marketcheck.com shows the median new EV was listed 9.8% below sticker price in February. By April, the median discount was 6.6%, and 4.7% in June. That’s a sign that dealers saw rising demand, not inventory to clear.

A run on used electric vehicles

Before the war, prices for used electric vehicles were still drifting down in the wake of the expired used EV federal tax credit. After the war began, they climbed 13% through late June 2026. For a typical used electric vehicle, that’s about $3,500 more.

Other data sources point in the same direction. Recurrent, a company that reports on batteries and used EVs, found that the price of a used 2023 Chevrolet Bolt rose almost 20% from January to June 2026.

And inventories of used electric vehicles dropped too, with only 31 days of supply in May, 23% below the year before.

A costly misreading

None of this means the electric vehicle market is healthy. High prices and uncertain access to charging stations are real stumbling blocks for people who are thinking about buying an EV.

But the data doesn’t support the claim that electric vehicle sales stalled in 2026 because Americans don’t want them. Rather, the sales stalled because there weren’t enough EVs available to buy – and there were plenty of hybrids as an alternative.

The distinction matters because automakers have treated a change in the policy landscape as a change in consumer demand, leading to shortages with real costs.

The average new car now sells for about $50,000 and the average new electric vehicle for about $55,000, according to Kelley Blue Book, a company that tracks car prices.

The current situation leaves drivers exposed to the volatility of oil prices with fewer alternatives. The U.S. is the world’s largest oil producer, yet a war in the Persian Gulf raised gas prices significantly in just three months. Oil trades on a global market, so American drivers pay global prices.

Seven months into the war, the pressure on drivers is still going full throttle. Oil was still above $100 a barrel in mid-October, and diesel hit a record $6.52 a gallon on Sept. 22.

Electric vehicle sales haven’t caught up. Argonne’s data show 86,000 of them sold in August, fewer than the 101,000 sold in May, while hybrid sales stayed above 216,000 a month all summer.

A look ahead

Rather than move to increase electric vehicle supply and make them more affordable, federal policy continues to hinder the U.S. electric vehicle sector.

The fuel economy rule released Sept. 28, 2026, loosens efficiency requirements for gas-powered vehicles and in 2028 ends a system that let automakers that beat the standards – mostly EV makers – earn credits for exceeding them and sell those to automakers that fell short. That means automakers will have fewer regulatory incentives to produce EVs going forward.

Regulators say buyers will save $1,289 on the purchase price of a new gas-powered vehicle from reduced engineering and manufacturing costs to make less efficient engines. But the same analysis estimates drivers will spend about $1,600 more on gas over the life of the car, and that’s using fuel price forecasts well below today’s prices. Economists say the administration’s math does not properly account for those fuel costs.

The U.S. has also effectively shut out Chinese automakers, even though nearly three-quarters of the world’s electric cars are built in China. In 2024, Chinese car buyers could choose from over 130 EV models priced under $40,000; American buyers had just four EV models under that threshold. Beyond tariffs of more than 100% on EVs made in China, a Commerce Department rule bars cars from Chinese-linked automakers starting with model year 2027, even if they are built in the U.S. A bill pending in Congress would widen the ban, blocking Chinese investment in U.S. auto factories altogether.

As long as gas stays expensive, the gap between the electric vehicles Americans want and the electric vehicles dealers can sell them is likely to remain. Decisions such as ending the tax credit, rolling back fuel economy standards and banning Chinese technology all make it harder to build them, which means Americans will continue to have fewer affordable electric vehicles to choose from.

title: Is industrial AI the key to resilient and sustainable electronics manufacturing? | ESG Dive
description:
John Mitchell is president and CEO of the Global Electronics Association, the world’s largest trade association for companies across the electronics ecosystem.
The electronics industry remains hyper-dependent on specific geographic hotspots for both raw materials and resource-intensive processing.
If a drought threatens a chip facility’s water supply, industrial AI can optimize production lines to run on fewer resources.
These use cases are part of a broader shift of companies using industrial AI to build operational insulation.
AI can make electronics more sustainable, and more circular electronics can reduce the material and energy burden of building the next generation of AI hardware.
text:
John Mitchell is president and CEO of the Global Electronics Association, the world’s largest trade association for companies across the electronics ecosystem. Views are the author’s own.

Semiconductor facilities in Taiwan — the current epicenter of global chip production – need to truck in water from external watersheds just to keep assembly lines moving. Forty percent of existing global semiconductor manufacturing capacity and up to 40% of all facilities currently under construction will face high to extremely high water risk by 2030, according to industry data.

This water problem signals a growing challenge for the electronics industry: the physical impacts of climate change are increasingly affecting operations and supply chains. This does not happen in a vacuum — rather, it compounds geopolitical and logistical vulnerabilities across the supply chain.

The electronics industry remains hyper-dependent on specific geographic hotspots for both raw materials and resource-intensive processing. When virtually every sector depends on these components, geographically contained crises trigger immediate worldwide volatility.

As shipping ground to a halt in the Strait of Hormuz over the past seven months, component prices spiked rapidly, with copper foil rising by 30% and printed circuit boards going up 40%, according to reporting by Reuters. Whether driven by climate-induced resource scarcity or geopolitical bottlenecks, these compounding shocks expose a vulnerability we must address.

While there is no single solution to solve every supply chain challenge at once, industrial artificial intelligence, which applies AI to manufacturing operations from factories to energy grids, is designed specifically for complex operational environments. This technology can safeguard the supply chain by changing how we respond to external shocks in real time.

If a drought threatens a chip facility’s water supply, industrial AI can optimize production lines to run on fewer resources. If military conflicts close a shipping lane or cause critical mineral costs to spike, industrial AI has the capability to diversify sourcing intelligence to find alternative routes and materials. By reducing primary material demands and increasing resource efficiency across the board, industrial AI can build an operational buffer that directly insulates companies from global instability.

Keep up with the story. Subscribe to the ESG Dive free daily newsletter

Industrial AI is already helping the electronics industry — from real-time factory planning and optimization to resource forecasting and AI “factories” with extensive electrification infrastructure. For instance, world models, also known as digital twins, are being used to actively simulate severe market disruptions and climate events. This application gives manufacturers the predictive intelligence needed to certify backup suppliers and adjust material volumes weeks before a crisis hits. Global Electronics Association member companies are reporting their deployment of industrial AI for quality control, predictive maintenance, sustainability reporting, carbon data collection and designing for circularity.

These use cases are part of a broader shift of companies using industrial AI to build operational insulation. A recent corporate survey from Siemens reports that 65% of respondents integrated industrial AI into manufacturing to save energy and 43% used the technology to better manage resources and waste. In a supply chain where energy price spikes and resource scarcity are triggered by events nearby or thousands of miles away, that kind of operational insulation can be a sustainability win and competitive hedge. These applications of industrial AI enhance companies’ strategic interdependence, creating a supply chain that bends under pressure rather than breaks.

However, there is also a need to confront the infrastructure required to build this operational resilience. The algorithms powering industrial AI models currently require massive data centers, which carry a large resource footprint of their own.

Read More in Sustainability

Global data center electricity consumption has grown 12% per year over the last five years, according to the International Energy Agency. U.S. data center electricity consumption is projected to increase 300% over the next decade. As the world enters an era of water bankruptcy, data centers are anticipated to consume 9.3 trillion liters of water by 2030, according to research by the U.N.

At the moment, the choices made about the fuels needed to power digital backbones accelerate extreme climate conditions and geopolitical energy dependencies that are already fracturing supply chains. That is an operational contradiction the industrial sector can no longer afford.

Industrial AI adoption must be guided by dual accountability. AI should accelerate sustainability by optimizing resources, reducing waste, improving energy efficiency, and scaling supply chain decarbonization. But the digital infrastructure that powers AI must also be sustainable — a challenge many across industries are working on.

Circular water practices, waste recovery and a commitment to 100% clean energy sourcing are the baseline for companies serious about employing industrial AI as a net-positive resilience tool.

The electronics industry has a unique role to play in creating this virtuous loop. Electronics are the foundation that makes AI possible, and AI can also become a powerful tool to make electronics design, manufacturing, use and end-of-life management more circular. In short, better electronics can make AI more efficient. AI can make electronics more sustainable, and more circular electronics can reduce the material and energy burden of building the next generation of AI hardware.

Read More in Sustainability

The electronics industry sits at the center of both the challenge and the solution because it influences the technologies that enable AI and the industrial systems where AI can deliver sustainability gains – and it’s an intersection more COOs, CFOs and CSOs should pay attention to.

text:
OTTAWA — HANNAH HUNTER, senior analyst with the Pembina Institute’s Sustainable Workforce program, made the following statement in response to the federal government’s announcement of more than $430 million in apprenticeship training funding over the next five years under Team Canada Strong.

“Canada’s growing clean economy offers major opportunities to create good jobs and drive economic growth. Realizing these opportunities will depend on having enough skilled workers to expand our electricity system and electrify more of our economy, from transportation and buildings to industry. Today’s investment in apprenticeship training is a welcome step. To make it worthwhile for workers and employers, Canada must ensure this investment goes towards jobs of the future, not the jobs of yesterday.

“The funding will help training centres expand, purchase modern equipment and develop new approaches to apprenticeship training through three streams of the Union Training and Innovation Program (UTIP): infrastructure expansion, training equipment and innovation. If allocated well, these investments can help to prepare learners for the advancing technologies and growing demand for skills in the clean economy, including modern construction methods, grid modernization, heat pump installation, and electric vehicle infrastructure.

“Canada has committed to doubling its electricity supply by 2050. To realize the full benefits of that investment, we also need to double electrification and energy efficiency. Achieving these ambitions will depend on having enough skilled workers with the right training and experience. As the government decides which initiatives to fund through UTIP, it should prioritize training that responds to growing demand in the clean economy and builds the skilled workforce needed to deliver on Canada’s economic ambitions.”

title: US is reviving shuttered nuclear plants to meet growing electricity demand and to power data centers
description:
The United States is making an unprecedented attempt to revive three shuttered nuclear plants to meet rising energy demand, including from large-scale data centers.
The Trump administration is pushing hard to deploy nuclear power for artificial intelligence and manufacturing.
It’s also lending billions of dollars for upgrades to produce more electricity from currently operating nuclear plants.
Holtec says its efforts will restore baseload power, strengthen energy security and demonstrate the role of nuclear energy in meeting the nation’s growing electricity demands.
Industry group says reactors shouldn’t close early The World Nuclear Association said restarting nuclear reactors should be celebrated, but preventing them from closing prematurely would be the best option.
text:
The United States is making an unprecedented attempt to revive three shuttered nuclear plants to meet rising energy demand, including from large-scale data centers.

No commercial nuclear reactor is known to have resumed generating electricity after beginning the decommissioning process that takes one out of service, though some reactors have restarted after long outages.

The Department of Energy is lending as much as $4.4 billion to restart the Palisades Power Plant in Michigan, the Crane Clean Energy Center on Pennsylvania’s Three Mile Island and the Duane Arnold Energy Center in Iowa to restore a combined 2.25 gigawatts of electricity, which can power roughly 2 million homes and businesses. All three of the plants closed before their licenses expired, largely because the electricity they produced was considered too expensive.

Not anymore. Two of the plants have contracts with Big Tech companies that will pay a premium to get large amounts of carbon-free energy for data centers. The Trump administration is pushing hard to deploy nuclear power for artificial intelligence and manufacturing. It’s also lending billions of dollars for upgrades to produce more electricity from currently operating nuclear plants.

Restarting a reactor is a fairly quick way to get a lot of electricity, and it’s cheaper than building a new, large reactor, said nuclear engineering expert Todd Allen.

“There’s a demand in the country for more power,” he said. “You have these assets that were previously hooked up. They were previously operable, and you can relatively quickly get them generating electricity again, compared to your other possibilities. For anyone who wants zero carbon, nuclear provides that. For the Trump administration, which really wants nuclear, this fits that story also.”

Restarting a reactor is kind of like restoring a car

Allen compared restarting a decommissioned nuclear plant to restarting a car that sat idle for a few years. The driver still needs a valid license and all the parts need to be working correctly.

“That’s what they’re trying to do with these nuclear plants, but it’s a much bigger, complicated system,” said Allen, associate dean for research at the University of Michigan’s College of Engineering.

With a nuclear plant, the owner has to bring nuclear workers back and ensure their training is current, make sure everything is working and that maintenance is up to date, ensure they have enough fuel and ask regulators to restore their operating license, he added.

Allen said it’s a lot to keep track of, but it’s relatively straightforward.

Expert says restarts are risky

Edwin Lyman, at the Union of Concerned Scientists, said the taxpayer money being used should go toward addressing safety risks. For example, most U.S. plants were built between 1970 and 1990 and were designed to withstand natural disasters of that era, said Lyman, director of nuclear power safety at UCS. But climate change is making extreme weather events more frequent and severe.

“It’s possible, if they set the right level of safety and spend the necessary funds to meet that, they could restore these plants to operable condition,” he said. “That’s not happening at this point.”

Iowa’s only nuclear facility, Duane Arnold, began operating in 1975. It was scheduled to permanently close in October 2020. Replacing it with cheaper energy sources, including wind, was projected to save Iowa customers $300 million in energy costs. The plant shut down early, in August 2020, when it was damaged during a powerful storm known as a derecho.

NextEra Energy owns Duane Arnold. Looking at its condition, CEO John Ketchum said company officials “felt really good about the ability to bring it back.”

Palisades plant is the furthest along

The Palisades plant operated from 1971 until 2022, when its owner, Entergy, left the nuclear power business. The plant’s operating license lasted until 2031.

Holtec International bought it and began dismantling it, though none of the steps were irreversible. Michigan officials, not wanting to lose nuclear jobs or energy, encouraged Holtec to pursue reopening the plant and provided state funding. The Biden administration in 2024 approved a $1.5 billion loan to restart the facility, and the Trump administration continued the payments.

In August, Holtec began loading nuclear fuel, one of the final major phases before a reactor can restart. The company paused the process after a fuel assembly tilted from its upright position and Holtec determined it needed to figure out why. Its power purchase agreements require Palisades to be in service by March 2027.

Holtec says its efforts will restore baseload power, strengthen energy security and demonstrate the role of nuclear energy in meeting the nation’s growing electricity demands.

Big Tech will purchase power for data centers

NextEra Energy and Google are collaborating to restart Duane Arnold by early 2029.

“This is a perfect example of data centers paying their own way,” Ketchum said in an interview. “We’re able to sign a long-term contract with a hyperscaler for that project. So none of the costs are being paid by residential customers in Iowa.”

Microsoft has a contract with the Crane Clean Energy Center on Three Mile Island just outside Harrisburg. The plant was the site of the nation’s worst commercial nuclear power accident in 1979. The accident destroyed one reactor, leaving the plant with one functioning. In 2019, Constellation Energy’s then-parent company Exelon shut down the functioning reactor, saying it was losing money and that Pennsylvania lawmakers had refused to subsidize it.

Constellation Energy announced in 2024 that it would spend $1.6 billion to restart the reactor under a 20-year agreement with Microsoft. It hopes to bring the plant back online in 2027. The Energy Department provided a $1 billion loan, and Deputy Energy Secretary James Danly took a tour last week.

Jack Spencer at The Heritage Foundation said he can’t think of a worse use of taxpayer money than using it to restart reactors. These are low-risk projects where there is a massive demand for the energy, so there is no reason to funnel federal dollars to these companies, said Spencer, director of the foundation’s Center for Energy, Climate and Environment.

Conversely, Jennifer Gordon at the Atlantic Council said she thinks it’s a terrific way of leveraging federal financing to get needed electricity. Gordon directs the council’s Nuclear Energy Policy Initiative.

Industry group says reactors shouldn’t close early

The World Nuclear Association said restarting nuclear reactors should be celebrated, but preventing them from closing prematurely would be the best option.

Palisades is expected to be the first nuclear plant in the world to resume generating power after beginning the decommissioning process, but other countries have restarted or refurbished reactors after long-term shutdowns, the association said. That includes Canada, Armenia, Belgium, Japan, India and South Korea. Others are considering or in the process of restarting reactors.

___

Associated Press writer Sarah Rankin in Richmond, Virginia, contributed to this report.

American Electric Power (AEP, Nasdaq: AEP) plans to invest about $4 billion in a 702-megawatt (MW) fuel cell generation project near Cheyenne, Wyoming. The project relies on a 20-year power purchase agreement (PPA) with Google. According to AEP, the transaction marks a step in its strategy to serve growing demand from large-scale customers.

A project company approximately 92% owned by AEP

Google will purchase power from Cheyenne Fuel Cell, LLC, which is approximately 92% owned and controlled by AEP. Funds advised by Basalt Infrastructure Partners, LLP hold nearly 8% of the company. AEP and its partners plan to start construction in 2026, and the facility is expected to be fully operational by the end of 2028.

Other recent announcements involve hydrogen technologies. EDF is preparing the sale of its hydrogen subsidiary Hynamics to HY24 in early 2027, while Ballard has won a 4.8 MW order from Siemens Mobility for Romania's hydrogen trains. Meanwhile, tesa has secured 500 tonnes of green hydrogen from EWE for Hamburg.

Bloom Energy technology without natural gas combustion

The facility uses fuel cell technology developed by Bloom Energy. According to AEP, the technology can be deployed rapidly and provide reliable, on-demand power for large-load customers. It generates electricity without combustion of natural gas, and the project includes plans to integrate carbon capture technology to deliver reliable, near-zero-emissions power.

"As power demand continues to grow, AEP is bringing together new technologies and strong partnerships to deliver reliable, innovative energy solutions quickly and at scale," said Bill Fehrman, AEP chairman, president and chief executive officer. The development and construction of the facility support Google's growing energy needs in the greater Cheyenne area. The project follows agreements reached between Google and Black Hills Corp., effective Sept. 30.

text:
Texas Border Business

SAN ANTONIO, Texas – The North American Development Bank (NADBank) announced the launch of the Access to Financing Program (AFP), a new financing tool that will expand access to funding for environmental projects in the U.S.-Mexico border region through qualified financial intermediaries.

NADBank will make up to US$300 million available for both public and private sector through financial institutions under the program.

Through this initiative, NADBank will expand support for investments in strategic sectors, prioritizing projects related to drinking water, wastewater, water conservation, solid waste management, air quality, energy and energy efficiency. Eligible initiatives include infrastructure and equipment for water projects, wastewater treatment, low-emission technologies, energy generation and storage, energy efficiency, and high-performance buildings.

“Approval of the AFP will allow us to reach more projects by mobilizing greater investment through financial intermediaries and expanding our impact in sectors that are critical to the development of the border region. In addition, it will support the efforts of the governments of the United States and Mexico to promote economic growth and competitiveness along the border. At the same time, it will help strengthen access to essential services such as water, sanitation and electricity that families rely on every day,” said John Beckham, Managing Director of NADBank.

Through financial intermediaries, the program will channel funding to smaller-scale initiatives that often face barriers to accessing long-term financing, allowing NADBank to expand the reach of its financing activities under its mandate. Loans under the AFP may be structured as senior secured and unsecured corporate loans, bond issuances or structured corporate financing through special-purpose vehicles (SPV) or with asset-backed securities (ABS).

Through the AFP, NADBank reaffirms its commitment to financing infrastructure and initiatives that protect the environment, strengthen regional development and generate benefits for border communities.

Buyers, for their part, rushed to beat the tax credit deadline, pushing EVs to 11.3% of new vehicle sales in September 2025. But by November 2025, after the tax credits ended,
their share dropped to 4.3%
.
As 2026 progressed and gas prices began to rise, so did EV demand. New EV inventories declined, shrinking from about
130 days of supply
in the first quarter of 2026 to
78 days
by August – just two days above the supply level of gas-burning cars.
Discounts on new EV models shrank too. My analysis of
online listings from marketcheck.com
shows the median new EV was listed 9.8% below sticker price in February. By April, the median discount was 6.6%, and 4.7% in June. That’s a sign that dealers saw rising demand, not inventory to clear.
A run on used electric vehicles
Before the war, prices for used electric vehicles were still drifting down in the wake of the expired used EV federal tax credit. After the war began, they
climbed 13% through late June 2026
. For a typical used electric vehicle, that’s about $3,500 more.
Other data sources point in the same direction. Recurrent, a
company that reports on batteries and used EVs
, found that the price of a
used 2023 Chevrolet Bolt rose almost 20%
from January to June 2026.
And inventories of used electric vehicles dropped too, with
only 31 days of supply in May
, 23% below the year before.
A costly misreading
None of this means the electric vehicle market is healthy. High prices and uncertain access to charging stations
are real stumbling blocks for people who are thinking about buying an EV
.
But the data doesn’t support the claim that electric vehicle sales stalled in 2026 because Americans don’t want them. Rather, the sales stalled because there weren’t enough EVs available to buy – and there were plenty of hybrids as an alternative.
The distinction matters because automakers have treated a change in the policy landscape as a change in consumer demand, leading to shortages with real costs.
The average new car now sells for about $50,000 and the average new electric vehicle for about $55,000, according to
Kelley Blue Book
, a company that tracks car prices.
The current situation leaves drivers exposed to the volatility of oil prices with fewer alternatives. The U.S. is the
world’s largest oil producer
, yet a war in the Persian Gulf raised gas prices significantly in just three months. Oil trades on a global market, so
American drivers pay global prices
.
Seven months into the war, the pressure on drivers is still
going full throttle
. Oil was still
above $100 a barrel
in mid-October, and
diesel hit a record $6.52 a gallon
on Sept. 22.
Electric vehicle sales haven’t caught up.
Argonne’s data
show 86,000 of them sold in August, fewer than the 101,000 sold in May, while hybrid sales stayed above 216,000 a month all summer.
A look ahead
Rather than move to increase electric vehicle supply and make them more affordable, federal policy continues to hinder the U.S. electric vehicle sector.
The
fuel economy rule released Sept. 28, 2026
, loosens efficiency requirements for gas-powered vehicles and in 2028 ends a system that let automakers that beat the standards – mostly EV makers –
earn credits for exceeding them
and sell those to automakers that fell short. That means automakers will have fewer regulatory incentives to produce EVs going forward.
Regulators say
buyers will save $1,289
on the purchase price of a new gas-powered vehicle from reduced engineering and manufacturing costs to make less efficient engines. But the same analysis estimates drivers will
spend about $1,600 more on gas
over the life of the car, and that’s using fuel price forecasts well below today’s prices.
Economists say
the
administration’s math does not properly account for
those fuel costs.
Chinese EV manufacturing is growing, but the U.S. market is mostly closed to those products and the companies that make them, and may get even more closed.
Kevin Frayer/Getty Images via The Conversation
The U.S. has also effectively shut out Chinese automakers, even though nearly three-quarters of the world’s electric cars
are built in China
. In 2024, Chinese car buyers could choose from over 130 EV models priced under $40,000; American buyers had
just four EV models under that threshold
. Beyond
tariffs of more than 100%
on EVs made in China, a
Commerce Department rule
bars cars from Chinese-linked automakers starting with model year 2027,
even if they are built in the U.S
. A
bill pending in Congress
would
widen the ban
, blocking Chinese investment in U.S. auto factories altogether.
As long as gas stays expensive, the gap between the electric vehicles Americans want and the electric vehicles dealers can sell them is likely to remain. Decisions such as ending the tax credit, rolling back fuel economy standards and banning Chinese technology all make it harder to build them, which means Americans will continue to have fewer affordable electric vehicles to choose from.

title: Can States Still Protect Public Health? The Risk of a Climate Regulatory Vacuum
authors: Erin Scott, Patrick Hauth, William Maione, Wendy E. Parmet, Shannon Rempe
description:
The case began in 2018 when Boulder County first filed its complaint against defendants, Exxon Mobil and Suncor (fossil fuel companies).
But both the state trial court and Colorado’s Supreme Court rejected defendant’s contention.
Suncor does not map cleanly on the traditional areas of preemption found in Supreme Court precedent.
However, if the Court finds state climate claims preempted, we may be left with a regulatory vacuum — especially as the Trump administration rolls back federal climate protections, and challenges to the EPA’s regulatory authority over greenhouse gases rise.
Again, state tobacco litigation illustrates the broader role state litigation can play in protecting public health when federal action falls short.
text:
On Oct. 5, 2026, the U.S. Supreme Court heard oral arguments in a case that has the potential to greatly impact state and local municipalities’ ability to fight widespread threats to public and environmental health. For more than eight years Boulder County, Colorado, has been locked in a protracted legal battle with prominent energy companies that produce, refine and market fossil fuels. The litigation, now Suncor Energy (U.S.A) Inc. v. County Commissioners of Boulder County, seeks to recover monetary relief to compensate the Plaintiff — Boulder County — for their past and future damages and costs related to mitigating the impact of climate change.

The case began in 2018 when Boulder County first filed its complaint against defendants, Exxon Mobil and Suncor (fossil fuel companies). Initially, the case bounced between state and federal court as judges grappled with venue challenges, leading to a recurring question about in which jurisdiction the case should be tried. Eventually, in 2023, the venue question was resolved when the Supreme Court denied the fossil fuel companies’ request to hear an appeal of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit’s decision remanding the case to state court where it was originally filed.

However, the fossil fuel companies were quick to present new challenges, this time based on preemption. But both the state trial court and Colorado’s Supreme Court rejected defendant’s contention.

Preemption, the concept that a higher level of government may limit or even eliminate the powers of a lower level of government, is a legal doctrine that on the federal level rests on the Supremacy Clause of the Constitution, which establishes federal supremacy over state law. Although preemption has been broadly used across the country and across party lines, in the last few years it has been used frequently by industry and in lockstep with the Trump Administration’s deregulatory agenda to weaken the ability of state and local governments to protect the health of their residents.

Suncor does not map cleanly on the traditional areas of preemption found in Supreme Court precedent. Typically, the Supreme Court has held that preemption can either be express, when it is called for in a specific provision in an act, implied from Congressional intent, or as a result of a conflict between state and federal law. The Clean Air Act does not contain any provision expressly preempting state regulation or tort liability for greenhouse-gas emissions, and there is no clear conflict between the federal and state laws in question nor any reason that both laws could not be followed simultaneously.

The fossil fuel companies argue that since pollution has an interstate impact, the states cannot regulate its emissions absent express authorization from Congress. If this argument is accepted by the Court, it could serve as rationale for preempting any state environmental laws or any other regulation not affirmatively authorized by Congress. This could dramatically eviscerate the states’ police power.

Suncor also argues that the states cannot act because the alleged harm relates to foreign affairs as greenhouse-gas emissions are “inherently transboundary.” From this, Suncor concludes that the issue falls within the federal government’s exclusive power over foreign relations. While previous Supreme Court cases like Crosby or Garamendi have found preemption of claims related to foreign affairs, extending that precedent to this case would again dramatically undercut the states’ police power, potentially barring a state from pursuing any civil justice claims for environmental harms as the EPA continues to leave gaps in enforcement.

Suncor marks one of many lawsuits seeking to hold fossil-fuel companies accountable for climate-related costs that the companies’ conduct has left states and local communities to bear. Local governments bear substantial costs associated with climate change, while fossil-fuel producers have historically not been required to pay or compensate for the costs created by fossil fuel-related climate change. These lawsuits seek to hold the companies responsible for the environmental and health harms they cause. The Supreme Court’s decision in Suncor could shape the future of many of these similar cases nationwide.

In many ways, this recent batch of climate change lawsuits echo state tobacco litigation in the 1990s, a comparison Justice Kagan also drew during oral arguments. Those lawsuits recovered billions of dollars from tobacco companies for harms caused by their products. That history helps explain the approach and appeal of climate suits seeking to hold a handful of companies accountable for profiting while leaving the public to bear the enormous costs of climate change.

However, if the Court finds state climate claims preempted, we may be left with a regulatory vacuum — especially as the Trump administration rolls back federal climate protections, and challenges to the EPA’s regulatory authority over greenhouse gases rise. If the Court accepts the fossil fuel companies’ argument that climate change’s national and global reach puts these claims beyond state power, communities could be left without meaningful federal protection or state remedies.

Again, state tobacco litigation illustrates the broader role state litigation can play in protecting public health when federal action falls short. When tobacco’s public health harms went largely unaddressed by the federal government, state lawsuits helped pressure tobacco companies to accept broad restrictions on advertising and marketing. Whether climate lawsuits can play a similar role is a question the Court may answer in Suncor.

Preemption, however, is not the only question before the Court in Suncor. The Court also opted to address Boulder County’s questions regarding whether the Court had jurisdiction (either by statute or Article III of the Constitution) to even review the Colorado Supreme Court’s interlocutory decision. But only Justices Sotomayor and Jackson seemed interested in pressing that issue at oral argument; most of the Court’s questions instead focused on preemption.

Ultimately, past preemption precedent does not offer a clear prediction of the outcome. On Sept. 28, Justice Alito, who faced pressure to step aside because he owns stock in two oil companies, recused himself. This leaves eight justices to decide on an issue that will impact state public health and environmental protection authorities’ ability to address the harms and protect their residents from the rising costs of climate change.

title: Environmental groups push back against EPA delays on regulating big oil, gas

text:
WASHINGTON — Judges grilled Environmental Protection Agency attorneys for more evidence supporting its decision to delay regulations on methane from gas and oil operators Wednesday at a federal appeals court.

In November 2025, the EPA issued a delay rule, pushing compliance deadlines for new sources of gas and oil emissions to January 2027. For existing sources, the rule gave states until January 2027 to submit compliance plans and gave operators up to 36 months, until January 2030, to carry them out, according to Alexandra Schluntz, a senior attorney at Earthjustice, an environmental organization that was among the groups that sued the EPA in 2025.

Attorneys for the groups, including the Environmental Defense Fund, called for the delay rule to be vacated, claiming the agency did not provide enough concrete evidence and data to show it considered the emissions consequences. Under legal precedent, the agency must undergo an extensive review before making substantive changes, Environmental Defense Fund attorney Grace Smith argued.

“Because of that lack of data, EPA cannot critically evaluate the petitioner’s statement,” Smith said.

Justice Department attorneys disputed this. Deputy Assistant Attorney General Robert Stander said the extensions were “limited” and rationalized by the EPA.

Stander said the agency considered emissions consequences, granting extensions after reviewing petitions with data and technical reports from industry representatives, who argued they could not meet the 2024 Rule.

“A comment from the industry is evidence,” Stander said.

However, judges cast doubt on whether the EPA provided enough evidence to back its extensions. Several asked for more explicit proof that the EPA had considered the emissions consequences of pushing back the deadlines.

Judge Judith Rogers pressed the EPA’s attorneys on how the agency reached its decision, noting the lack of public health discussion in the agency’s brief. She said she saw no analysis in the agency’s five-volume brief that explained the EPA’s decision.

“The natural question is why is that (decision) not arbitrary,” Rogers said.

Judges also questioned the practicality of reinstating the original deadlines after vacating the delay rule. Judge Bradley Garcia questioned whether operators had enough time to comply after the old deadlines snapped back into place.

The case is one of several pending lawsuits challenging environmental rollbacks by the Trump administration across multiple industries. In March 2025, the EPA announced it would reconsider regulation of the oil and gas industry, as part of a larger push for environmental deregulation.

The announcement marked a departure from the 2024 Rule, which expanded environmental regulation under the Biden administration. The rule set compliance deadlines for both new and existing oil and gas facilities, aiming to cut methane and other volatile organic compounds that contribute to ozone depletion, air pollution and public health concerns.

Schluntz said she thinks that the delay rule could be a precursor to a more sweeping rollback on the 2024 Rule.

“The delay rule was an attempt by the administration to buy time as a stopgap measure to pause these compliance requirements while they undo the underlying substantive requirements,” Schluntz claimed.

However, Ohio Chief Deputy Solicitor General John Kerkhoff defended the extended timeline, arguing that Ohio needed more time to comply with environmental regulations because of its many oil and gas operations.

Max Sarinsky, legal director of the Institute for Policy Integrity at New York University, a nonpartisan think tank that filed an amicus brief in support of the environmental groups, said the institute weighed in because of the overall benefits to combatting climate change and improving public health.

“They’ve basically taken decades of science and economics that EPA has honed over time and thrown it out the window with very little explanation,” Sarinsky said.

However, Stanford University professor Deborah Sivas, co-director of the Environmental Law Clinic, said even if environmental groups prevail, the road to full compliance from companies and states could drag because operators aren’t moving toward compliance and are waiting for the Trump administration to propose a new rule that would not just delay, but remove regulation.

On Oct. 7, the EPA said it was “days away” from unveiling its proposal for rolling back regulation on oil and gas companies.

“It could be a short-lived victory if EPA comes out with a new rule,” Sivas said.

title: US is reviving shuttered nuclear plants to meet growing electricity demand and to power data centers
description:
The United States is making an unprecedented attempt to revive three shuttered nuclear plants to meet rising energy demand, including from large-scale data centers.
The Trump administration is pushing hard to deploy nuclear power for artificial intelligence and manufacturing.
It's also lending billions of dollars for upgrades to produce more electricity from currently operating nuclear plants.
Holtec says its efforts will restore baseload power, strengthen energy security and demonstrate the role of nuclear energy in meeting the nation's growing electricity demands.
Industry group says reactors shouldn't close early The World Nuclear Association said restarting nuclear reactors should be celebrated, but preventing them from closing prematurely would be the best option.
text:
The United States is making an unprecedented attempt to revive three shuttered nuclear plants to meet rising energy demand, including from large-scale data centers.

No commercial nuclear reactor is known to have resumed generating electricity after beginning the decommissioning process that takes one out of service, though some reactors have restarted after long outages.

The Department of Energy is lending as much as $4.4 billion to restart the Palisades Power Plant in Michigan, the Crane Clean Energy Center on Pennsylvania's Three Mile Island and the Duane Arnold Energy Center in Iowa to restore a combined 2.25 gigawatts of electricity, which can power roughly 2 million homes and businesses. All three of the plants closed before their licenses expired, largely because the electricity they produced was considered too expensive.

Not anymore. Two of the plants have contracts with Big Tech companies that will pay a premium to get large amounts of carbon-free energy for data centers. The Trump administration is pushing hard to deploy nuclear power for artificial intelligence and manufacturing. It's also lending billions of dollars for upgrades to produce more electricity from currently operating nuclear plants.

Restarting a reactor is a fairly quick way to get a lot of electricity, and it's cheaper than building a new, large reactor, said nuclear engineering expert Todd Allen.

“There's a demand in the country for more power,” he said. “You have these assets that were previously hooked up. They were previously operable, and you can relatively quickly get them generating electricity again, compared to your other possibilities. For anyone who wants zero carbon, nuclear provides that. For the Trump administration, which really wants nuclear, this fits that story also.”

Restarting a reactor is kind of like restoring a car

Allen compared restarting a decommissioned nuclear plant to restarting a car that sat idle for a few years. The driver still needs a valid license and all the parts need to be working correctly.

“That’s what they’re trying to do with these nuclear plants, but it’s a much bigger, complicated system,” said Allen, associate dean for research at the University of Michigan's College of Engineering.

With a nuclear plant, the owner has to bring nuclear workers back and ensure their training is current, make sure everything is working and that maintenance is up to date, ensure they have enough fuel and ask regulators to restore their operating license, he added.

Allen said it's a lot to keep track of, but it's relatively straightforward.

Expert says restarts are risky

Edwin Lyman, at the Union of Concerned Scientists, said the taxpayer money being used should go toward addressing safety risks. For example, most U.S. plants were built between 1970 and 1990 and were designed to withstand natural disasters of that era, said Lyman, director of nuclear power safety at UCS. But climate change is making extreme weather events more frequent and severe.

“It’s possible, if they set the right level of safety and spend the necessary funds to meet that, they could restore these plants to operable condition,” he said. “That's not happening at this point.”

Iowa’s only nuclear facility, Duane Arnold, began operating in 1975. It was scheduled to permanently close in October 2020. Replacing it with cheaper energy sources, including wind, was projected to save Iowa customers $300 million in energy costs. The plant shut down early, in August 2020, when it was damaged during a powerful storm known as a derecho.

NextEra Energy owns Duane Arnold. Looking at its condition, CEO John Ketchum said company officials “felt really good about the ability to bring it back.”

Palisades plant is the furthest along

The Palisades plant operated from 1971 until 2022, when its owner, Entergy, left the nuclear power business. The plant's operating license lasted until 2031.

Holtec International bought it and began dismantling it, though none of the steps were irreversible. Michigan officials, not wanting to lose nuclear jobs or energy, encouraged Holtec to pursue reopening the plant and provided state funding. The Biden administration in 2024 approved a $1.5 billion loan to restart the facility, and the Trump administration continued the payments.

In August, Holtec began loading nuclear fuel, one of the final major phases before a reactor can restart. The company paused the process after a fuel assembly tilted from its upright position and Holtec determined it needed to figure out why. Its power purchase agreements require Palisades to be in service by March 2027.

Holtec says its efforts will restore baseload power, strengthen energy security and demonstrate the role of nuclear energy in meeting the nation's growing electricity demands.

Big Tech will purchase power for data centers

NextEra Energy and Google are collaborating to restart Duane Arnold by early 2029.

“This is a perfect example of data centers paying their own way,” Ketchum said in an interview. “We’re able to sign a long-term contract with a hyperscaler for that project. So none of the costs are being paid by residential customers in Iowa.”

Microsoft has a contract with the Crane Clean Energy Center on Three Mile Island just outside Harrisburg. The plant was the site of the nation’s worst commercial nuclear power accident in 1979. The accident destroyed one reactor, leaving the plant with one functioning. In 2019, Constellation Energy’s then-parent company Exelon shut down the functioning reactor, saying it was losing money and that Pennsylvania lawmakers had refused to subsidize it.

Constellation Energy announced in 2024 that it would spend $1.6 billion to restart the reactor under a 20-year agreement with Microsoft. It hopes to bring the plant back online in 2027. The Energy Department provided a $1 billion loan, and Deputy Energy Secretary James Danly took a tour last week.

Jack Spencer at The Heritage Foundation said he can't think of a worse use of taxpayer money than using it to restart reactors. These are low-risk projects where there is a massive demand for the energy, so there is no reason to funnel federal dollars to these companies, said Spencer, director of the foundation's Center for Energy, Climate and Environment.

Conversely, Jennifer Gordon at the Atlantic Council said she thinks it's a terrific way of leveraging federal financing to get needed electricity. Gordon directs the council's Nuclear Energy Policy Initiative.

Industry group says reactors shouldn't close early

The World Nuclear Association said restarting nuclear reactors should be celebrated, but preventing them from closing prematurely would be the best option.

Palisades is expected to be the first nuclear plant in the world to resume generating power after beginning the decommissioning process, but other countries have restarted or refurbished reactors after long-term shutdowns, the association said. That includes Canada, Armenia, Belgium, Japan, India and South Korea. Others are considering or in the process of restarting reactors.

___

Associated Press writer Sarah Rankin in Richmond, Virginia, contributed to this report.

text:
Global EV sales reached 2.15 million in in September 2026, a 17% month-on-month increase but a 2% year-on-year decrease.

This is according to the latest forges from Benchmark Mineral Intelligence (BMI), which published its EV sales figures today. In the first nine months of the year, total EV sales reached 15.5 million, up from year-to-date sales of 13.4 million in August and up 3% from the same period in 2025.

However, while China was the only country to sell more than one million EVs, the China sales figures of 1.11 million are down 13% over the same period in 2025, which BMI attributed to “subdued” demand from domestic consumers, which has encouraged Chinese manufacturers to export their products overseas.

Passenger car NEV exports out of China reached 558,000 in September, a record figure, but BMI noted that an upcoming cap on imports of hybrid vehicles from China to Europe at 350,000 a year—agreed between China and the EU this week and to take effect from December—could interfere with this trade dynamic. The European Commission expects this to more than halve shipments of EVs from China to the EU, which stood at around 800,000 prior to the cap.

Strong sales in Europe, year-on-year declines in North America

Meanwhile, Europe and the rest of the world saw a 30% and 93% year-on-year increase, respectively, to almost 600,000 and 310,000. BMI data manager Charles Lester said that the European sales were its “strongest month on record”.

“Europe had its strongest month on record, with almost 600,000 EVs sold in September, 10% above the previous high set in June,” said Lester. “Sales were up 39% year-on-year, led by battery electric vehicles, which grew 50%, while plug-in hybrids grew a more modest 16%. The UK, France, Spain, Portugal and Finland all posted record monthly EV sales.”

Lester’s comments are supported by data from New AutoMotive, which put battery EV registrations in the UK in September at 99,827, a record figure. Across Europe more broadly, sales rose 62% month-on-month and 39% year-on-year, with battery EVs driving much of this growth, with a 50% year-on-year increase in sales. Plug-in hybrid sales, meanwhile, had a more “modest” year-on-year growth figure of 16%.

North America saw the lowest number of year-to-date sales in the regions covered by the BMI figures, with 1.2 million sales in the first nine months of the year. This is a 24% year-on-year decline in sales over this period, and September alone saw 44% fewer EV sales than September 2025.

BMI attributed this decline not to poor performance in 2026 per se, but better-than-expected sales figures in 2025. Last September, US buyers rushed to purchase EVs ahead of the end of tax credit support at the end of the month. While some customers saw their tax credits extended into October, the policy disruption drove significant purchasing activity in September, which BMI says makes it difficult to make fair year-on-year comparisons.

“From October onward, year-on-year figures will be measured against the first months without the tax credit in the US, when EV sales collapsed, so the region’s year-on-year declines should narrow significantly,” said BMI in a statement.

description:
If there was ever a moment for Americans to switch to electric vehicles, this was it.
But the data doesn’t support the claim that electric vehicle sales stalled in 2026 because Americans don’t want them.
A look ahead Rather than move to increase electric vehicle supply and make them more affordable, federal policy continues to hinder the U.S. electric vehicle sector.
