text:
Within three months of the U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran on Feb. 28, 2026, the average price of gasoline for American drivers climbed from US$2.94 to $4.35 a gallon. If there was ever a moment for Americans to switch to electric vehicles, this was it.

From March to May 2026, in fact, sales of hybrid electric vehicles were 18% higher than over the same months in 2025.

But sales of fully electric vehicles were 16% lower from March to May 2026 compared with the same months in 2025. Some observers took that as evidence that high gas prices alone wouldn’t push Americans toward fully electric cars, but that conclusion misses half the story.

I study car buyers and their preferences, and there is an important distinction between what consumers want and what they can actually buy. Sales reveal what cars people actually bought, but not necessarily what they actually wanted.

When the supply of some kinds of cars can’t keep up with demand, prices rise, and that’s exactly what happened for electric vehicles in 2026.

An industry in retreat

In 2026, hybrids and all-electric vehicles faced the same jump in demand from the oil crisis. While there were plenty of hybrids available to meet that demand, the same was not true for EVs.

Hybrid production had been growing for years, led by Toyota, which sells about half of the hybrids bought in the United States. As a result, even as sales surged, hybrid inventories on dealer lots were 19% higher in March 2026 than they had been a year earlier.

However, EV production had been in retreat since the tax and spending law President Donald Trump signed in July 2025 ended federal tax credits for EVs. Buyers had been able to get up to $7,500 for new EVs and $4,000 for used ones, but that ended after Sept. 30, 2025.

Automakers responded by cutting back their EV production. General Motors laid off more than 3,400 workers at its EV and battery plants and shifted its Tennessee plant to make batteries for energy storage, not cars. Ford wrote off $19.5 billion from its EV business, ended production of the all-electric F-150 Lightning and converted a Tennessee EV plant to build gas-powered trucks.

Buyers, for their part, rushed to beat the tax credit deadline, pushing EVs to 11.3% of new vehicle sales in September 2025. But by November 2025, after the tax credits ended, their share dropped to 4.3%.

As 2026 progressed and gas prices began to rise, so did EV demand. New EV inventories declined, shrinking from about 130 days of supply in the first quarter of 2026 to 78 days by August – just two days above the supply level of gas-burning cars.

Discounts on new EV models shrank too. My analysis of online listings from marketcheck.com shows the median new EV was listed 9.8% below sticker price in February. By April, the median discount was 6.6%, and 4.7% in June. That’s a sign that dealers saw rising demand, not inventory to clear.

A run on used electric vehicles

Before the war, prices for used electric vehicles were still drifting down in the wake of the expired used EV federal tax credit. After the war began, they climbed 13% through late June 2026. For a typical used electric vehicle, that’s about $3,500 more.

Other data sources point in the same direction. Recurrent, a company that reports on batteries and used EVs, found that the price of a used 2023 Chevrolet Bolt rose almost 20% from January to June 2026.

And inventories of used electric vehicles dropped too, with only 31 days of supply in May, 23% below the year before.

A costly misreading

None of this means the electric vehicle market is healthy. High prices and uncertain access to charging stations are real stumbling blocks for people who are thinking about buying an EV.

But the data doesn’t support the claim that electric vehicle sales stalled in 2026 because Americans don’t want them. Rather, the sales stalled because there weren’t enough EVs available to buy – and there were plenty of hybrids as an alternative.

The distinction matters because automakers have treated a change in the policy landscape as a change in consumer demand, leading to shortages with real costs.

The average new car now sells for about $50,000 and the average new electric vehicle for about $55,000, according to Kelley Blue Book, a company that tracks car prices.

The current situation leaves drivers exposed to the volatility of oil prices with fewer alternatives. The U.S. is the world’s largest oil producer, yet a war in the Persian Gulf raised gas prices significantly in just three months. Oil trades on a global market, so American drivers pay global prices.

Seven months into the war, the pressure on drivers is still going full throttle. Oil was still above $100 a barrel in mid-October, and diesel hit a record $6.52 a gallon on Sept. 22.

Electric vehicle sales haven’t caught up. Argonne’s data show 86,000 of them sold in August, fewer than the 101,000 sold in May, while hybrid sales stayed above 216,000 a month all summer.

A look ahead

Rather than move to increase electric vehicle supply and make them more affordable, federal policy continues to hinder the U.S. electric vehicle sector.

The fuel economy rule released Sept. 28, 2026, loosens efficiency requirements for gas-powered vehicles and in 2028 ends a system that let automakers that beat the standards – mostly EV makers – earn credits for exceeding them and sell those to automakers that fell short. That means automakers will have fewer regulatory incentives to produce EVs going forward.

Regulators say buyers will save $1,289 on the purchase price of a new gas-powered vehicle from reduced engineering and manufacturing costs to make less efficient engines. But the same analysis estimates drivers will spend about $1,600 more on gas over the life of the car, and that’s using fuel price forecasts well below today’s prices. Economists say the administration’s math does not properly account for those fuel costs.

The U.S. has also effectively shut out Chinese automakers, even though nearly three-quarters of the world’s electric cars are built in China. In 2024, Chinese car buyers could choose from over 130 EV models priced under $40,000; American buyers had just four EV models under that threshold. Beyond tariffs of more than 100% on EVs made in China, a Commerce Department rule bars cars from Chinese-linked automakers starting with model year 2027, even if they are built in the U.S. A bill pending in Congress would widen the ban, blocking Chinese investment in U.S. auto factories altogether.

As long as gas stays expensive, the gap between the electric vehicles Americans want and the electric vehicles dealers can sell them is likely to remain. Decisions such as ending the tax credit, rolling back fuel economy standards and banning Chinese technology all make it harder to build them, which means Americans will continue to have fewer affordable electric vehicles to choose from.

text:
XBM and SiCAM Technologies join forces to develop a sustainable, ultra-high-density battery technology using locally sourced materials for drones and electric aircraft.

Lithium-sulfur cathode developer Xponential Battery Materials (XBM) and silicon-carbon anode specialist SiCAM Technologies have entered into a technology partnership to create a new silicon-sulfur battery materials platform tailored for US battery original equipment manufacturers (OEMs).

The collaborative platform will combine SiCAM’s silicon-carbon (Si-C) anode material with XBM’s lithium-sulfur (Li-S) cathode technology and cell architecture.

According to the two companies, silicon-sulfur batteries offer significantly higher theoretical energy density compared to conventional lithium-ion cells. The primary components are widely available within the region: silicon is the second most abundant element in the Earth’s crust, while sulfur is produced as a byproduct of US petroleum refining.

Whereas most Si-C anode developers rely on silane via a chemical vapour deposition (CVD) process, SiCAM employs trichlorosilane within a fluidized-bed CVD setup. This fluidized-bed method is engineered to form a bonded silicon-composite primary structure, helping to mitigate the 300% swelling typically experienced by silicon during charge and discharge cycles. SiCAM holds the exclusive licence for this patented anode material and is currently working towards commercialising the technology and establishing manufacturing facilities in the US.

XBM’s CarbonX cathode material is derived from lignin, a byproduct of the US paper pulping industry. The cathode utilises porous carbon created through a proprietary sol-gel process and infused with sulfur and catalysts, a design intended to enhance sulfur utilisation, extend cycle life, and boost cell-level energy density.

Phillip Roberts, co-founder of both SiCAM Technologies and XBM, noted that the collaboration represents a natural step in advancing a sustainable battery vision that bypasses traditional chemistries reliant on mined, costly, and foreign-controlled supply chains.

Jon Shan, Chief Technology Officer at XBM, stated that the immediate objective is to refine the high-capacity Li-S cathode and Si-C anode integration. The resulting silicon-sulfur platform will initially target lightweight, high-energy-density eMobility applications, including electric vertical take-off and landing (eVTOL) aircraft and drones.

text:
By Amir Orusov

Oct 16 (Reuters) – Global demand for electric vehicles fell 2% in September, ending six consecutive months of growth, as ​record sales in Europe were not ‌enough to offset sharp declines in North America and China, data from UK-based research firm Benchmark Mineral Intelligence showed on Friday.

The data highlights growing ‌divergence ​across major EV markets. Europe ⁠is benefiting from ⁠strong consumer demand and policy support, while China’s domestic market remains weak and North America continues to feel the impact of ​the expiration of US federal EV tax credits at the end of September ⁠2025.

• Global EV sales ⁠slid to 2.15 million vehicles ​in September, while year-to-date volumes are up 3% at ​15.5 million units

• “Europe had its strongest month ‌on record, with almost 600,000 EVs sold in September, 10% above the previous high set in June,” BMI data manager Charles ⁠Lester said

• North American sales fell 44%, the steepest monthly decline this year, reflecting the strong ⁠year-ago period ‌when buyers rushed to dealerships ⁠before the tax credits expired

• From ​the ‌fourth quarter, these comparisons will ease ​as they ⁠lap the post-tax-credit slump, Lester said

• Sales in China dropped 18% to 1.11 million vehicles, prompting carmakers to increasingly rely on exports

(Reporting by Amir Orusov in Gdansk, editing by ​Milla Nissi-Prussak)

description:

Solar photovoltaics (PV) alone accounted for 234 projects and Rs 401 crore ($42 million), more than hydrogen, energy efficiency, transport and CCUS combined.

text:
India spent about Rs 1,443 crore ($151 million) on 1,359 publicly funded clean energy research, development and demonstration (RD&D) projects between 2019 and 2024, but the funding remains concentrated in a few technologies and is yet to adequately build the production capabilities needed to support the country’s clean energy manufacturing ambitions, according to a new study.

The projects, spread across more than 90 institutions, cover renewables, other power and storage, hydrogen and fuel cells, transport and electric mobility, energy efficiency, and carbon capture, utilisation and storage (CCUS). The database is one of the first consolidated assessments of India’s publicly funded clean energy RD&D ecosystem.

The report by the Sustainable Futures Collaborative (SFC) and the Climate Policy Lab at The Fletcher School, Tufts University, found that renewables accounted for 421 projects and Rs 580 crore (61 million), followed by other power and storage with 333 projects and Rs 492 crore (52 million). Together, the two categories absorbed about three quarters of declared funding. Solar photovoltaics (PV) alone accounted for 234 projects and Rs 401 crore ($42 million), more than hydrogen, energy efficiency, transport and CCUS combined.

The findings come as green industrialisation takes centre stage ahead of the 31st Conference of the Parties (COP31) in Turkey next month. The report’s assessment is that India’s challenge is no longer simply how much it spends on clean energy RD&D, but whether that spending is building the technological capabilities needed for its energy, industrial and climate objectives.

The authors caution that the database is based on publicly available information and is therefore a large sample rather than a complete census of India’s clean energy RD&D. It does not capture the substantial body of private sector research and innovation, while some industry linked and demonstration activity may not be visible in public disclosures.

The concentration is sharper when funding rather than project numbers is considered. Budget information was available for about 85 per cent of the portfolio. The Department of Science and Technology was the largest funder, accounting for Rs 401 crore (42 million) across 705 projects, or 52 per cent of the portfolio by project count. The Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (37 million) across only 39 projects. The Council of Scientific and Industrial Research accounted for Rs 170 crore (18 million), while the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology accounted for Rs 66 crore (8 million), largely concentrated in batteries, the report said.

The study found that the portfolio is strongest in early stage laboratory research, materials development and component level innovation, with comparatively less visible activity at the prototype, pilot scale and demonstration stages. This creates a gap between research and deployment, commonly referred to as the “valley of death”.

A key concern is the type of innovation being funded. The report said public RD&D is increasingly important as India’s ambitions move beyond installing clean energy capacity towards making technologies domestically, competitively and at scale. Achieving that requires knowledge of production processes, materials, systems integration and scale up.

The report argues that spreading limited resources across technologies without explicit choices on concentration and sequencing can produce breadth without sufficient depth. Funding systems designed for small investigator-led research grants are less suited to pilot manufacturing, process development and demonstration, which require larger budgets, longer time horizons and sustained collaboration among laboratories, firms and equipment suppliers.

This is particularly relevant given India’s continuing dependence on imported clean energy technologies and components. The report points to reliance on imported polysilicon, wafers and production equipment in solar, as well as limited domestic supplies of battery cell materials. It also cites research showing that a battery manufacturing programme designed to establish 50 gigawatt hours (GWh) of domestic cell capacity had commissioned only 1.4 GWh, or 2.8 per cent of its target, with zero incentives disbursed. Domestic dependence on imported battery cells remained close to 100 per cent.

“RD&D builds the knowledge base that makes industrial policy productive,” the report said, noting that public research can help domestic institutions accumulate expertise in design, process engineering, materials science and systems integration.

The study also found that project funding is relatively uniform despite differences in the type of research being undertaken. Many projects receive relatively small grants, while projects requiring pilot-scale development or manufacturing demonstration need substantially larger, longer-term support. The report said India’s RD&D system would benefit from a broader mix of funding instruments suited to different stages of innovation.

The report concluded that India needs to identify where deeper domestic technological capability is required, where adapting existing technologies is sufficient, and how research can connect more effectively with manufacturing, demonstration and deployment.

text:
Brian McLain is a co-chair of the Iowa Democratic Party’s Platform Committee and former chair of the party’s Progressive Caucus.

Every two years, hundreds of Iowa Democratic Party members come together to determine the direction they want the Party to go. It is a long process requiring hours of meetings, debate, and discussion that eventually culminates in a single document, offering a picture of where the base stands on the issues at the time. It is truly one of the most democratic processes that one can take part in and a testament to what can be achieved in a party whose members don’t always see eye to eye with each other.

Typically this document is available on the Iowa Democratic Party website after the bi-annual convention. However, for some unknown reason the 2026 platform has not been published yet. So in honor of the hard work that the Platform Committee has put into this document, we are taking it upon ourselves to bring the platform to you through this medium.

Unlike the Republican Party’s platform, there is an incredible amount of nuance in the Iowa Democratic Platform, which comes from its members’ lived experiences. That can make the platform difficult to comprehend and intimidating. For that reason, some have called for shortening or eliminating the document. title: From Metal Casting to Batteries--Different Products, Same Commitment to Craftsmanship
description:
As Toyota expanded its in-house production of battery electric vehicle (BEV) batteries, the company needed a new site capable of mass production.
Only two were from the Myochi Plant, with the rest having been gathered from Shimoyama and other facilities throughout the company.
To determine the position of every pillar and every door, GM Kato and his team made countless visits to the site and ran many simulations using design software.
Three years after construction began, the building began operating as a battery plant.
The shift to a battery plant also meant big changes for those who work there.
text:
Myochi reached a major turning point around 2020. As Toyota consolidated its driveline production to strengthen competitiveness, CV joints and other components made at sister plant Miyoshi were transferred to JTEKT, while Miyoshi was reorganized as a hub specializing in driveline production.

As part of this consolidation, differentials and other components produced at Myochi were moved to Miyoshi. The remaining production lines, including those for the Land Cruiser 250, are scheduled to be transferred to JTEKT Gear Systems by the end of 2028. Plant General Manager Kazuaki Takahashi recalls the growing sense of urgency as work at Myochi declined.

As production was consolidated, empty spaces began to appear throughout the plant. Takahashi realized that these scattered pockets of vacant floor space would make it difficult to respond quickly when new work arrived. Therefore, he consolidated the remaining lines into one area, creating a large, continuous space for future production.

Despite their uncertain future, Takahashi continued to reassure his Genba employees.

Just as the shift toward electrification was accelerating, Myochi was freeing up space. As Toyota expanded its in-house production of battery electric vehicle (BEV) batteries, the company needed a new site capable of mass production.

Through repeated changes, such as driveline transfers and the consolidation of casting operations, Myochi strengthened its people and production capabilities, preparing itself for whatever came next.

The task of carrying out this “plant within a plant” approach fell to Global Battery Manufacturing Division GM Yoshikazu Kato, who began his career as a Foundry Division technician and had chiefly worked on automation equipment within the Myochi Plant.

One Saturday in May 2022, GM Kato was at work on a day off when his supervisor suddenly informed him of the assignment: “Within three years, a battery line will start up at either Myochi or Shimoyama, and we want you to play a key role there.” The assembled team had fewer than ten members. Only two were from the Myochi Plant, with the rest having been gathered from Shimoyama and other facilities throughout the company. None had any experience working with batteries.

Kato’s job was to design a layout that managed to incorporate the PPES Himeji Plant’s equipment specifications within the confines of the Myochi building. Previously used as a foundry, the structure’s footprint was 30% smaller than the Himeji Plant, and its existing pillars could not be moved. He also found pillars that were irregularly spaced, as well as walls and pipes that did not show up in the drawings.

Kato recalls those early days:

For certain production steps, the equipment required a height of nearly 12 meters. Where there was not enough vertical clearance, even newly finished floors had to be dug up.

To determine the position of every pillar and every door, GM Kato and his team made countless visits to the site and ran many simulations using design software. After much painstaking deliberation, GM Kato presented his layout proposal to Plant General Manager Takahashi.

Once coated in layers of sand and dust from casting molds, the building was now stripped of all walls and interior fixtures, transforming into a vast, empty space whose only features were the exposed steel beams. Workers repaired the leaky roof, and one by one dug up the old pipes and metal frames missing from the blueprints, diligently stripping away half a century of grime as they went.

Three years after construction began, the building began operating as a battery plant.

Inside the transformed building lay the polar opposite of a foundry, a world where everything must be meticulously controlled. Foreign particles are controlled down to just a few dozen microns—roughly half the thickness of a human hair.

The temperature and humidity are tightly controlled, and employees cannot even drink water while working because introducing moisture can affect the environment. Covered head to toe in dust-proof suits and masks, employees are barely recognizable to their colleagues. The shift to a battery plant also meant big changes for those who work there.

text:
When nearly 1,000 maritime leaders gathered recently in New Orleans for the American Association of Port Authorities' annual convention, discussion focused on how small modular reactors, or SMRs, can help power U.S. ports and the maritime industry. This conversation featured top federal officials, port leaders from around the country and leading industry executives.

Currently, nearly 22 million workers help move more than 2 billion metric tons of cargo every year through U.S. ports. Everything in the average American home, from laptops to couches to medicine, moves through ports. It’s no surprise that American ports contribute $2.9 trillion to the U.S. gross domestic product. To move the goods for a growing economy and population, ports need more cranes, more terminals and more workers. Ports are adding electric cargo-handling equipment, power for docked vessels and cold storage for perishables. Ports must also operate through extreme weather, grid disruptions and other emergencies. So how do we power these 370 ports spread across 41 states, especially with growing demands?

SMRs for ports are a new type of nuclear reactor that can be manufactured faster, are far safer, are easier to transport than typical large-scale nuclear power plants and would reduce competition for electricity with other critical sectors. Given the nexus of energy and ports, there was no better place to have this conversation than New Orleans.

Fortunately, there is an undeniable momentum for nuclear energy at ports. For example, under the leadership of U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Maritime Administrator Stephen Carmel, the ports of Long Beach and Corpus Christi recently became the first U.S. ports to sign agreements with the Maritime Administration, or MARAD, to explore SMR technology for both commercial vessels and port operations. These partnerships will examine port microgrids, shoreside power and emerging vessel propulsion technology applications.

While nuclear energy may propel cargo ships across oceans, these partnerships envision broader potential for SMRs. A barge-mounted reactor at a port could power cranes during the day and an entire neighborhood at night. A reactor based at a port could also power communities impacted by a hurricane. SMRs will undoubtedly create new jobs for American workers.

One of my proudest accomplishments during my tenure as deputy maritime administrator was helping to lay the groundwork for the Port of Long Beach’s historic memorandum of cooperation with MARAD. While visiting ports across the country, I saw firsthand what can happen when federal officials, port leaders and private-sector innovators come together with an open mind.

A room with the right people, the right ideas and enthusiasm is a recipe for creative solutions. That spirit of collaboration, as demonstrated in New Orleans, is exactly what America needs as our ports continue to consider the next generation of maritime infrastructure.

The Port of New Orleans highlighted the critical importance of investment in our ports. In 2024, marine cargo activity through the port supported 342,150 U.S. jobs and generated $101.5 billion in economic value nationwide. Looking to the future, the port’s CEO, Beth Ann Branch, and her team sought and secured federal permitting from the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers to construct the $1.8 billion Louisiana International Terminal, or LIT, in St. Bernard Parish, which will significantly expand Gulf Coast container capacity.

Projects like LIT raise the important question of how additional energy requirements will be met. This question confronts ports across the country. A diverse energy portfolio, including expanded grid connections, energy storage, microgrids and other emerging technologies like SMRs, will be the answer.

Undoubtedly, nuclear technology must meet rigorous safety, security, environmental and regulatory standards. AAPA has called for clear federal permitting responsibilities and strong emergency-response protocols developed with the U.S. Coast Guard through meaningful public and stakeholder engagement.

America's ports are gateways to the global economy. They support jobs, manufacturing, agriculture, energy and national security. Our ports, however, require reliable, resilient and sufficient power to keep American commerce moving.

text:
Newsletters, Real Solutions

Low-Energy Friday: Permissionless Solar

As we all wait for voting on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 to commence, it seemed appropriate to discuss an idea and technology that has taken hold in other countries and is beginning to be adopted in the United States: Permissionless Solar.

In short, “permissionless solar” refers to solar panels specifically designed to integrate with the broader electric system without a permit or “permission” from a regulatory body. Most are simple enough that you don’t even need an electrician to install them. In practice, this means you can purchase a panel at your local big box retailer along with a gallon of milk. When you get home, you can stow the milk in the fridge and unbox the panel, appropriately orient it towards the sun, and plug it into the wall. Just as simply as you could plug in other appliances, whether a TV or a deep freezer.

It is well established that it costs more to install rooftop solar in the United States than in either Europe or Australia, even when the hardware costs are nearly the same. One component driving that difference is the cost of permitting and installation. And permitting is an important step when you’re affixing panels to roofs and hardwiring inverters and panels into a system that could potentially add power to the grid. On top of that, if you want to install rooftop solar, you need to own the roof, which only 53% of Americans do. If you’re in the 47% who don’t own your own home, solar is not an option, even in the face of increasing utility costs.

At least it wasn’t an option. Now that’s starting to change. Utah started a trend in 2025 with the passage of HB 340. Since then, 10 other states have passed legislation authorizing various forms of plug-in solar. Many others had bills introduced in 2026, with twenty-one of them likely to be reintroduced in 2027.

What does this look like in practice in Utah? The system can have an output no greater than 1,200 watts (about enough to power a microwave), has to have a standard 120 volt plug to plug into the wall, must be certified by an appropriate testing laboratory (UL or equivalent), compliant with the National Electric Code, and must contain anti-islanding protection (a safety feature that automatically shuts it down or disconnects it from the grid during power losses).

This last bit is critical, and a key piece of why this plug-in solar can be permissionless. When the power grid goes down, due to a squirrel making a questionable decision or a lightning strike causing a tree to topple some lines, the distribution system de-energizes for safety. When linesmen come to inspect the damage and determine the appropriate fix, they rely on those lines being “cold” so they can safely work with the lines and poles and return everything to service as quickly as possible. Without the anti-islanding protection scheme in the solar hardware, there is a risk the solar could push a current to the grid and seriously injure or kill a linesman. With it, the local utility can be assured of the safety of their linesmen.

So where did this all come from? Germany. In 2022, after the invasion of Ukraine, European energy prices increased dramatically in part due to an overreliance on Russian natural gas. In order to help mitigate the costs, Germany reduced the regulatory burden of installing “Balkonkraftwerk,” or balcony power plant. Consequently, they went from an estimated 40,000 systems in 2017 to potentially four million systems in 2025. To be clear, this was about energy affordability, not clean power for the sake of it. The Germans limited the size of their systems to 2000 watts for panels. In the United States, that might offset between 12 and 18 percent of monthly kilowatt-hours purchased from the local utility by the target customer or renter.

So as the calendar turns, and legislatures return to state capitals, permissionless solar should be a part of the affordability conversation. Customers should be able to choose what they do behind their meter while maintaining the safety of the broader grid. They say necessity is the mother of invention, but in this case it was also the mother of deregulation. Permissionless solar isn’t going to upend the electric grid, but it is a way to help consumers save a little cash while providing a hedge against power market volatility. Allowing it should be an easy call.

title: Global EV Sales Hit 2.15 Million in September 2026 - Electric Cars Report
description:
According to Benchmark Mineral Intelligence, global EV sales increased 17% month-on-month but fell 2% year-on-year.
Year-to-date EV sales growth in Europe reached 30% through September, up from 29% at the end of August.
China EV Sales Decline as Exports Reach Record High China’s EV market continued to weaken in September, with sales falling 18% year-on-year.
Global EV Market Faces Diverging Regional Trends September’s figures reveal a global EV market increasingly shaped by regional differences.
With global EV sales reaching 15.5 million units in the first nine months of 2026, the market remains larger than a year ago despite September’s modest annual decline.
text:
Global electric vehicle (EV) sales rebounded in September 2026, reaching 2.15 million units as Europe recorded its strongest month ever, offsetting weaker demand in China and a sharp decline in North America.

According to Benchmark Mineral Intelligence, global EV sales increased 17% month-on-month but fell 2% year-on-year. Despite the September decline, year-to-date sales reached 15.5 million units, representing a 3% increase compared with the same period in 2025.

The latest figures highlight diverging trends across the world’s largest EV markets. Europe continues to accelerate its transition to electric mobility, while China’s domestic market faces mounting pressure and North America adjusts to the removal of US federal EV tax credits.

RegionSept-26, milliony-o-ym-o-mYTD, millionsYTD-26 vs YTD-25China1.11-18%7%8.1-13%Europe0.6039%62%3.930%North America0.13-44%-8%1.2-24%RoW0.3181%6%2.393%Global2.15-2%17%15.53%

Europe Sets New Monthly EV Sales Record

Europe emerged as the strongest-performing major EV market in September, with almost 600,000 electric vehicles sold. Sales climbed 39% year-on-year and 62% compared with August, surpassing the previous monthly record set in June by 10%.

Year-to-date EV sales growth in Europe reached 30% through September, up from 29% at the end of August. Battery electric vehicles (BEVs) led the expansion, with sales rising 50% year-on-year, while plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEVs) recorded more modest growth of 16%.

Several countries achieved new monthly records. The UK, France, Spain, Portugal and Finland all posted their highest-ever monthly EV sales.

France recorded an especially strong performance, with sales increasing 78% year-on-year to almost 80,000 units. Germany also delivered substantial growth, with EV sales rising 61% to 117,000 units.

In the UK, sales increased more than threefold compared with August, partly reflecting the traditional September registration plate change. However, EV penetration remained broadly stable at around 40%, indicating that electric vehicles continue to represent a substantial share of new-car sales.

Europe’s record performance reinforces the region’s position as a major growth engine for the global EV industry, even as other markets encounter headwinds.

China EV Sales Decline as Exports Reach Record High

China’s EV market continued to weaken in September, with sales falling 18% year-on-year. Although monthly sales increased 7% compared with August, the annual decline widened from 11% in the previous month.

The Chinese market remained down 13% year-to-date. Plug-in hybrids were particularly affected, with sales declining 25% compared with the same period last year. Battery electric vehicles performed better, recording a more moderate 6% decline.

Despite weaker domestic demand, Chinese manufacturers have maintained production levels and increased their focus on international markets. Passenger car new energy vehicle (NEV) exports reached a record 558,000 units in September, highlighting the growing importance of overseas markets for China’s automotive industry.

However, two upcoming policy changes could complicate the export outlook in 2027.

The European Union and China have agreed on a proposed arrangement to limit imports of Chinese-built full and plug-in hybrid vehicles into the EU. Subject to approval by EU member states, the measure would introduce an annual cap of 350,000 units from 2027 for four years, with the limit increasing by 6% annually from the second year.

The arrangement targets a rapidly expanding segment of the European market. According to Benchmark Mineral Intelligence, Chinese-made vehicles accounted for approximately 14% of PHEVs sold across the EU, EFTA and UK in 2025. That share increased to 29% year-to-date in 2026.

China is also preparing to reduce its NEV export VAT rebate from 13% to 9% starting April 1, 2027. The change could increase export costs and squeeze manufacturers’ overseas profit margins, adding further pressure as domestic competition remains intense.

North American EV Sales Fall 44% After Tax Credit Expiration

North America recorded the sharpest annual decline among the major EV markets in September, with sales plunging 44% year-on-year and falling 8% from August.

The deterioration pushed the region’s year-to-date performance to a 24% decline, compared with a 21% drop at the end of August.

However, the figures require context. September 2025 was the final month before the expiration of the US federal EV tax credit, prompting many buyers to bring forward purchases to benefit from the incentive.

The unusually strong comparison period is therefore a major factor behind September’s steep decline. The latest figures do not necessarily indicate an equivalent deterioration in underlying demand.

Benchmark Mineral Intelligence expects the year-on-year comparison to become more favourable from the fourth quarter of 2026. Sales will be measured against the months immediately following the tax credit’s removal, when US EV demand dropped sharply.

As a result, reported annual declines across North America could narrow significantly, although the region’s recovery will depend on market conditions and consumer demand in the absence of the former federal incentive.

Global EV Market Faces Diverging Regional Trends

September’s figures reveal a global EV market increasingly shaped by regional differences. Europe’s record sales demonstrate continued momentum, supported by strong growth in battery electric vehicles and rising adoption across several major countries.

China, meanwhile, faces weaker domestic demand but continues to expand its international presence through record exports. Upcoming European import restrictions and changes to China’s export incentives could influence how manufacturers allocate vehicles and compete overseas.

North America remains under pressure following the expiration of US federal EV tax credits, although the impact of last year’s buying surge makes recent annual comparisons particularly severe.

With global EV sales reaching 15.5 million units in the first nine months of 2026, the market remains larger than a year ago despite September’s modest annual decline. The coming months will show whether Europe’s momentum and China’s export strength can offset continued weakness in North America and China’s domestic market.

[source: Benchmark Mineral Intelligence]

title: Data Center Permits Face EPA Oversight Shift - EarthTimes
description:
Federal policy on data center permits shifted in 2026 through a mix of issued guidance, proposed rule changes, and longer-term planning documents from the Environmental Protection Agency.
EPA documents and statements described a goal of reducing permitting friction for data centers, backup generators, and dedicated power facilities.
That matters for data center permits because large facilities increasingly raise questions about whether new power generation is part of the electric grid, part of a private industrial project, or both.
Other Clean Air Act provisions, state permitting rules, and local requirements may still apply, depending on the project and location.
What Data Center Permits Still Leave Unresolved As of October 15, 2026, the EPA had clearly moved toward faster and more flexible permitting for data centers and the power systems that support them.
text:
Federal policy on data center permits shifted in 2026 through a mix of issued guidance, proposed rule changes, and longer-term planning documents from the Environmental Protection Agency. As of October 15, 2026, some actions had already taken effect as agency guidance, while others remained proposals or policy commitments rather than final binding rules.

The common thread is speed. EPA documents and statements described a goal of reducing permitting friction for data centers, backup generators, and dedicated power facilities. The agency has said its approach does not rewrite pollution limits themselves, but changes how projects move through permitting and review. That distinction matters: a procedural change can still affect how much information the public receives, when a project starts construction, and how easily communities can challenge assumptions about air, water, and local infrastructure.

The policy debate is not limited to one statute. The EPA actions described in 2026 touched the Clean Air Act’s Acid Rain Program, New Source Review, hazardous air pollutant rules for emergency engines, minor-source air permits, National Environmental Policy Act procedures, and the agency’s FY 2026–2030 Strategic Plan. For those interested in further exploring the broader federal policy context, you can check out more articles at The US Report.

Why Data Center Permits Changed In 2026

Data Center Permits And The Acid Rain Program

On July 27, 2026, the EPA under Administrator Lee Zeldin issued guidance stating that the Clean Air Act’s Acid Rain Program does not apply to “islanded” power generation facilities that are not connected to the public grid and are used to supply data centers. The EPA said those facilities are outside the Acid Rain Program when they operate independently of the grid, according to the agency’s July 27 guidance.

That matters for data center permits because large facilities increasingly raise questions about whether new power generation is part of the electric grid, part of a private industrial project, or both. The guidance did not say islanded generators are free from all environmental obligations. It addressed one program: Acid Rain Program requirements. Other Clean Air Act provisions, state permitting rules, and local requirements may still apply, depending on the project and location.

A Faster Start Before Major Review

On May 11, 2026, the EPA proposed redefining “Begin Actual Construction” for major New Source Review permitting. Under the proposal described in the research record, non-emitting components or structures, including wiring, piping, and cement pads, could be built before a major NSR permit is obtained. The change would be significant for construction sequencing because developers could perform some site work earlier while still waiting for approval of emitting equipment.

The legal and practical effect would depend on final rule language. If finalized as described, the proposal would not authorize a source to operate emitting equipment without required permits. It would, however, move some early construction activity outside the trigger point that historically has constrained major industrial projects. For communities, that may make a project feel more advanced before the most consequential air-permit decisions have been made.

Air Rules Shift From Emissions To Procedure

Emergency Engines And Grid Support

Also in May 2026, the EPA clarified rules for stationary emergency engines under the National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants. The clarification confirmed that certain emergency engines may operate up to 50 hours annually in non-emergency conditions to help stabilize the electric grid for data centers. The figure is narrow, but it is relevant because backup power is a central feature of large computing campuses.

Backup generators are usually discussed as reliability assets. In air-quality terms, they can also be emission sources, especially where a site uses many diesel-fired units. The EPA clarification did not create an unlimited operating window. It identified a bounded allowance for certain non-emergency use. Whether that allowance increases local pollution exposure depends on site-specific factors, including engine type, operating hours, fuel, controls, weather, and proximity to homes, schools, or health facilities.

NEPA Timing And Scope

On June 24, 2026, the EPA proposed changes to National Environmental Policy Act reviews. As described in the research record, the proposal would set firmer deadlines, reduce average Environmental Impact Statement timelines from about four years to two years, limit page counts, narrow the scope of reviews, and expand low-risk categorical exclusions.

NEPA does not itself set emission limits. It is a disclosure and decision-making law for federal actions. Shorter reviews may reduce delay, but narrower reviews can also limit the range of alternatives and effects assessed in the public record. For data centers, that could matter where federal permits, funding, land decisions, or infrastructure approvals connect a private project to federal review.

Public Notice Became The Flashpoint

Minor Sources And State Discretion

The most contested 2026 proposal involved air pollution permits for “minor” sources. A July 2026 proposal, identified in the research as EPA docket EPA-HQ-OAR-2025-1212, would remove the federal requirement that states notify the public and seek comment before issuing minor-source air permits, including for some data center backup generators and related equipment. The comment period closed on August 21, 2026. Reporting by the Texas Tribune described the proposal as giving states discretion over public notice and comment for those permits.

The word “minor” can be misleading in public debate. In Clean Air Act permitting, it generally refers to regulatory thresholds, not whether a facility has no local effect. Multiple smaller sources at or near a large campus may still be relevant to nearby residents, especially in areas that already experience industrial emissions or heavy electricity demand.

What Public Input May Lose

Critics of the minor-source proposal warned that it could reduce public involvement before permits are issued. Supporters of faster permitting argue that duplicative process can delay infrastructure needed for computing demand, electric reliability, and artificial intelligence development. The confirmed procedural question is narrower: whether federal rules should require public notice and comment for those minor-source permits, or whether states should decide when notice is appropriate.

That distinction leaves several unresolved issues. States could retain public notice requirements, reduce them, or apply different rules by permit type. Communities would then face a patchwork system. Developers might gain more predictable timing in some states, but not others. Public-health agencies and local governments could receive less consistent information unless state rules fill the gap. EarthTimes has separately tracked the same issue in coverage of public input on permits.

What Communities And Developers Still Need To Know

The Strategic Plan Signals More Action

In October 2026, the EPA’s FY 2026–2030 Strategic Plan committed the agency to “common-sense regulation” that supports data center development. The plan identified areas including Clean Air Act sections 111 and 112, the New Source Review program, siting and permitting guidance, and water usage efficiency for data center infrastructure.

A strategic plan is not the same as a final rule. It signals agency priorities and can guide future rulemaking, enforcement discretion, and technical guidance. The plan therefore matters less as an immediate legal change and more as a map of where the EPA may keep pressing: air standards, permitting timing, siting, and resource efficiency.

Water And Siting Remain Less Settled

The research record identifies water usage efficiency and siting guidance as part of the EPA’s planned work, but it does not provide final standards or numeric limits for those areas. That uncertainty is significant. Data centers can affect local water demand through cooling systems and local electricity demand through continuous operation. The environmental effect varies by design, climate, energy source, and grid conditions.

For local officials, the absence of final federal rules means near-term decisions may still depend heavily on state permits, utility planning, zoning, water authorities, and local public-health review. For developers, the policy direction is favorable to faster processing, but it does not eliminate the need to document compliance with applicable environmental laws.

What Data Center Permits Still Leave Unresolved

As of October 15, 2026, the EPA had clearly moved toward faster and more flexible permitting for data centers and the power systems that support them. The confirmed actions include issued guidance on islanded power generation and clarified treatment of certain emergency engines. Other changes, including the construction-start proposal, NEPA revisions, and the minor-source public-notice proposal, were described as proposed rather than final in the research record.

title: Amherst County hits the trifecta of issues: off-track betting, data centers and nuclear energy
description:
The most politically fascinating place in Virginia right now might be Amherst County, with Campbell County coming in second.
That $1.6 million figure for tax revenue seems on track with what other Rosie’s outlets have generated in smaller communities.
Data center There are possibly two data center projects that will soon come before Amherst County supervisors.
Transmission lines The Campbell County supervisors recently voted to oppose the proposed Valley Link transmission line that would go from Joshua Falls to Culpeper County.
Back across the river in Amherst County, 67.6% of voters there backed Trump.
text:
The most politically fascinating place in Virginia right now might be Amherst County, with Campbell County coming in second.

Multiple forces are converging on both counties — and, admittedly, some others — that will require public officials there to make some decisions that most localities don’t have to. Many of these involve a subject that’s complicated, often misunderstood and usually politicized: energy.

Let’s start with Amherst County.

Many county taxpayers are still reeling from reassessments that are driving their tax bills higher. The board of supervisors reduced the tax rate but not by enough to hold tax bills the same. Just as the prices you and I pay at the store are going up, so, too, are the prices that governments must pay. That sticker shock from reassessments should make Amherst a prime candidate to hear options on how to hold down tax bills — and now it has some.

Off-track betting

Five years ago, Amherst voters were asked if they wanted to approve off-track betting for a Rosie’s Gaming Emporium. They said no, by a margin of 54.1% to 45.9%.

Now Rosie’s is trying again. Will the post-assessment political landscape in Amherst produce a different result? We’ll see. (Pulaski County also has its own referendum on off-track betting.)

A study by Mangum Economics commissioned by the Lynchburg Regional Business Alliance forecasts that such a facility would generate $1.9 million in tax revenue during its first year of operation — $1.6 million from the tax on pari-mutuel wagering, the rest through other taxes such as meals taxes and sales taxes and whatnot. That $1.6 million figure for tax revenue seems on track with what other Rosie’s outlets have generated in smaller communities. The three most comparable ones are in Collinsville (outside Martinsville), Vinton (outside Roanoke) and Emporia.

Here’s what they generated last year:

Collinsville: $254,636

Emporia: $1,574,946

Vinton: $3,478,266

Those localities were allowed to keep half that money; the rest was shared with New Kent County, home of the Colonial Downs racetrack. That law has now been changed to allow host localities to keep all the tax revenue.

If Amherst were to reject off-track betting a second time, that would not be unprecedented: Manassas Park has voted it down three times, in 1996, 2004 and 2023.

The off-track betting question might be simple compared to the other issues coming before Amherst.

Data center

There are possibly two data center projects that will soon come before Amherst County supervisors.

Data centers have become politically unpopular, to put it mildly. However, they also generate enormous sums of tax revenues, which is why some localities prize them. Mecklenburg County’s Microsoft complex has generated so much revenue that the county has been able to build new schools — every school is now built in this century — and lower its real estate tax rate to the lowest in the state.

Some may see this as a Faustian bargain: Amherst could generate lots of tax revenue (the exact amount is unclear) with a data center. Is Amherst so opposed to data centers that it’s willing to turn away millions in revenue? If Amherst says “no” to both a data center and to Rosie’s, then how does the county propose to generate new revenues? That’s not an argument to approve either if people don’t want them, but it is an argument that Amherst will need revenue options if taxpayers don’t like their bills going up. If Rosie’s and a data center aren’t those options, then what is?

And then there’s this:

Nuclear reactors

Amherst and Campbell counties now find themselves in the middle of a nationwide debate over how we should generate electricity. Gov. Abigail Spanberger’s recent energy plan lays out some uncomfortable facts: Depending on which forecast you believe — low, moderate or high — Virginia will need to double, triple or quadruple the amount of power it produces.

And yes, data centers are a big factor in what’s driving those energy demands.

Under every option the governor’s plan lays out, Virginia needs more nuclear energy. The advantage of nuclear is that you can produce a lot of power in a small space — unlike, say, solar energy, which requires a lot of land to produce power only part of the time. The disadvantage is that nuclear has been expensive and time-consuming to build. And then there are those who are freaked out by the idea of splitting atoms.

Nuclear development slowed to almost nothing after the Three Mile Island accident in Pennsylvania in 1979. It’s also been politically polarizing, with the right more receptive to it than the left. Now nuclear is seeing something of a renaissance with a push for small reactors that, in theory, can be built more quickly and cheaply. We’re also seeing a political realignment, with some on the left coming to see nuclear as the only realistic way to retire lots of carbon-belching energy facilities.

There are now three proposals to build small nuclear reactors in Virginia: Dominion Energy and Amazon are exploring one that would go at Dominion’s existing North Anna nuclear station in Louisa County. That seems about as non-controversial as you can get. The place has two big reactors now and is authorized for a third anyway. (Disclosure: Dominion is one of our donors, but donors have no say in news decisions; see our policy. You can become a donor and test that proposition.)

The other two reactor proposals are both in the Lynchburg area: Appalachian Power is looking at one at its Joshua Falls substation in Campbell County, and now a Charlotte, North Carolina-based energy company is pitching a facility that could involve multiple small reactors (sounds like two from the energy estimates) in Amherst County, almost directly across the James River from Joshua Falls.

If there’s any place in Virginia that understands nuclear power — or, at least, isn’t automatically spooked by it — it should be the Lynchburg area. The region has long been home to not one but two nuclear companies, BWX Technologies and Framatome. These two proposals will test just how open-minded the Lynchburg area is about nuclear.

With all these proposals, the questions start mounting: If Amherst approves a data center, can it realistically oppose the Beck Creek Energy project? It seems hypocritical to approve a big energy-drinking facility and then reject an energy generation site. After all, energy has to be produced somewhere. The two projects are separate and not a package deal — Amherst could easily approve a data center and oppose a nuclear facility, but that’s just creating a problem for somebody else that will have to host some kind of energy production. Amherst could reject all three things — Rosie’s, the data center, the nuclear site — but it still hasn’t answered the revenue question.

The questions get trickier on the other side of the James River in Campbell County.

Transmission lines

The Campbell County supervisors recently voted to oppose the proposed Valley Link transmission line that would go from Joshua Falls to Culpeper County. This is completely understandable. Transmission lines are ugly. Nobody wants one near them. I don’t. You don’t. None of us do. Valley Link is said to have nothing to do with Appalachian’s nuclear proposal — this is simply envisioned as a way to move electricity from the Midwest to Northern Virginia, with Joshua Falls as one link in the chain before the power moves on to another utility, in this case, Dominion. If Appalachian builds a nuclear reactor in Joshua Falls, that power is going to have to move out, too.

The governor’s energy plan says we need more transmission lines. Campbell County may not like this particular governor — only 26.6% of the voters there cast ballots for Spanberger — but nobody is really disputing that we need more energy and more transmission lines. Campbell County may not like the idea of having to bear the brunt of moving energy to data centers in Northern Virginia, but 73.6% of Campbell County voters backed Donald Trump in 2024 and he’s been an enthusiastic champion of artificial intelligence, which will require more data centers somewhere and more energy production somewhere and more transmission lines somewhere. Back across the river in Amherst County, 67.6% of voters there backed Trump.

The remaining percentages of voters who backed Kamala Harris aren’t off the hook, either, because the Biden-Harris administration also pushed for more transmission lines — the only real difference between the Biden administration and the Trump administration on this is that they had different preferences for what type of power they wanted to move over those lines. Biden wanted more carbon-free energy, Trump is quite fine with carbon-based energy. And yet … both administrations have strongly backed more nuclear development.

The point here isn’t to say that Amherst and Campbell have to be for all these things — a Rosie’s, a data center and a nuclear facility in Amherst, a nuclear facility and transmission lines in Campbell. However, it is to say that many of them are connected and none of them can be viewed in isolation.

If Amherst voters reject Rosie’s and/or a data center, then they either need to reconcile themselves to their current tax bills or find other ways for the county to generate revenue. If they approve a data center, they can’t blissfully assume that some other county somewhere else will host the power generation. If Campbell doesn’t want Valley Link, then it may need to ask whether it wants a nuclear facility that will produce power that has to get out to market. And all of us might want to ask exactly how we’re going to make a society work where we’re using an average of 58 to 87 data centers each day and power demands are rising geometrically but none of us want a data center, an energy production site or a transmission line nearby.

text:
See more from Canary Media’s ​“Chart of the Week” column.

Clean energy installations have persisted at record levels despite President Donald Trump’s best efforts to stop them. But the first year of Trump’s second term did leave a mark on U.S. jobs in the sector.

Clean energy jobs fell in 2025 after four years of steady growth, according to a new analysis of federal jobs data by business-focused environmental advocacy group E2. The U.S. had 3.52 million clean energy jobs at the end of 2025, down nearly 37,000 from the year before. That drop represents just about 1% of the clean energy workforce, but was enough to erase about 40% of the previous year’s job growth.

The big caveat is that overall energy employment also fell between 2024 and 2025. The clean energy job losses closely track clean energy’s share of overall energy jobs, suggesting that the drop, while a substantial break from the previous four years, might have more to do with broader energy sector trends than the unique challenges facing clean energy.

It’s been hard to say definitively how well clean energy has fared under the current administration; federal policy has turned against renewables and electric vehicles again and again, yet raw clean energy deployment numbers have continued their dominant streak from the Biden years. Solar is the No. 1 pick for new power plants getting built in America, followed by batteries and wind. Factories have continued to open, reshoring production of batteries, solar panels, and even cells.

But clean energy employers have had to adjust to new policy obstacles and prepare for a less certain future. Halfway through 2025, the Republican majority in Congress passed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, stripping away renewable energy tax credits that were supposed to run for roughly another decade, plus consumer-facing incentives to help Americans electrify their cars and homes. The executive branch also froze or clawed back billions of dollars earmarked by Congress to fund efficiency and clean energy installations for communities.

There are many variables at play here, but the job changes do track with the areas targeted by federal policy.

The One Big Beautiful Bill ended the EV tax credit first, in September 2025. U.S. automakers subsequently backed away from their earlier EV plans, shuttering planned and operating production lines and reorienting battery manufacturing to make grid storage products. Clean vehicles lost the most jobs in relative terms compared to the other clean energy categories — 2.4% or 9,619.

Energy efficiency, hit hard by the funding clawbacks, lost the most in absolute terms — 21,443 — though that is less than 1% of the sub-sector’s nearly 2.4 million jobs. ​“Storage and grid modernization” provided the brightest spot in the report, growing by 3.2%; grid batteries retained their tax credits in the budget law, and have continued to enjoy bipartisan support.

What this data doesn’t represent is the many planned jobs that will never come to fruition due to the Trump administration’s attacks on clean energy. text:
By Martin McConnell

Spanish EV charging firm Wallbox and Quebec-based EDP Électrique have partnered to deploy public EV charging infrastructure at Montreal Metropolitan Airport, the companies announced Oct. 15.

Located at the airport’s YHU terminal, the project has installed 120 Wallbox Pulsar Pro charging stations. Once the airport’s new building is complete, the two firms will install an additional 48 charging stations, bringing total deployment to 168 chargers around the airport campus.

“Transport hubs such as airports are an important part of the next phase of EV charging infrastructure, where scale, reliability and intelligent energy management become increasingly important,” says Ignasi Alastuey, chief business officer of Wallbox. “Together with edp électrique and the broader project team, we are helping YHU build charging infrastructure that addresses current needs while providing the flexibility to continue expanding as EV adoption grows.”

Wallbox, EDP, Foresta, EG Électrique, and Westburne developed the EV charging project in collaboration, the companies say. The brain trust brings together expertise across EV charging technology, as well as infrastructure management, electrical installation, and distribution.

Supporting sustainability

The companies chose Wallbox’s Pulsar Pro for its power sharing capabilities, which will play a key role, the companies say. The installation will make use of the power sharing across groups of chargers, which will allow power to move between multiple charging points for more efficiency.

The new deployment is part of the Montreal Metropolitan Airport’s wider efforts toward supporting both EV transition efforts and wider sustainability practices. As demand for EV charging ports increase throughout Canada, the new charging infrastructure will support a wide range of airport users and operations, representatives from the companies say.

“This project is a strong example of what can be achieved through close collaboration between all stakeholders,” says Sabryna Barabé-Favreau, sales representative of electrical products at EDP Electrique.

“By working closely with the airport, Wallbox and the wider project team, we were able to bring together the different components required to deliver a scalable charging infrastructure that meets the customer’s high standards and can continue growing alongside future demand.”

The project also aims to provide a fully scalable model for future EV charging deployments, the company says. By combining smart power solutions and management with sustainable and scalable infrastructure, the airport’s charging stations will be able to grow alongside that demand.

title: Bipartisan permitting bill in Congress could speed energy projects, but draws green critics
description:
WASHINGTON —Suddenly there’s hope for cutting the reams of red tape that can make getting new energy projects a seemingly endless slog.
Reformers will have to fight environmental groups, who tend to appreciate today’s detailed, often lengthy process for reviewing energy projects.
The bill offers new laws governing the issuance of permits and approvals to energy and infrastructure projects.
Critics have complained that the 1970 National Environmental Policy Act’s provisions have meant unnecessary delays.
The bill attempts to speed the process for environmental review without changing the standards for review.
text:
WASHINGTON —Suddenly there’s hope for cutting the reams of red tape that can make getting new energy projects a seemingly endless slog.

Top Republican and Democratic senators have unveiled a 417-page bill to overhaul the approval process, a pathway for what’s known as “permitting reform.” A debate is likely when lawmakers return for their lame-duck session in November, though getting to a finish line anytime soon won’t be easy.

Reformers will have to fight environmental groups, who tend to appreciate today’s detailed, often lengthy process for reviewing energy projects. They worry that streamlining reviews will make it easier for energy-gulping and air-and-water-polluting projects to proceed.

It’s a battle that is likely to continue for months and perhaps even years. But at least now there’s a real starting point, a bipartisan group of powerful senators eager to find common ground and a widespread congressional — and national – consensus that the process is broken.

“Long awaited is not an exaggeration,” said an analysis from the Bipartisan Policy Center of the effort to spur changes.

“There is widespread recognition that a permitting system created to protect the environment against industrial pollution more than 50 years ago has morphed into a system that is bad for both the economy and the environment,” it said.

An uncertain future

The bill faces a bumpy, unpredictable path. Lots of amendments are likely. The White House’s reluctance to embrace renewable energy is a potential roadblock.

Getting through the House, where Democrats who might be in the majority next year are signaling broad skepticism, could be tough.

“No issue was an easy issue,” said Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., top Democrat on the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, describing for reporters the challenges he and his colleagues faced in writing the bill and continue to tackle.

The strongest opposition is coming from environmental groups.

“The entire gist and purpose of this bill is to get to yes as fast as possible for every project under the sun. It doesn’t matter if it’s a good project or a bad project,” Brett Hartl, government affairs director at the Tucson, Arizona-based Center for Biological Diversity, told States Newsroom.

These groups see the bill as a massive concession to those who have thwarted efforts to promote renewable energy.

“Making a deal with the devil fails the American people,” said Eric Schlenker-Goodrich, executive director of the New Mexico-based Western Environmental Law Center.

Whitehouse saw the bill very differently..

“The wins from this could be very very big ones. This should lower electricity costs measurably for Americans. This should increase clean power significantly for Americans. This should significantly add construction and jobs across the country,” he said.

What the bill would do

The Senate bill is co-sponsored by four of the most powerful energy and environmental voices in the chamber: Energy and Natural Resources Chairman Mike Lee, R-Utah; top committee Democrat Martin Heinrich, D-N.M.; Environment and Public Works Chair Shelley Moore Capito, a West Virginia Republican; and Whitehouse.

The bill offers new laws governing the issuance of permits and approvals to energy and infrastructure projects.

It would put new restrictions on the process federal regulators use to take a serious look at environmental impact before approving a project. Critics have complained that the 1970 National Environmental Policy Act’s provisions have meant unnecessary delays.

Here’s what the reforms could mean for:

Data centers. Companies would have to pay for the electricity infrastructure they use to operate the centers. While they’ve pledged to protect consumers from paying additional costs, signing an agreement with the White House, nothing in that deal is mandatory. Traditionally, those who use the electricity share the costs, since they too benefit from the new or expanded power plant and/or transmission lines. This bill says data centers will pay all those additional center-related costs.

Power plants and transmission lines. The bill would cut down the amount of time allowed for government review and approval of such facilities. It would be easier for federal and state reviews to proceed simultaneously, shortening the review period.

Wind and other renewable energy. President Donald Trump has been opposed to such projects. The bill would apparently bar the executive branch from denying permits for political reasons, though lawmakers are still in discussions with administration officials on how to proceed.

Historic preservation. Reviewing a project’s impact on a historic property can take years — there’s no deadline for review. The bill would streamline the process in a number of ways.

Legal challenges. Opponents would have 150 days to file legal challenges to most of the act’s provisions. Currently lawsuits can be filed within six years.

Environmental protection. The bill attempts to speed the process for environmental review without changing the standards for review.

Pipelines. The bill makes it harder for a single state to block an interstate gas pipeline or electric transmission line that the administration views as essential to national security or significant economic reasons.

One reason permitting itself can take a long time, said the Bipartisan Policy Center, is that “agency staff try to write environmental review documents that will survive legal challenges, which is quite different from doing a more careful review of potential harms.”

Roadblocks

The promising news for the effort is being led in the Senate by the four top committee members.

“We once built projects like the Hoover Dam, the Golden Gate Bridge, and the Empire State Building in years, not decades,” said Lee in a statement. “America still has the resources and the talent, but what too often stands in the way is a permitting system that takes too long and costs too much.”

Whitehouse had a somewhat different emphasis. “If we can pass this bill, we will flood the grid with clean, affordable energy and make data centers start paying their fair share,” he said.

But in the House, Rep. Jared Huffman, D-Calif., said that while the senators have “done some good work,” their bill “raises significant questions and concerns that would have to be resolved before most Democrats could support it.”

While he supports smoothing the process for transmission and clean energy projects, he had environmental concerns.

“We can’t throw states, tribes, impacted communities, and threatened and endangered wildlife under the bus,” said Huffman, top Democrat on the House Natural Resources Committee.

Environmental groups agreed.

Holly Bender, chief program officer at the Sierra Club, worried that the bill would benefit oil and gas companies “while communities stand to lose critical protections for clean air, water, and wildlife.”

Her views were shared in a letter to top Senate Democrats from representatives of 122 clean air and water advocacy organizations. They stretched from coast to coast, including the Chesapeake Bay Foundation, Detroit Riverkeeper, Los Angeles Waterkeeper, Conservancy of Southwest Florida, Oregon Wild, Orleans Audubon Society, Ohio River Foundation and more.

Alaska pipeline project

Hartl cited a proposed pipeline project in Alaska as an example of how the bill could have a profound impact.

The LNG project, championed by the Trump administration, would send natural gas from Alaska’s North Slope to a terminal in the southern part of the state.

“That pipeline will cross lands, streams, rivers, down to Anchorage. A project like that in a normal world would have a pretty serious environmental review. If this (bill) were to pass I think they could approve it with almost no review,” Hartl said.”That project will be rubber stamped.”

Ariana Kretz, policy analyst at the Climate Justice Alliance, which promotes efforts to reduce the impact of climate change, cited as an example of the bill’s danger how the administration has dealt with the Santa Ynez Unit, an offshore oil production operation off the Southern California coast. It was shut down 11 years ago after an oil spill.

In March, Energy Secretary Chris Wright directed it to reopen after a presidential executive order aimed at producing more domestic oil.

“Today’s order will strengthen America’s oil supply and restore a pipeline system vital to our national security and defense, ensuring that West Coast military installations have the reliable energy critical to military readiness,” he said at the time.

If the new legislation became law, Kretz told States Newsroom, “a future administration would have a very difficult time reversing Secretary Wright’s decision.”

More opinions

Energy interests have offered strong praise for the bill. It’s a “generational opportunity” to streamline a balky process, said Mike Sommers, American Petroleum Institute president and CEO.

Others are being somewhat more circumspect.

The National Governors Association is “encouraged” by the bill’s introduction. CEO Brandon Tatum said he looks forward to “working with Congress to further develop this legislation. “

Whitehouse said issues such as wind projects — which the Trump administration tried to halt but was thwarted by a federal judge — remain under discussion.

“We need more clarity on that and when we have more clarity there will be back and forth,” he said. So far, he found White House staff’s proposals and discussion “not outside the bounds of ordinary legislative disagreement.”

The bill is a starting point, he and others said, and there are many amendments and negotiations still to come. But at least there is a starting point, Whitehouse suggested, and so “today begins a process.”

text:
The Louisiana Department of Transportation and Development (DOTD) formally named the new hybrid-electric vehicle ferry Holly Beach on Wednesday, October 14.

Holly Beach is the first of two ferries being built by Thoma-Sea Marine Constructors under a US$49.7 million project. Completion of sister vessel Cameron is expected in late November, with entry into service planned for December.

The DOTD said Holly Beach will enter public service within 30 days of the dedication. The two ferries will take the place of the 1964-built Cameron II on the Calcasieu Ship Channel crossing.

If Cameron II is unavailable for maintenance or mandatory drydocking, the route uses a temporary side-loading ferry that is unable to carry trucks longer than 50 feet (15 metres).

Trucks over that length must travel a 100-mile (160-kilometre) detour, adding more than two hours to their journey.

The DOTD said the new vessels will also assist with hurricane evacuations and emergencies arising from other weather events.

Operation and maintenance of the crossing are being transferred to New Orleans-based LabMar Ferry Services under a contract approved by the Louisiana Transportation Authority, with DOTD retaining ownership of the vessels and terminals.

The ferries were designed by the Elliott Bay Design Group to US Coast Guard Subchapter H requirements. Each vessel will have a capacity for up to 34 vehicles.
