text:
Energy Department issues emergency power order, IRS moves to tighten access to health tax credits, and more…

IN THE NEWS:

U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright issued an emergency order to mitigate blackout risks in the Mid-Atlantic amid rising electricity demand and planned power plant and transmission outages. Issued under Section 202(c) of the Federal Power Act, the order directs PJM Interconnection, a regional grid operator serving 13 states and Washington, D.C., to operate designated generators as needed to maintain grid reliability. The order also authorizes PJM to deploy backup generation as a last resort during severe grid emergencies. The order followed the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s rejection of PJM’s proposal to curtail electricity supplies to certain large data centers during shortages, citing concerns about federal authority over retail electricity sales.

The Internal Revenue Service (IRS) proposed a rule tightening eligibility for the premium tax credit, which helps people pay for health insurance purchased through the Affordable Care Act exchanges, to implement changes made by the One Big Beautiful Bill. The IRS would deny the credit for any month in which an exchange fails to verify an enrollee’s eligibility for reasons related to residency, citizenship, lawful immigration status, household income, and access to other health care coverage. Under the proposal, the IRS would bar some lawfully present immigrants from receiving the credit, including low-income immigrants who are ineligible for Medicaid because of their immigration status. The rule would also eliminate the cap on how much taxpayers must repay at tax time when advance subsidy payments exceed the credit they are owed.

The Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) announced it plans to list two potent opioid compounds found in kratom-derived products in the most restrictive category of the Controlled Substances Act, on a temporary basis. The DEA explained that the kratom market has expanded to include concentrated and semi-synthetic products sold online and in gas stations and vape shops, often marketed as lower-risk “botanical” products. Assistant Secretary for HHS Brian Christine recommended limiting restrictions to products with high concentrations of the compounds, so that natural kratom products containing trace amounts can stay on the market. The DEA will adopt HHS’s recommendations next month temporarily.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) proposed rescinding a rule that directs federal officers reviewing work authorization applications to give deference to earlier approvals involving the same applicant and the same facts. Under the current rule, when people apply to renew their work or stay authorizations, DHS defers to previous eligibility determinations, unless the previous decision involved clear error. If the deference policy is rescinded, however, officials would consider the facts of each case without giving weight to previous decisions based on the same facts. DHS argued that the change is necessary to ensure that the applicant bears the burden of proving continued eligibility to work or stay in the United States.

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) announced a new initiative to develop a regulatory framework for drugs and biologics treating rare diseases. The Rare Disease Framework Initiative aims to tailor regulatory requirements to individual diseases, patient needs, and the evidence available from small patient populations. FDA plans to improve regulatory predictability, incorporate patient perspectives into drug reviews, and expand the use of innovative scientific and statistical methods. The agency noted that only approximately five percent of rare conditions have an FDA-approved treatment. The initiative could lead to revised agency guidance, regulations, and review procedures.

A new rule proposed by the U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) would require train operators to provide advance notice of any person arriving or departing the United States by train. Currently, operators must report to CBP when trains arrive in the United States from a foreign location and can choose to provide advance information about individual travelers. CBP argued, however, that the current system creates security risks because the government does not have enough time to determine if travelers are violating immigration or customs laws. Under the proposed rule, CBP would inspect traveler lists and could recommend that train operators not allow individual travelers to board if CBP determines that the individuals pose security risks.

The U.S. Department of Agriculture issued a rule amending the administrative review process for actions implementing land and resource management plans on national forests and grasslands. When the Forest Service proposes certain projects on public land, the public can file objections and request administrative review of the projects. The new rule amends the review process by reducing the windows of time in which individuals can object to, and submit comments on, projects. The Department of Agriculture claimed that the changes are necessary to increase the efficiency of the review process.

The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network of the U.S. Department of the Treasury assessed a $1.2 billion civil penalty against Bank of America for willful violations of the Bank Secrecy Act, including failures to detect and report suspicious financial activity. The penalty ranked as the third largest ever issued in Treasury history. The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network found that deficiencies in Bank of America’s anti-money-laundering program caused it to miss or delay reporting more than $5 billion in suspicious transactions, including activity linked to Chinese money laundering networks and illicit finance along the southwest border. Bank of America admitted to inadequate transaction monitoring, insufficient due diligence on foreign financial institutions, and failures to file required suspicious activity reports. Federal regulators imposed an additional $750 million penalty for related compliance deficiencies.

WHAT WE’RE READING:

In a recent Brookings Institute essay, Rachel M. Perera, a fellow in the Brown Center on Education Policy at Brookings, argued that guidance from the U.S. Department of Education regarding school discipline mischaracterized federal law. In July, the Education Department rescinded regulations that held schools liable for disparate impacts–conduct that affects students of different races differently–even without evidence of intentional discrimination. The Education Department then released nonbinding guidance stating that if a school chose to change its policies because the policies affected students of different races differently, the school had engaged in racial discrimination. Perera claimed that the guidance misrepresented federal law, because the new regulations imply that disparate impact by itself is insufficient to prove racial discrimination, but the guidance goes further to suggest that schools can never consider the disparate effects of their policies. Perera noted that the guidance is not legally binding, but argued that it puts pressure on schools to change their policies.

In a recent Brookings Institution essay, Anil Hurkadli, a former nonresident senior fellow at Brookings, and Josie Stewart, a senior research and communications assistant at Brookings, argued that existing federal privacy laws provide students inadequate protection from expanding school surveillance technologies. The authors explained that the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act restricts disclosure of certain student records but does not regulate data collection, and the Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act protects only children under 13. These gaps, they warned, leave sensitive student information vulnerable to misuse by technology companies and law enforcement. Although states such as California and Minnesota have enacted additional protections, Hurkadli and Stewart contended that inconsistent state laws leave students exposed. They urged stronger data privacy and minimization safeguards to protect students as schools adopt surveillance technologies.

In a recent report, the U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO) found that interest in geothermal energy development on federal lands has surged since 2020, noting that the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) approved 68 geothermal drilling permits in 2024, more than the previous five years combined. Nevertheless, GAO cautioned that developers face inconsistent permitting requirements across the BLM’s field offices, in part because the agency’s geothermal handbooks have remained in draft since at least 2022. GAO found that the BLM lacks a unified system to track permit applications, leaving developers uncertain about the status of their permits. GAO recommended that the BLM publish its handbooks, create a system to track permits, and set goals for processing times.

EDITOR’S CHOICE:

In an essay in The Regulatory Review, Peter T. Grossi, an adjunct professor at the University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School, argued that HHS should conduct a financial “stress test” before expanding the National Vaccine Injury Compensation Program, which compensates people injured by childhood vaccines, to cover autism claims. Grossi noted that recent HHS actions—including removing a federal statement that vaccines do not cause autism and replacing half of the staff at its Advisory Commission on Childhood Vaccines—suggest the agency will soon attempt such expansion. Grossi cautioned that covering even 2 to 5 percent of profound autism cases would exhaust the program’s funding. Grossi recommended that HHS commit to testing any proposal against existing autism data and release the results for independent review before issuing a change.

title: Mercedes-Benz goes digital first to make GLA variants at Rastatt
description:
In September this year Mercedes-Benz launched series production of its new electric GLA compact SUV at its Rastatt plant in Germany, alongside the existing GLA combustion-engine model.
To manage that complexity at Rastatt, Mercedes-Benz is using its Microsoft Azure MO360 production ecosystem, which integrates artificial intelligence and digital twin technology with its Mercedes-Benz Operating System (MB.OS).
The investment strengthens Rastatt's role within the global Mercedes-Benz production network and supports further digitalisation and flexibility of manufacturing.
All sites work with the MO360 digital production ecosystem, while the MO360 Data Platform analyses their production data across the network.
“The start of production of the new GLA marks another important chapter for the Mercedes-Benz Rastatt plant,” said Torsten Höink, chairman of the Works Council at the Rastatt plant at the production launch in September.
text:
In September this year Mercedes-Benz launched series production of its new electric GLA compact SUV at its Rastatt plant in Germany, alongside the existing GLA combustion-engine model. The Rastatt plant also makes the CLA Coupé and CLA Shooting Brake. Before the end of the year, it will be adding a hybrid variant of the GLA with 48-volt technology. Mercedes-Benz says that its flexible production system enables it to build conventional internal combustion, hybrid and fully electric vehicles on the same line. This allows Mercedes-Benz to react quickly to changes in customer demand. That flexibility continues to strengthen Rastatt's role as a centre of excellence for compact vehicle production within the global production network.

Predictive Maintenance has a rare-failure problem

Automotive downtime now costs $2.3m an hour, yet fewer breakdowns mean less data to learn from. The plants getting Predictive Maintenance right are pooling knowledge, prioritising critical assets and earning the trust of the technicians who act on alerts.

“Our global production network is designed for high flexibility, allowing us to respond quickly to market fluctuations while ensuring efficient utilisation of our production lines,” says Marco Zwick, site manager and head of production for Mercedes-Benz’s Rastatt plant.

Advertisement

Mercedes-Benz has been making cars at Rastatt since 1992 but manufacturing has become more complex as the different drive systems have been introduced. To manage that complexity at Rastatt, Mercedes-Benz is using its Microsoft Azure MO360 production ecosystem, which integrates artificial intelligence and digital twin technology with its Mercedes-Benz Operating System (MB.OS).

The existing GLA is currently being made in Assembly Hall 4.1 but Mercedes-Benz is now investing “a low three-digit million euro amount” in converting that hall for production of the next-generation GLA and its various drivetrain variants starting in 2027. “This includes the adaptation of production equipment, assembly stations and logistics processes, supported by digital planning and simulation tools to ensure an efficient and flexible production setup,” says Zwick.

The investment strengthens Rastatt's role within the global Mercedes-Benz production network and supports further digitalisation and flexibility of manufacturing.

Digital twin

The carmaker said that for the conversion of Assembly Hall 4.1 it is using a digital twin to configure and optimise the production line, enabling it to cut construction time and save costs. The strategy has precedent, as Mercedes-Benz used a digital twin to successfully convert Assembly Hall 4.0 in record time in 2023.

Applying a simulation of the production process enables Mercedes-Benz to create a highly precise virtual representation of the production environment before physical conversion work begins. It enables engineers to digitally configure and optimise production lines, machine positioning, logistics routes and process flows in advance.

“By simulating manufacturing scenarios before implementation, we can identify optimisation opportunities early, reduce construction time, minimise disruption and improve cost efficiency,” says Zwick.

Mercedes-Benz is using the Nvidia Omniverse platform for the industrial digital twins being used at Rastatt. According to Zwick, it enables engineers to plan, simulate and validate production equipment and processes virtually before any changes are made on the shop floor. This is central to the carmaker’s Digital First strategy, aimed at integrating new models and technologies faster, with greater planning accuracy and lower costs. At the Rastatt plant, where all-electric and hybrid models are built flexibly on one line, individual production systems have already been implemented as digital twins.

Advertisement

Cloud data

Mercedes-Benz’s MO360 digital production ecosystem is used across the entire global production network. The plants themselves are connected via the cloud-based MO360 Data Platform, which analyses production data across the network in real time. Insights gained at one site can therefore benefit others, and proven solutions can be rolled out quickly. Rastatt benefits directly from this. At the same time, as a pioneer of the Digital First approach, the plant combines artificial intelligence and digital twin technologies to effect better transparency, data driven decision-making and continuous optimisation of manufacturing processes, says Zwick.

BMW trades breadth for margin and puts AI to work

At its Capital Market Day, BMW set out a route back to an 8% to 10% Automotive EBIT margin, built on regional production, agentic AI in the plant and 20% fewer divisions and management roles.

Mercedes-Benz connects its global production network through the Microsoft Azure-based MO360 Data Platform. “The cloud brings together production and supply chain data that was previously held in separate systems, which creates greater transparency and predictability across the network,” says Zwick. “Teams can identify potential bottlenecks earlier and allocate production resources dynamically. The cloud also provides the computing power to apply artificial intelligence and data analytics globally, while meeting regional cybersecurity and compliance standards.”

Cross-plant configuration

Mercedes-Benz uses high-precision digital simulation techniques to plan, configure and validate production equipment and processes virtually before they are implemented on the shop floor. The carmaker says the approach has proven itself in practice: in 2023, the production line in Rastatt's assembly hall 4.0 was converted, configured and optimised within just a few weeks by means of virtual commissioning. This reduced risk during ramp-up and ensured that new equipment integrated smoothly into existing workflows.

The digital manufacturing execution system also helps coordinate production between Rastatt and the Kuppenheim and Untertürkheim plants to effectively manage the delivery of components electric drive units and body parts just-in-time.

The electric drive units and axles for the latest GLA are produced in Untertürkheim, at Mercedes-Benz’s Hedelfingen and Mettingen plants. Each drive unit is made of three subsystems: an electric motor, power electronics and the gearbox. The power-transmitting wheelset and other components, such as the control system, are also manufactured there. The assembly of these components into a complete system takes place at the Untertürkheim plant. Mettingen is also responsible for assembling the electric axles for the GLA, which are then delivered to Rastatt as a complete system.

Advertisement

The GLA’s high-voltage batteries come from Mercedes-Benz’s subsidiary Accumotive in Kamenz, Saxony.

Body-in-white components as well as structural and body parts are made at the Mercedes-Benz Kuppenheim plant, located 10km from Rastatt, which is now organised as part of Rastatt operations.

“The electric drive units and axles for the new GLA are supplied by the Untertürkheim plant and its Mettingen and Hedelfingen sites,” explains Zwick “Body-in-white components as well as structural and body parts come from Kuppenheim, which has been part of the Rastatt plant since the beginning of 2026.”

Logistics for the network is coordinated through the Mercedes-Benz International Consolidation Center (ICC) in Bischweier (a district of Rastatt). Together, Rastatt, Kuppenheim and Bischweier form the automotive region there. All sites work with the MO360 digital production ecosystem, while the MO360 Data Platform analyses their production data across the network.

Chip-to-cloud platform

In Rastatt, production is also directly linked to the Mercedes Intelligent Cloud via MB.OS, so every vehicle leaves the plant with up-to-date software. The carmaker describes the MB.OS as a chip-to-cloud software platform that connects the vehicle’s hardware to the cloud and manages a range of functions. That includes in-car functions for drivers but it also helps with manufacturing quality, connecting manufacturing and production data, streamlining how software configurations are flashed and tested during assembly. The chip-to-cloud architecture transfers the vehicle software via a central server of the Mercedes-Benz Intelligent Cloud instead of via various hardware modules, so that the vehicles always roll off the assembly line with the latest version.

“Rastatt was the first Mercedes-Benz plant to implement MB.OS in production, which serves as the blueprint for plants worldwide,” says Zwick. “The experience gained from the production launches of the CLA and GLA, as well as from the use of digital twins, also feeds back into the entire production network.”

MB.OS centralises software operations in Mercedes-Benz vehicle production. Production is directly connected to the Mercedes Intelligent Cloud (MIC), which is responsible for software update packages and the installation processes. “As a result, vehicle software is continuously updated during production, and every vehicle leaves the plant always up to date", says Zwick.

Within the development, production and fleet operations network, the MIC is directly linked to the MO360 Data Platform, so the current software status of each vehicle is transparent at all times. Rastatt was the first Mercedes-Benz plant to implement MB.OS in production, starting with the CLA. Following this successful start, MB.OS has now been fully rolled out in the plant's second assembly hall as well, and serves as the blueprint for plants worldwide. This latest investment by Mercedes-Benz reinforces the Rastatt. plant's role as a key hub for Mercedes-Benz's future production of electric, hybrid and software-defined vehicles.

“The start of production of the new GLA marks another important chapter for the Mercedes-Benz Rastatt plant,” said Torsten Höink, chairman of the Works Council at the Rastatt plant at the production launch in September. “This vehicle represents modern mobility and the successful transformation of our production. The decision to manufacture the GLA in Rastatt strengthens our competitiveness and secures the future for our colleagues.”

title: San Francisco Is Ground Zero for AI. How Would Congressional Candidates Push for Regulation?
description:
Currently, there is no comprehensive federal framework regulating AI, and experts following AI development closely say it’s time for lawmakers in Washington to set up guardrails even as President Donald Trump has suggested AI companies will regulate themselves.
His first attempt at an AI safety bill included a “kill-switch” for disastrous scenarios and other safeguards; however, that bill was vetoed by Gov.
Along the campaign trail, Wiener has leaned into that legislative experience and touted being an early advocate for AI safety.
“No more tax breaks for these billionaires and tech corporations.” She’s also criticized her opponent’s AI safety bill, calling it “watered down” and influenced by big tech interests.
For whichever candidate wins, the questions around AI safety are not likely going away soon.
text:
At the center of the artificial intelligence boom, candidates looking to represent San Francisco in Washington appear aligned on a common goal: AI must be regulated. But how to do that is where the debate really heats up.

State Sen. Scott Wiener and San Francisco Supervisor Connie Chan are vying for Rep. Nancy Pelosi’s seat in Congress as the former House speaker prepares to retire after nearly four decades. They’re competing for votes at a time when concerns are rising around AI, from mass job loss to automated data privacy hacks and computer-driven nuclear war.

“Consumers have not seen such rapid change with any new technology. I mean, you could look to the internet, you could to railroads, you can go all the way back and look at industrialization in the 1800s, but we’ve just never seen this sort of rapid development,” said Michele Neitz, a professor of law, technology and social transformation at the University of San Francisco School of Law.

Currently, there is no comprehensive federal framework regulating AI, and experts following AI development closely say it’s time for lawmakers in Washington to set up guardrails even as President Donald Trump has suggested AI companies will regulate themselves.

“That rapid development is happening more quickly than our political system can keep up,” Neitz said.

Wiener has long been vocal about the need to regulate and increase transparency around AI, and authored the country’s first AI transparency bill, which California passed in 2025. His first attempt at an AI safety bill included a “kill-switch” for disastrous scenarios and other safeguards; however, that bill was vetoed by Gov. Gavin Newsom.

The bill that did pass, SB 53, has since been adapted around the country, including by New York City, and other places like Connecticut have gone on to add even more comprehensive AI legislation focused on areas like education and workforce mandates.

Along the campaign trail, Wiener has leaned into that legislative experience and touted being an early advocate for AI safety. His vision for Congress is to create a federal regulatory body to oversee AI security, increase guardrails and protect whistleblowers, and expand unemployment to brace for waves of job displacement.

In a video advertisement, Wiener tells viewers that “AI is getting more powerful by the day, and the risks are very real.” He said that in Washington, he would continue to seek the kill-switch approach, along with more legal liability and safety standards and cooperation with other countries on AI safety.

Wiener has also said that AI data centers should pick up the tab for their environmental costs, and he supports transitioning data centers towards greener energy, rather than a full ban on new facilities.

Chan meanwhile has taken what Neitz said is the more “populist” approach, calling for a full moratorium on data centers and giving unions and AI workers a voice in regulation.

In her own video on the topic, Chan pointed to a $3.9 billion tax break that Meta received last year to build data centers. “We’re going to regulate artificial intelligence to make sure we can protect our workforce and prioritize safety for the American people,” she said. “No more tax breaks for these billionaires and tech corporations.”

She’s also criticized her opponent’s AI safety bill, calling it “watered down” and influenced by big tech interests. The bill also did not prevent major cyberattacks this year, where AI models hacked into other platforms and breached government websites. Chan said the companies overseeing the models, OpenAI and Anthropic, should “absolutely” be held liable for the attacks.

“Instead of waiting for something catastrophic to happen and to have a so-called kill switch, it is important to have human oversight during the developmental phase of the technology,” Chan said at a debate this week hosted by Mission Local and the New York Times. “Can we trust the AI industries to police and regulate themselves? And can we trust any politicians who are bankrolled by the AI industry? I say no.”

The advocacy group Public First Action, which is pushing for more AI regulation and has received money from the AI company Anthropic, has poured $3 million into Abundant Future, an independent expenditure committee supporting Wiener, Punchbowl News first reported.

Wiener, in the debate this week, said, “That PAC supports candidates who are pro-AI regulation, and because I have actually regulated AI and will lead in regulating AI in Congress, that is my understanding of why that PAC is supporting me.”

He went on to defend his record, saying he “went to war with big tech to pass AI regulation in California.”

In September, tech titans including Anthropic’s Dario Amodei and OpenAI’s Sam Altman, both leading San Francisco-based companies, made headlines for sounding the alarm about potentially devastating impacts of AI on humanity and called for regulations.

But AI CEOs are not all in agreement on the issue. Others are advocating for self-regulation in order not to hinder development of the technology or risk falling behind China’s AI advancements.

President Donald Trump has pushed back against regulatory guardrails for AI, previously calling doomsday threats a “hoax.” In September, he signed a document with executives at Google, Anthropic, Meta, OpenAI, Nvidia and SpaceX that calls for “robust internal processes and controls to ensure that their technology behaves as intended.”

Both Chan and Wiener don’t trust the idea.

“We must not allow the tech companies to write their own self-regulation,” Wiener said. “We need Congress to step up and regulate tech to make sure technology is serving the public and not harming the public, and that will be a priority for me.”

Slowing down AI development has become the biggest political issue for many in the Bay Area. Wynd Kaufman, a retired former engineering teacher at City College of San Francisco, was one of several protesters arrested outside of the OpenAI headquarters last year, months before its CEO came out warning about the technology’s potential downsides.

“The concentration of talent, venture capital, leading universities and innovative companies continues to make the Bay Area the premier destination for AI development and investment,” said Colin Yasukochi, executive director of CBRE Tech Insights.

For whichever candidate wins, the questions around AI safety are not likely going away soon.

According to Neitz, “2027 is going to be a big year in AI legislation regardless of the outcome of the midterms because the people are clamoring for it and Congress will need to respond.”

text:
This audio is auto-generated. Please let us know if you have feedback.

Dive Brief:

The U.S. International Trade Commission found in a Wednesday vote that U.S. solar manufacturing has been injured by imports of crystalline silicon photovoltaic cells from India, Indonesia and Laos, aligning with the Department of Commerce’s finding last month and setting up the Commerce Department to finalize anti-dumping and countervailing duty orders.

“Duty margins are very substantial on all three countries,” said Wiley Rein partner Tim Brightbill, who represents the Alliance for American Solar Manufacturing and Trade, during a Wednesday press call. The alliance petitioned for the AD/CVD investigation. “For India, there were dumping margins of 123% for all producers, countervailing duty rates of 126%... We think those will be, and are, prohibitive rates.”

The Alliance for American Solar Manufacturing and Trade is led by the U.S. solar manufacturers First Solar, Hanwha Qcells USA and Mission Solar Energy. Brightbill said the alliance expects the final AD/CVD orders will be issued by the Commerce Department on Nov. 2.

Dive Insight:

The ITC’s finding follows a 2023 determination from the ITC and the Commerce Department that manufacturers had operated in Malaysia, Thailand, Cambodia and Vietnam to dodge tariffs on Chinese-made solar components. Commerce set subsidy rates in that case, in 2025, which went as high as 3,403.96% for four Cambodian solar exporters.

With Wednesday’s finding, “what happens next is that orders will be issued by the Commerce Department, and the duties will be locked in, and that will formally close off this route that many Chinese-owned companies who had set up shop in Indonesia and Laos had used to get around the prior solar trade cases,” Brightbill said.

He noted that when new cases are successful, “we often see evasion attempts to evade duties or circumvent the duties ... Notably, Ethiopia is currently the third-largest source of solar imports, and imports from Ethiopia have surged more than 3,000% in the last 12 months.”

The alliance is alleging that “many of these Ethiopian imports are not actually manufactured there,” he said, and are instead “largely” Chinese-manufactured products that are seeking to circumvent existing tariffs on China and “engaging in whack-a-mole behavior and simply shifting operations.”

The alliance has an inquiry into those Ethiopian solar imports underway with the Commerce Department, Brightbill said.

Commerce Department import statistics show that the U.S. imported 232 million watts of solar cells in 2022, then 2 billion watts in 2024. In the same time frame, imports from Laos went from zero to 1.9 million watts.

Brightbill said during the press call that it is “too early to tell” if the Trump administration’s Section 232 tariff on polysilicon, which will go into effect Dec. 4, will end the need for further petitions with Commerce.

“We are hopeful that these Section 232 actions can help address the whack-a-mole problem, but I don’t think we’ll know for some time to come if we continue to see unfair trade practices that might need to be addressed. So we’re monitoring very closely,” he said.

The solar industry has historically been divided on whether or not the government should take action against cheap solar imports. U.S. solar manufacturers have generally taken the position that it should, while clean energy groups and solar trade associations have opposed these petitions, saying that crackdowns on imports could create market uncertainty or “chill” the industry.

When the probe into imports from Malaysia, Thailand, Cambodia and Vietnam was first announced in 2022, Heather Zichal, then-CEO of the American Clean Power Association, called the investigation a “disaster” that “effectively freezes development in the U.S. solar industry,” according to reporting from E&E News.

Brightbill noted in the Wednesday call that it is difficult for the U.S. to compete with China on the cost of solar components. “So we also need smart domestic policy that builds American manufacturing at scale, and we’re starting to see that now on modules and cells,” he said.

title: Korean battery makers shift to domestic LFP cathodes amid US IRA rules - CHOSUNBIZ
description: Korean battery makers shift to domestic LFP cathodes amid US IRA rules  Domestic battery companies are diversifying their procurement of cathode mater
text:
Domestic battery companies are diversifying their procurement of cathode materials, a key material for lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries that have relied on Chinese companies, to domestic corporations. This move is seen as a response to the prohibited foreign entity (PFE) rules related to the advanced manufacturing production tax credit (AMPC) under the U.S. Inflation Reduction Act (IRA), and to raise domestic industry contribution scores in bid evaluations for the domestic energy storage system (ESS) central contract market.
According to the battery industry on the 16th, LG Energy Solution is in the final stage of negotiations to sign LFP cathode supply contracts with POSCO FUTURE M and L&F. If LG Energy Solution secures LFP cathodes from the two companies, it can diversify a supply chain that has relied on Chinese materials.
In 2024, LG Energy Solution signed a long-term contract with China's ShangzhuliYuan to supply LFP cathodes. Now, by pursuing supply contracts with domestic material companies as well, it has embarked on diversifying cathode procurement sources.
A view of the LFP cathode material plant in Guji-myeon, Dalseong-gun, Daegu, built in May by L&F's dedicated subsidiary for lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery cathode production, L&F Plus. /Courtesy of L&F
Before LG Energy Solution, Samsung SDI and SK On signed contracts to purchase LFP cathodes from POSCO FUTURE M and L&F. On Oct. 6, Samsung SDI signed a contract with POSCO FUTURE M to receive 6 trillion won worth of LFP cathodes from 2027 to 2032. In March, it signed a contract with L&F to receive about 1 trillion won worth of LFP cathodes for three years starting in 2027.
SK On decided to procure 1 trillion won worth of LFP cathodes from POSCO FUTURE M and 160 billion won worth from L&F.
Battery cell companies are turning to Korean material suppliers because they are about to expand LFP battery production. LG Energy Solution is currently producing LFP batteries for ESS (energy storage systems) at its plants in China and the United States. Next year, it will produce ESS-use LFP batteries with an annual capacity of 1 gigawatt-hour (GWh) in Ochang, North Chungcheong.
Samsung SDI will begin mass-producing LFP batteries for ESS in Indiana in the fourth quarter of this year and plans to supply LFP batteries starting next year. SK On is converting part of its Seosan, South Chungcheong plant facilities into ESS-use LFP production lines. It also plans to use part of its Georgia, U.S., plant facilities to produce LFP batteries for ESS. SK On's mass production of ESS-use LFPs is expected to begin next year.
Behind battery cell companies' push to secure domestically produced LFP cathodes are U.S. rules related to prohibited foreign entities. The rules for the advanced manufacturing production tax credit place limits on supply chains linked to prohibited foreign entities. Using parts subsidized by countries designated as prohibited foreign entities can exclude a company from eligibility for the tax credit.
POSCO FUTURE M plans to start mass-producing LFP cathodes at its Pohang plant at the end of this year. C&P New Material Technology, a joint venture established by POSCO FUTURE M with Chinese precursor corporations CNGR and CNGR's Korean subsidiary Fino, is building an LFP cathode plant in the Yeongilman 4 General Industrial Complex in Pohang
L&F is expanding LFP cathode production capacity in Daegu through its wholly owned subsidiary L&F Plus. L&F Plus completed its plant in May. It announced plans to start mass production at an annual scale of 30,000 tons (t) by the end of the third quarter this year. It then plans to establish an annual production system of 60,000 t by the first half of 2027.
Bidding in the ESS central contract market is also cited as a factor encouraging the adoption of domestically produced LFP cathodes. The Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment and the Korea Power Exchange announced in September the third ESS central contract market bidding with a total scale of 1,180 megawatts (MW). In bid evaluations, the weights for price and non-price indicators are 50% each. Of the 100 points for non-price indicators, 25 are allocated to industrial and economic contribution, which evaluates factors such as domestic production of materials and parts and contribution to supply chains.
A battery industry official said, "Not only in the United States but also in Europe, there are moves to create regulations on battery materials, so it is meaningful to secure a balanced supply of key materials, including LFP cathodes, encompassing domestic products."

text:
As a follow-up to a special Washington Wire that NAED released earlier this month, several other industry associations are now asking Congress to pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, a 417-page proposal intended to modernize federal environmental review and permitting processes for energy, infrastructure, and other major projects.

Several provisions could be particularly significant for NAED members. tED magazine took a deeper dive into permitting reform in it’s cover story of the August issue, showing this is a multi-trillion-dollar opportunity for our supply chain.

Bill Owens, chairman of the National Association of Home Builders (NAHB) and a home builder and remodeler from Worthington, Ohio, issued the following statement after Senators Mike Lee (R-UT), Shelley Moore Capito (R-WV), Martin Heinrich (D-NM), and Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI) released the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act.

“NAHB applauds Senators Lee, Capito, Heinrich and Whitehouse and for their leadership and bipartisan approach to crafting the most meaningful reforms in decades to several key federal environmental permitting programs.

“The housing sector stands to benefit from many of these federal permitting reforms, including an increase in acreage thresholds under the Clean Water Act’s (CWA) Nationwide Permit program along with extending the statutory timeframe from five to 10 years for the CWA permit programs. These provisions provide the industry with needed clarity and consistency during the federal permitting process.”

The National Electrical Contractors Association (NECA) released the following statement from CEO David Long:

“This bipartisan agreement is an important step toward making our nation’s permitting process more efficient and predictable. Improving transmission planning and siting, accelerating interconnections and streamlining approvals will help move critical projects from planning to construction faster.

NECA contractors are already building the infrastructure that powers America, from transmission and substations to power generation, schools, hospitals, manufacturing facilities and the electrical systems that support communities nationwide. Permitting reform will help ensure the regulatory process can keep pace with the tremendous investment and growing demand across our industry.

We appreciate Senators Lee, Capito, Heinrich and Whitehouse for working together on this agreement, as well as the Administration’s engagement in the process. NECA looks forward to continuing to work with Congress and the White House to advance comprehensive permitting reform and get America building.”

Associated Builders and Contractors issued a letter of support for S. 5653, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026. ABC urged the U.S. Senate to quickly pass the legislation, which includes reforms that ABC has long sought for the construction industry and would also benefit taxpayers, communities and owners.

“The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act’s comprehensive and balanced reforms to the National Environmental Policy Act and the Clean Water Act would address bureaucratic and procedural inefficiencies that deter and delay development,” said Kristen Swearingen, ABC vice president of government affairs. “By streamlining reviews, increasing transparency and setting clearer timelines, the legislation would create a more predictable permitting process that helps contractors plan work, invest in their workforce and deliver housing, infrastructure and other critical projects while continuing to protect the environment.

“ABC applauds Senate Environment and Public Works Committee leaders Sens. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., and Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., and Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee leaders Sens. Mike Lee, R-Utah, and Martin Heinrich, D-N.M. for reaching this bipartisan agreement,” Swearingen said. “The Senate must now pass this important permitting reform bill to help contractors put people to work and deliver the projects communities need.”

The National Association of Manufacturers, joined by members of its Council of Manufacturing Associations, Conference of State Manufacturers Associations and other leading manufacturing and business organizations, sent a coalition letter urging Congress to swiftly pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act. Representing businesses across the country and industries throughout the manufacturing economy, the coalition called on lawmakers to advance the bipartisan permitting deal to reduce costly delays, provide greater certainty for investment and make it easier to build and expand manufacturing operations in America.

The undersigned organizations, members of the NAM’s Council of Manufacturing Associations and Conference of State Manufacturers Associations and other aligned manufacturing and business organizations, represent businesses, manufacturers, and energy producers that employ millions of Americans in every industrial sector and in every state, as well as U.S. territories and Puerto Rico. We write in strong and unified support for S. 5653, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act and respectfully urge you to bring it to the Senate floor for immediate consideration.

Our organizations applaud the hard work that the bipartisan negotiators have done to find practical solutions to the challenges our industry faces in permitting projects to expand and grow manufacturing. It is a testament to our democracy that leaders from both parties can come together to seek common ground and address the major challenges that are facing our industry in the United States. Reforming our permitting processes will make it easier and more cost-efficient for manufacturers to get shovels in the ground on job-creating projects.

Finalizing and passing S. 5653, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, is an historic opportunity to deliver long-overdue reforms to our nation’s permitting process while maintaining America’s commitment to environmental stewardship. Manufacturers cannot afford inaction.

Our nation’s broken permitting system affects projects in every industry and of every energy source, directly contributing to the rising cost of electricity to homeowners and businesses. Right now, in the United States, it takes 80% longer to get a permit authorized for a manufacturing facility than it does in any other free market economy.

Permitting delays cost manufacturers at least $8 billion every year. That’s money not being spent on hiring new workers, expanding shop floors, or going back into the local economy. Manufacturers are ready to build in America; we just need the certainty and a modernized permitting process to make it happen.

Should the Senate pass this critical legislation, we would call on the House to move expeditiously to consider the bipartisan comprehensive agreement and deliver this manufacturing win to the American people.

Now is the time for action. Manufacturers are ready to build, and modernized permitting will help us race to the future. Thank you for your leadership and dedication to supporting manufacturers in the United States.

title: Green Jobs, Not Glass Ceiling: Women Powering Southeast Asia's Clean Energy Transition
description:
We created the HerPOWER Leadership Cohort in Viet Nam to change that.
Too often, I have walked into rooms where the future of the energy transition was being discussed almost entirely by men.
Building on that model, we launched the first cohort in 2025 as a joint initiative of Devtale Partners, the World Bank, GIZ Viet Nam, Women in Energy Viet Nam (WEVN), and the WePOWER network.
That internship led her to apply to HerPOWER Viet Nam.
HerPOWER Viet Nam's first cohort is a bet that the transition moves faster, and more fairly, when women help lead it.
text:
By Md Arif Raihan Maahi, Chief Impact Officer, Devtale Partners

Ask who is designing Viet Nam's wind farms, running its solar plants, or setting the policies that will govern its energy transition, and the answer is still mostly men, though a growing number of women are pushing that door open. Viet Nam ranks 72nd out of 146 countries on the World Economic Forum's 2023 Global Gender Gap Index, and women hold only 22% of jobs in the country's fast-growing green industries, still concentrated in administrative roles rather than the technical and leadership positions that will define how the transition unfolds. We created the HerPOWER Leadership Cohort in Viet Nam to change that.

Too often, I have walked into rooms where the future of the energy transition was being discussed almost entirely by men. I have seen how the absence of diverse voices narrows the conversation and slows the progress we all want. That experience convinced me that the only way to balance those rooms is to bring more women into the sector itself.

The pattern extends well beyond Viet Nam. Globally, women make up only around 32% of the renewable energy workforce, concentrated in administrative functions rather than the engineering, policy, and leadership roles that shape the sector's direction. Viet Nam, meanwhile, has committed to one of the region's most ambitious energy transitions: under its revised Power Development Plan VIII (PDP8), renewable sources excluding hydropower are set to supply 28–36% of the country's power mix by 2030, rising to as much as 74–75% by 2050. Our premise is straightforward: that transition will only be as fast, and as fair, as the number of women who help lead it.

HerPOWER Viet Nam is the first Southeast Asian chapter of a leadership model that began in Bangladesh in 2022 as Shoktikonna (Power Woman), which we co-created at Devtale Partners with the World Bank. HerPOWER Viet Nam combines self-paced online coursework on the World Bank's official learning platform and through sponsored Coursera courses from the University of Illinois, with live sessions delivered by more than 10 international experts. The experts are drawn from institutions including the World Bank's Energy Sector Management Assistance Program (ESMAP), the Asian Development Bank, the European Commission, and the European Investment Bank, as well as universities such as the University of Utah and the Florence School of Regulation.

Building on that model, we launched the first cohort in 2025 as a joint initiative of Devtale Partners, the World Bank, GIZ Viet Nam, Women in Energy Viet Nam (WEVN), and the WePOWER network. When the cohort graduated, leaders from every partner came together in Ha Noi and Ho Chi Minh City to celebrate and to reaffirm a shared commitment to a more inclusive green transition.

Nguyen Xuan Dieu Linh, a Sustainability and ESG Specialist at KLINOVA, completed the program and was recognized as a leader at the graduation ceremony in June 2026. Her colleague Nguyen Thi Minh Hue took part in the same cohort cycle from the other side of the room, as a guest speaker on ESG for future energy leaders. To me, it is a small sign of how quickly the program is drawing energy-sector professionals in as mentors as well as participants.

Not every graduate arrives already set on a career in energy. For some, the program is what turns an early interest into a firm decision. Nguyễn Trần Ngọc Như, an undergraduate studying International Relations at Ho Chi Minh City University of Social Sciences and Humanities, first found her way into the sector through an internship with GIZ's Energy Support Programme. She spent six months working on the Project Development Programme that changed how she saw her own prospects in the field. "I realized that renewable energy is a field with great potential and meaningful impact," she said. "I also saw that someone with a non-technical background like mine in International Relations can still contribute to the energy transition."

That internship led her to apply to HerPOWER Viet Nam. "That experience encouraged me to explore the sector further through HerPOWER, and now I am confident that this is the career path I want to pursue," she said.

Ngô Phương Linh, a recent International Business Administration graduate of Foreign Trade University, shared a standout memory of her time in the first cohort. "The best memory for me was during the final project of the program, which was the Solve-A-Thon. I got to work with people who share the same vision and goals as me," she said. With limited work experience, she found it a rare chance to put ideas into practice. "I don't have a lot of work experience yet. But through this opportunity, I was truly able to be a part of a very practical project focused on sustainability, carbon, and things like that, which I really enjoyed," she said. What stayed with her most, though, was a sense of community: "Thanks to HerPOWER, I realized that I am not alone on this journey, because there are many others out there just like me."

Stories like these are exactly why we built the program the way we did.

More than 40 women were selected for Viet Nam's first cohort. They were final-year STEM undergraduates and young professionals from universities, companies, and vocational institutes across the country, chosen from a competitive applicant pool. Alongside the coursework, participants take part in a Solve-A-Thon in which teams pitch solutions to real energy-sector problems, a Green Skills Summit, and a graduation ceremony that closes out the cohort.

It is genuinely inspiring to see how the program's success in Bangladesh has translated into Viet Nam: not just replicated, but building on itself and multiplying its impact. Women remain significantly underrepresented in the energy and green transition workforce, and closing that gap takes deliberate, strategic skill-development initiatives and strong collaboration across borders. The more gender-balanced we make this workforce, the faster the transition itself accelerates.

Viet Nam's first cohort joins a network that is still young but growing quickly. We aim to build a track record that others in the region can follow: women equipped not just to work in the energy sector, but to lead it, in engineering teams, in policy rooms, and in the decisions that will shape Viet Nam's clean-energy future. As the country works toward the power mix set out in PDP8, that future will need to look a great deal more like the population it serves.

HerPOWER Viet Nam's first cohort is a bet that the transition moves faster, and more fairly, when women help lead it. I believe it is a bet worth making.

description:

Clean streets are not a luxury.
He will then send the Legislature a Clean Streets California Act establishing clear standards and accountability for cities and counties across California.

text:
Steve Hilton’s Plan to Clean Up California

The Problem

California should be the cleanest, most beautiful state in America. Instead, too many communities are covered in graffiti, litter, illegal dumping and abandoned junk. The state of our streets is too often utterly disgusting. Stench, squalor, the complete collapse of civilized standards and public order. All in the richest state in the richest country on earth. Under one party rule California has become a living example of JK Galbraith’s dictum “Private affluence and public squalor.”

Californians pay the highest taxes in America. We should not have to accept filthy streets and public spaces in return. We are shamed by streets that stink of urine and feces.

State and local governments already spend heavily on cleanup. But the system is fragmented. Residents are sent from one agency to another. Reports disappear without explanation. Local governments measure performance differently, if they measure it at all. No one can clearly see which cities are responding quickly and which are allowing public spaces to deteriorate.

Clean streets are not a luxury. They affect public safety, local businesses, property values and whether people take pride in their community. Keeping public spaces clean is one of the most basic jobs of government.

Steve Hilton’s Plan

As governor, Steve will initiate a Clean-Up California Challenge, to be completed within one year of taking office. It will begin by fixing the cleanup systems controlled by state government. He will then send the Legislature a Clean Streets California Act establishing clear standards and accountability for cities and counties across California.

Steve’s commitment is clear: “One way or another, California will be cleaned up by the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028. The work starts the day I take office and reaches every community across the state. Local leaders who get the job done will have my support. Where they fail, the state will step in.”

The plan will operate through existing state agencies and redirect existing cleanup and beautification funding toward measurable results. It will draw on lessons from around the world where rapid clean-up has been successfully achieved, for example Singapore in the 1960s, Kigali, Rwanda and New York City in the 1990s. Steve’s approach will be based on his belief in the decentralization of power: local action where possible.

But there will be a state backstop: the current situation is completely unacceptable and if local politicians do not clean up their cities quickly, Steve will act. “Carrot where possible - stick where necessary” will be the guiding principle.

1. Start by Holding State Government Accountable

On taking office, Steve will issue an Executive Order directing Caltrans and the California Environmental Protection Agency to consolidate and improve the state’s existing systems for reporting litter, graffiti, illegal dumping and other maintenance problems on state-managed property.

Every report involving a state highway or other state-managed public space will receive a trackable service ticket. Residents will be able to see when the report was received, assigned and resolved.

State agencies will be required to publish their response times, unresolved reports and repeat problem locations. A report will not be marked resolved without photographic evidence or a documented inspection showing that the work was completed.

2. Put People to Work Cleaning Up California

Steve will use existing cleanup funding to expand paid street-cleaning crews for Californians who are ready and able to join the Clean-Up California Challenge. These crews will remove litter, clear graffiti and clean public spaces. Steve will create partnerships with statewide and local community and volunteer organizations, mobilized into a California Clean-Up Force. We will use creative ways to make Clean-Up California fun and effective, for example through focused days of action, prizes, and cultural activation. Steve will challenge the business community to partner in these efforts.

3. Give Residents One Place to Report Squalor

The Clean-Up California Challenge will establish one statewide platform for reporting serious cleanliness problems on public property.

Residents will be able to:

Report graffiti, litter, illegal dumping, abandoned furniture and similar problems.

Submit a photo with the location and time automatically attached.

Receive a service ticket showing which public agency is responsible.

Track when the report was received, assigned and resolved.

See evidence that the problem was actually addressed.

The platform will connect with local 311 systems instead of forcing cities to discard systems that already work. Reports will be routed automatically to the city, county or state agency responsible for that location.

Cities and counties will be required to return basic service information to the statewide platform so residents are not forced to navigate different government systems or wonder whether anyone received their report.

4. Grade Cities and Counties on Results

The Governor’s Clean-Up California Challenge will include a consistent standard for measuring the condition of local streets and public spaces.

Inspectors - including volunteers and existing community organizations - will regularly examine randomly selected public locations across every city and county. Inspections will be limited to public streets and public spaces. The program will not use drones or conduct surveillance of homes or private property.

Inspection results will be combined with actual service data, including:

Response times.

Unresolved complaints.

Repeat problem locations.

The accuracy of reports marked as completed.

Whether cleanliness is improving or deteriorating.

Every city and county will receive a public rating: Spotless, Clean, Needs Work or Squalid.

The methodology, underlying data and rankings will be public. Residents will be able to compare their community with others and see whether local officials are delivering results.

5. Reward Success and Impose Consequences for Failure

The Clean Streets California Act and Steve’s first state budget will direct future discretionary cleanup and beautification funding toward communities that demonstrate strong performance or real improvement.

California will publicly recognize its cleanest and most improved communities.

State agencies, cities and counties will publish interim cleanup targets and report their progress every quarter against the July 2028 deadline.

A city or county repeatedly rated Squalid will be required to publish a corrective action plan with specific cleanup targets and deadlines. If deadlines are missed, direct state action will ensue. We will not shy away from using the stick as well as the carrot.

Communities that improve will become eligible for greater support. Local governments that repeatedly fail, conceal their performance or refuse to participate will go to the back of the line for future discretionary funding. Or be fined. Or be taken into emergency measures run by the state. Squalor is not acceptable and will not be accepted.

Mayors, county supervisors and other local officials will have to answer publicly for the condition of the streets they manage. If they preside over continuing squalor, they will face the consequences.

A Basic Standard for Every Community

Government does not need more excuses or another sprawling bureaucracy. It needs clear standards, public accountability and consequences for failure.

California should be the cleanest, most beautiful state in America. Steve Hilton will make it easy to report a mess, require government to respond and show everyone which communities are getting the job done.

Steve’s Clean-Up California Challenge will ensure that one way or another, California is cleaned up by the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028.

text:
Mayor Lori Stone asked the Warren City Council to "hear out" a company's proposal for developing a climate action plan during her annual State of the City address Thursday, Oct. 15.

Some cities in Michigan have made climate action plans, or documents for measuring and reducing greenhouse gas emissions and adapting to a changing climate, according to ClimateCheck. Stone has been seeking to create such a plan.

Through a competitive process, the city has a consultant developing a climate action plan. The council tabled an agenda item last year to approve funding for the company, Blue Strike Environmental.

"Please take it off the table and act to move it forward," Stone said. "Only City Council can award a contract for climate action planning."

Stone's remarks were part of her annual address Thursday, in which she promoted Warren's recent accomplishments, including the opening of Eckstein Skatepark and the renovation of the Community Center auditorium, where Stone's speech was held. She highlighted state or federal funding the city is pursuing or has recently secured, including over $8 million in funding from the Federal Emergency Management Agency.

Stone said the climate action plan, which she said creates a framework for improvements, is "essential" to drawing down grant funding that "will allow taxpayer dollars to go further" in implementing sustainability initiatives, she said.

In October 2025, the council tabled an agenda item to approve an award to Blue Strike Environmental Inc. for furnishing a climate action plan in an amount not to exceed $150,000. The Monterey, California-based company was found through a request for the proposal process and was the recommendation of a city committee.

"I am asking Warren City Council to hear out the company that was ... recommended by the RFP committee," Stone said.

Councilman Jonathan Lafferty said while the climate action plan has "a relatively small charge" compared to the overall city budget, he said the projects it would generate would total "in the millions of dollars to Warren residents." He said when the council tabled the item, it asked the Mayor's Office for a list of the objectives and plans for sustainability in the city.

"What is the the city doing already?" he said. "What are our objectives to be sustainable? What are we doing to be a healthier climate city? And that's over a year ago that I put that request in, so that we can say, 'What's our benchmark? ... If we want to improve, where are we at right now?'"

He said the information has yet to be presented to the council.

Warren seeks infrastructure funding

Stone said Warren is pursuing $12 million in funding from the state's Drinking Water State Revolving Fund. The low-interest loan would support efforts to replace lead service lines and other water lines.

"This could provide Warren with critical financial resources to address aging infrastructure while minimizing the financial burden on taxpayers," Stone told the audience.

Stone said Warren also has secured FEMA grants, including a $4.4 million grant for Section 2 sanitary sewer improvements and a $4.1 million grant for Jackson Avenue and Rivard Avenue sanitary sewer replacements. The city was notified in the last few months that it was being awarded the grants.

"Together, this represents more than 8 million in investment on Warren's sanitary sewer infrastructure, strengthening the systems beneath our neighborhoods and reducing risk for flooding in our households," she said.

Warren City Engineer Tina Gapshes said the city is designing the project, and construction will start in the spring.

text:
Americans spend a lot of money on energy every year. In fact, it's actually one of the largest household expenses for the average American homeowner. But some states have gotten better at implementing energy-efficient habits in hopes of saving some extra cash.

To determine which state is the most energy-efficient, WalletHub ranked each state based off how efficient its energy was both at home and in the car.

How much does energy cost?

Dig deeper:

According to WalletHub, the average family in the U.S. spends at least $2,000 on utilities such as heating and cooling. On top of that, the average resident in the U.S. spends roughly $2,400 per year on gasoline.

By implementing simple energy-efficient measures in your home could cut some utility expenses by up to 25%, while switching to a fuel-efficient vehicle can save drivers over $1,000 per year, according to the U.S. Department of Energy.

How energy-efficient in the Midwest?

Local perspective:

Landing at the top of the list for the Midwest was Minnesota, which ranked as the ninth most energy-efficient state in the country. The North Star state finished ranked 9th for home energy efficiency and 19th for auto energy efficiency.

Not far behind was Wisconsin at No. 11, which finished 18th for home energy efficiency and 9th for auto efficiency.

Other Midwest states near the top include South Dakota at No. 15, with the best home energy efficiency rank in the country, Illinois at No. 17, Michigan at No. 20 and Iowa at No. 21.

Check out the full list of how every Midwest state ranked from most to least energy-efficient:

No. 9: Minnesota — 9th for home energy efficiency and 19th for auto energy efficiency

No. 11: Wisconsin — 18th for home energy efficiency and 9th for auto energy efficiency

No. 15: South Dakota — 1st for home energy efficiency and 46th for auto energy efficiency

No. 17: Illinois — 28th for home energy efficiency and 8th for auto energy efficiency

No. 20: Michigan — 25th for home energy efficiency and 14th for auto energy efficiency

No. 21: Iowa — 6th for home energy efficiency and 45th for auto energy efficiency

No. 29 : Ohio — 33rd for home energy efficiency and 20th for auto energy efficiency

No. 32: Indiana — 36th for home energy efficiency and 21st for auto energy efficiency

No. 33: North Dakota — 17th for home energy efficiency and 47th for auto energy efficiency

Rest of the country

Big picture view:

As for the rest of the U.S., California landed at the top of the list with the 3rd best home energy efficiency rank and 2nd for auto energy efficiency.

Vermont finished just behind at No. 2, followed by New York at No. 3, and Washington at No. 4.

On the other end, South Carolina finished with the worst energy efficiency in the country, with Alabama as the second-worst.

text:
Guilford County, the City of Greensboro and the City of High Point today announced the adoption of the North Carolina Commercial Property Assessed Capital Expenditure Program, commonly known as NC C-PACE.

Following action by the Guilford County Board of Commissioners on Thursday, Oct. 15, and coordinated implementation with Greensboro and High Point, C-PACE will give eligible property owners in participating Guilford County jurisdictions a new way to finance qualifying improvements to existing buildings and new construction.

C-PACE allows willing owners of eligible commercial, industrial, agricultural, nonprofit, and multifamily properties with five or more dwelling units to obtain long-term financing from private capital providers. Eligible projects may include energy-efficiency upgrades, water-conservation measures, renewable-energy systems, and improvements that make buildings more resilient.

The Economic Development Partnership of North Carolina is the statewide administrator for the C-PACE Program. Guilford County, Greensboro, and High Point will work with the statewide administrator to support local participation and inform interested property owners.

“C-PACE gives Guilford County another way to help businesses and property owners invest in their buildings and in our community," said Board of Commissioners Chairman Melvin "Skip" Alston. "It can help them make improvements that lower energy costs, make buildings stronger and more efficient, and prepare them for the future. At the same time, it encourages private investment, supports jobs, and helps grow our local economy without putting the cost on County taxpayers. This is about giving businesses another tool to succeed while helping Guilford County continue to grow in a smart and responsible way.”

“C-PACE expands Greensboro’s development toolbox by creating another financing option that can support quality development and reinvestment in our commercial areas," said City of Greensboro Mayor Marikay Abuzuaiter. "It gives property owners and developers greater flexibility to pursue efficient, resilient building improvements while advancing the City’s broader economic development and sustainability goals.”

"C-PACE provides our commercial and industrial companies and developers in High Point with a competitive financing option for their next expansion or building improvement, helping create new jobs and continually improve our building stock," said City of High Point Mayor Cyril Jefferson. "We look forward to working with these partners to invest in resiliency, energy efficiency, and building improvements that add value to the High Point community."

C-PACE financing is secured through a voluntary assessment and lien on the participating property. The assessment is not a tax, and the property owner initiates participation. Private capital providers, not Guilford County, Greensboro, or High Point, provide the financing. State and local governments do not guarantee the financing or pledge public funds or their taxing authority to repay it.

Potential qualifying improvements include:

Heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning systems

Building-envelope and insulation improvements

Energy-efficient lighting and equipment

Water-efficiency and conservation measures

Solar and other renewable-energy systems

Resiliency improvements that protect properties from storms, flooding, and other hazards

Property owners select their own qualified contractors and private capital providers. Existing mortgage holders and other qualifying lienholders must provide written consent before a C-PACE assessment can be placed on a property.
